output.text_response:
## Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

### Correction of the survey's premise

Before the guide itself: the delegation states that "nothing civil exists" for 1820–1850 because Massachusetts didn't require vital registration until 1841. The FamilySearch Wiki on Massachusetts Vital Records contradicts this — Massachusetts mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths from **1639**, and those original records remain with the clerk of each town. The 1841 statewide act created a *parallel centralized system*; it did not originate vital record-keeping. A digitized FamilySearch volume of Berkshire County "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records" covering 1761–1850 (image group 004500891, 512 images) confirms civil records exist throughout the period. This guide treats town-level vital records as a primary source for all of 1820–1850.

---

### Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761 from Hampshire County, Massachusetts
- **Borders relevant to this family:** New York State to the west; Vermont to the north
- **Pre-1761 records:** Filed under Hampshire County

---

### Available Record Types

#### 1. Town-Level Civil Vital Records (throughout 1820–1850)

- Town clerk registers (births, marriages, deaths, marriage intentions) have been legally required since 1639; originals remain with each town clerk's office.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 — 3,456,789 records indexed).
- **FamilySearch browse-only volume:** Image group 004500891 — "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," Berkshire County, 1761–1850, 512 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**; must be browsed image by image.
- **Published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series:** Covers 200+ Massachusetts towns with indexed access — confirm whether the specific Berkshire town has a volume (via NEHGS or FamilySearch).
- **Marriage intentions** were recorded in the bride's home town; check the groom's town as well, and both sides of any state line.
- **Statewide layer (1841–1850 only):** A parallel state-level register begins in 1841, but it did not include marriage intentions. For 1820–1840, only town registers exist; for 1841–1850, both series run in parallel.

#### 2. Church Records

- **Congregational, Pittsfield (tool-confirmed):** FamilySearch image group 004500892 — "Church Records (Congregational)," Pittsfield, Berkshire County, 1791–1850. 274 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**; must be browsed image by image.
- **Statewide church records collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 — 987,654 records) — may include other Berkshire County denominations.
- Other denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker, etc.) were not confirmed by this survey's tool results; consult NEHGS and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records directly.

#### 3. Cemetery Records

- **Online:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers Berkshire County cemeteries with inscriptions and photographs.
- **Physical:** Sexton's registers are held by individual churches or town offices; none were confirmed as digitized in this survey.
- Cemetery inscriptions are especially valuable for the 1820–1840 window where town-clerk compliance may be uneven.

#### 4. Federal Census Records

- 1820, 1830, and 1840: Named only household heads for free persons.
- **1850 (at the period's close):** First census naming all free household members with ages, birthplaces, and occupations — the richest census source for the period.
- **1850 Mortality Schedule:** Records deaths in the preceding 12 months (1849–1850); supplements death records for that window.
- Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

#### 5. Probate Records

- Berkshire County Probate Court holds records from 1761 (wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories).
- **FamilySearch:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 — 567,890 records).
- Intestate estates may name children and other heirs not documented in vital records.

#### 6. Military Records (War of 1812 pensions — especially valuable)

- War of 1812 pension files at NARA frequently include family affidavits naming the veteran's wife, children, and their ages — a critical supplement to uneven 1820s–1830s vital records.
- Mexican-American War (1846–1848) also falls within the period.
- **Online:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); originals at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).

#### 7. Land Records

- Metes-and-bounds system; deeds recorded at the county level since 1761 at the Berkshire County Registry of Deeds.
- No digitized Berkshire County deed collection was returned by this survey — in-person or mail access required.

#### 8. Immigration and Naturalization

- "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (FamilySearch collection 1784312) covers the full period.
- "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (FamilySearch collection 1459213) — pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court, including Berkshire County courts.

#### 9. Newspapers

- Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical Berkshire County papers; obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices may supplement missing register entries.

#### 10. Tax Records

- Town tax lists (property and poll tax) confirm residence in years between censuses; originals are at town clerk offices or the Massachusetts Archives, Boston. None were confirmed as digitized in this survey.

---

### Repository Guide

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (online) | Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (coll. 2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (coll. 1921657); Probate 1635–1991 (coll. 1678901); Passenger Lists 1820–1891 (coll. 1784312); Naturalization 1790–1906 (coll. 1459213); browse-only county vital vol. 004500891; browse-only Congregational vol. 004500892 | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal Census 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 / NARA | Military service, pension, bounty land files | Subscription / free in-person |
| Berkshire County town clerks | Original town vital registers 1820–1850 | Contact individual towns |
| Berkshire County Probate Court | Wills, administrations, guardianships from 1761 | In-person or mail |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds | Deed books from 1761 | In-person |
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | State-level originals; colony-era records | In-person or online request |
| NEHGS, Boston | Largest regional genealogical library; published town histories, finding aids | In-person |

---

### Cross-Border Research (New York and Vermont)

For a family near both state lines:

- **New York (western border):** Deeds, church records, and probate may appear in adjacent New York counties. New York did not require civil vital registration until 1880; church registers are the primary source across the border. Run a separate locality guide for the specific adjacent New York county.
- **Vermont (northern border):** Vermont began statewide vital registration in 1857; town-level recording existed earlier but unevenly. Run a separate locality guide for the adjacent Vermont county.
- Cross-border circuit ministers may have recorded events in registers now held in a New York or Vermont archive.
- If either party to a marriage lived across the state line, the Massachusetts marriage intention may be absent entirely, with the record in a neighboring state's town clerk book.

---

### Records NOT Online (require in-person or mail access)

- Town vital registers 1820–1840 at individual Berkshire County town clerk offices
- Church records beyond Pittsfield Congregational (not confirmed digitized in this survey)
- Land deeds at the Berkshire County Registry of Deeds
- Town tax lists at town clerks or the Massachusetts Archives
- Cemetery/sexton registers at individual churches or town offices

### Key Warnings

1. Both FamilySearch volumes for Berkshire County (004500891 and 004500892) are **0% indexed** and **not full-text searchable** — budget time for image-by-image browsing.
2. An online negative result is **not evidence of absence**. Most Berkshire County records for 1820–1850 are undigitized. After any failed online search, go directly to the town clerk, Berkshire County Probate Court, Registry of Deeds, or NEHGS.
3. Town-level vital records are the primary civil source **throughout 1820–1850**, not only after 1841. Always check the town clerk's register before concluding a civil record does not exist.

Marriage intentions were typically recorded in the bride's home town; additional copies may appear in the groom's home town and current residence. FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (id: 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550, collections_search: 3,456,789 records) is an indexed statewide collection covering 1820–1850. Marriage intentions were NOT included in the 1841 statewide system. For 1820–1840, only town-level records exist; for 1841–1850, both series exist in parallel. Boston was excluded until 1850 under a stricter regulation — this does not apply to Berkshire County towns.

- **Federal census:** The 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 censuses all fall within or at the period's end. The 1820, 1830, and 1840 censuses named only heads of household for free persons; the 1850 census (at the period's close) is the first to name all free household members, with ages, birthplaces, and occupations. output.text_response:
## Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

*Note: The FamilySearch Wiki and place-search tools experienced a service outage during this research session, so no specific collection numbers, registration-year dates, or volume counts could be confirmed from tool output. All repository and collection details below should be verified directly at the sources cited. No collection is named that wasn't returned by a tool result, per standing instructions.*

---

### Jurisdiction Overview

**Billy civil parish** sits in the barony of Cary, County Antrim, Province of Ulster — the Bushmills area on the north Antrim coast. After 1921 it passed into Northern Ireland; records custodianship shifted from Dublin (the former Public Record Office of Ireland, destroyed 1922) to the **Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)** in Belfast.

**Dominant denomination in the area:** Ulster Scots / Presbyterian, with a Church of Ireland gentry class and smaller Catholic and Reformed Presbyterian populations.

**Key historical events affecting records:**
- The 1798 United Irishmen rising affected Ulster heavily
- The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most pre-1900 wills, the pre-1901 census returns, and centrally-deposited Church of Ireland registers — the defining record loss for all Irish genealogy
- The Great Famine (1845–1852) reduced population and may account for record gaps

---

### Record Types Available

#### Church Records *(most important for a Presbyterian family before civil registration)*
- **Presbyterian baptisms, marriages, burials, session minutes, communicants' rolls, and removal certificates**
- **Congregations most likely to cover Billy parish:** Bushmills Presbyterian Church and Dervock Presbyterian Church (both within the Route Presbytery covering north Antrim)
- **Where held:** PRONI, Belfast — many on microfilm; some on FamilySearch. Consult PRONI's online catalogue and the FamilySearch catalog at catalog.familysearch.org
- **Tip:** Session minutes and communicants' rolls are as important as baptism registers — they record admissions, discipline, and certificates of removal when members moved congregations. The **Route Presbytery minutes** are a secondary source that can confirm when a congregation was active.
- **Caution:** Also check **adjacent parishes** (Ballintoy to the east, Dunluce to the south-west) — a family may have worshipped in a chapel across the civil-parish boundary, and their register is filed under a different parish at PRONI.
- Church of Ireland and Roman Catholic registers also held at PRONI and the Representative Church Body Library (Dublin)

#### Civil Registration *(does not begin until the mid-19th century)*
- Pre-registration, church records are the only vital records source
- **IrishGenealogy.ie** holds civil registration BMD records and some church registers; **GRONI** (General Register Office Northern Ireland) holds statutory BMD registrations

#### Census Substitutes *(critical — Irish census returns largely destroyed)*
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Listed occupiers of tithable land townland-by-townland; directly brackets the c. 1825 birth year. Available at the National Archives of Ireland (NAI) and partly at PRONI/Ancestry
- **Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864):** Comprehensive survey of all occupiers and their landholders across every townland — the standard census substitute for the mid-19th century. Finding your ancestor's family here establishes their townland address, which then routes every subsequent search
- **1901 and 1911 Irish censuses:** Fully online at census.nationalarchives.ie — the only near-complete household enumerations to survive; work backward from these

#### Probate and Wills
- Pre-1858: Ecclesiastical probate courts (prerogative and diocesan); most destroyed 1922 — surviving fragments and abstracts at NAI and PRONI
- Post-1858: Principal Probate Registry and district registries; testamentary calendars listing who proved a will survive even when the will itself is gone
- Held at PRONI and NAI

#### Land and Estate Records
- North Antrim was landlord territory; large estate collections at PRONI include leases, rent rolls, and correspondence naming tenant families by name and townland
- **Ordnance Survey memoirs (1830s):** Detailed parish-level descriptions of townland composition (Royal Irish Academy, Dublin; not fully online)

#### Tax Records
- Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation (see Census Substitutes above)

#### Military Records
- British Army service records, pension files, muster rolls (National Archives UK at Kew; some at NAI)

#### Newspapers
- North Antrim served by papers including the *Coleraine Chronicle* and *Ballymena Observer*; marriage notices, death notices, and estate administration notices are genealogically valuable; access is institution-specific

#### Immigration / Emigration
- North Antrim emigrants typically sailed from Londonderry/Derry or Belfast, some via Liverpool to North America
- US arrival passenger lists at the National Archives (US); Famine-era assisted-emigration records

---

### Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** (nidirect.gov.uk/proni) | Church registers; estate papers; valuation records; post-1858 wills; court records | In-person + much online for free |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | Civil registration BMD; some church registers | Free online |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church register microfilms; Tithe Books; some civil registration | Free; consult catalog.familysearch.org |
| **National Archives of Ireland, Dublin** (nationalarchives.ie) | Tithe Applotment Books; surviving wills; 1901/1911 censuses | In-person + online |
| **GRONI, Belfast** | Civil registration births, marriages, deaths (statutory) | Fee-based; some at IrishGenealogy.ie |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland, Belfast** | Congregational records; session minutes | In-person by appointment |
| **Representative Church Body Library, Dublin** | Church of Ireland diocesan and parish records | In-person; some on PRONI/FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Royal Irish Academy, Dublin** | Ordnance Survey memoirs (1830s) | In-person |

---

### Known Record Losses

- **1922 Four Courts fire:** Destroyed the great majority of pre-1900 surviving Irish wills, almost all pre-1901 census returns, and many Church of Ireland parish register copies deposited centrally. Presbyterian and Catholic registers (held locally, not in Dublin) largely survived.
- **Pre-1901 census returns:** The 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 returns are almost entirely gone — Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books are the standard replacements.

---

### Recommended First Steps

1. **Search PRONI's online catalogue** for the Bushmills and Dervock Presbyterian congregation registers (baptisms, marriages, session minutes) covering 1780–1870.
2. **Identify the ancestor's townland** using Griffith's Valuation — this address routes every subsequent search to the right register and estate collection.
3. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books** for the same townlands to establish where the family was in the 1820s–1830s.
4. **Work backward from the 1901/1911 census** (fully online at census.nationalarchives.ie) to anchor the family before pushing into earlier records.
5. **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly** at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Antrim_Genealogy for Ireland-specific registration dates and indexed collection details (the wiki was unreachable during this session).

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Civil parish:** Billy, barony of Cary, County Antrim, Province of Ulster
- **Town of interest:** Bushmills, the main settlement within the parish
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, Province of Ulster, Ireland (now Northern Ireland, United Kingdom since 1921)

- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Ulster Scots (Presbyterian) in the rural north Antrim hinterland, with an Anglican (Church of Ireland) gentry and farming class and a smaller Catholic population.
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian (dominant among tenant farmers), Church of Ireland (the established church), Roman Catholic, and smaller Reformed Presbyterian / Covenanting congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The 1798 United Irish rising affected Ulster heavily and may account for record disruptions; the Great Famine (1845–1852) severely reduced the Catholic and poorer Protestant population; the 1922 destruction of the Public Record Office of Ireland in Dublin eliminated most pre-registration vital records held centrally.

## Boundary changes

- **Presbyterian congregations in the Bushmills / Billy area:** Billy civil parish falls within the Route Presbytery. The congregations most likely to cover a family in this parish in 1780–1870 are **Bushmills Presbyterian Church** and **Dervock Presbyterian Church**. However: a tool result did not assign either congregation to Billy parish specifically, and no tool result settled the parish boundary question. This guide cannot confirm which congregation's registers cover a given family. The researcher must check each congregation's own records and cross-reference with PRONI's church records holdings.
- **Where held:** Presbyterian registers for County Antrim are held at PRONI (Titanic Quarter, Belfast) and many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. This survey could not confirm specific film or collection numbers — place search and volume search tools returned no results for County Antrim.

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), Belfast | Church registers, valuation records, estate papers, court records, post-1858 wills | In-person; many records searchable and viewable online at nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| General Register Office Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast | Civil registration births, marriages, deaths (statutory records) | GRO search service; some records online at IrishGenealogy.ie |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Pre-1922 surviving records; Tithe Applotment Books; some surviving wills | In-person; some records online at nationalarchives.ie |
| Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland, Belfast | Presbyterian congregational records; session minutes; historical records | In-person by appointment |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland diocesan and parish records | In-person by appointment; some records on PRONI/FamilySearch microfilm |
| Royal Irish Academy, Dublin | Ordnance Survey memoirs (1830s), manuscript collections | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1858 wills for County Antrim (largely destroyed 1922; surviving fragments and abstracts at NAI and PRONI)
- Estate papers and landlord rent rolls (held at PRONI in physical form; not comprehensively indexed)
- Presbyterian session minutes (access varies by congregation; many at PRONI on microfilm, not all digitized online)
- Ordnance Survey memoirs (at the Royal Irish Academy; not fully online)
- Local newspaper runs from 1780–1830 (access is institution-specific; many exist only on microfilm at libraries)

## Known record losses
- **1922 Four Courts fire:** The destruction of the Public Record Office of Ireland in Dublin during the Civil War wiped out the great majority of pre-1900 surviving Irish wills and probate papers, almost all pre-1901 census returns, and many Church of Ireland parish register copies that had been deposited centrally. This is the defining record loss for Irish genealogy and directly affects all research into County Antrim families before 1900. Substitutes include Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation, testamentary calendars, estate papers, and surviving Presbyterian and Catholic church registers (which were held locally, not in Dublin, and thus largely survived).
- **Pre-1901 census returns:** The 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 Irish census returns were almost entirely destroyed, making Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books the primary census substitutes for a family born around 1825.
- This survey could not confirm specific record losses for Billy parish beyond those above from tool results; consult PRONI directly for parish-level survival information.

## Research tips
- **Start with Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books for Billy townlands.** These two surveys bracket the c. 1825 birth year of your ancestor and will tell you which townland the family occupied and under which landlord — essential orientation before searching any other record class. Both are accessible (at least in part) through the PRONI website and Ancestry; this survey could not confirm specific collection numbers from tool results.
- **For a Presbyterian family, the session minutes and communicants' rolls are as important as the baptism register.** Presbyterian session records recorded admissions, discipline, certificates of removal (when members moved to another congregation), and deaths in ways the baptism register does not. PRONI holds many County Antrim Presbyterian session collections on microfilm.
- **The Route Presbytery is the administrative body** covering north Antrim congregations including Bushmills and Dervock. Its historical records (minutes, ordination records, reports from congregations) are a secondary source that can confirm whether a congregation was active and when registers begin.
- **Search for the family in adjacent civil parishes** — Ballintoy to the east and Dunluce to the south-west also border the Bushmills area. A family could have worshipped in a congregation whose chapel stood just across the civil-parish line; the register that covers them may be filed under a different civil parish at PRONI.
- **The 1901 and 1911 Irish censuses are fully available online** (at nationalarchives.ie and census.nationalarchives.ie respectively) and are the only near-complete household-level enumerations to survive for Ireland. Working backwards from a family found there is the standard approach to anchoring earlier research.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki could not be reached during this survey.** The pages at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Antrim_Genealogy contain Ireland-specific guidance on registration dates, indexed collections, and research strategies that this guide cannot replicate. Consult them directly before treating any absence noted here as confirmed.

---

This guide covers Billy civil parish, County Antrim (the Bushmills area) for 1780 to 1870, a period when civil registration had not yet begun and church registers — especially Presbyterian ones — are the primary source for births, marriages, and deaths. The most important immediate sources are the Presbyterian registers for Bushmills and Dervock congregations (held at PRONI in Belfast and partly on FamilySearch microfilm), Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books for land occupation, and the surviving 1901/1911 censuses to anchor a family before working backwards. The great caution for all Irish research is the 1922 destruction of the central Public Record Office, which eliminated most pre-1900 wills and the pre-1901 census returns — Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Books are the standard replacements. The FamilySearch Wiki and collection search tools were unreachable during this survey session, so no specific collection numbers or registration-year dates could be confirmed from tool output; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy and the PRONI website (nidirect.gov.uk/proni) directly before searching.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Province:** Munster, Ireland (administered within the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland during this period)
- **County seat:** Cork City
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural; Cork City and Cobh (Queenstown) served as major Atlantic ports — central to Famine-era emigration
- **Religion:** Predominantly Roman Catholic; Church of Ireland (Anglican) also present

---

## Key Historical Context
The **Great Famine began in 1845**, profoundly affecting County Cork through death and mass emigration. **Cobh (then called Queenstown)** became the primary emigration port for the whole island.

---

## Available Records by Type

### ⚠️ Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **State registration did NOT exist for Catholics in the 1830s–1840s.** Civil registration for Roman Catholic marriages began 1 January 1864; non-Catholic marriages from 1845.
- **What to use instead:** Church parish registers are the only substitute for this period.

---

### Church Records *(Primary vital-record source for this period)*
| Denomination | Record Types | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| Roman Catholic | Baptisms, marriages | National Library of Ireland — digital images free online, covering registers to 1880 |
| Church of Ireland | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Representative Church Body Library, Dublin |

- **Survival varies by parish** — some Cork Catholic parishes have registers dating to the 1810s–1830s; others do not survive for this period.
- **Key step:** Identify the specific townland and civil/Catholic parish your ancestor came from — that determines which register series to search.

---

### Census Records
| Census | Status |
|---|---|
| 1841 | **Destroyed** — 1922 Four Courts fire in Dublin |
| 1851 | **Destroyed** — same fire |

**A failed census search is expected for this period — not a research failure.**

#### Census Substitutes *(confirmed)*
1. **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** — List occupiers of tithe-liable land; function as a de facto 1830s census. The best starting point for placing a family in a specific townland.
2. **Griffith's Valuation (Cork, early 1850s)** — Lists every householder; the major substitute for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses. Slightly outside the target window but captures families who had not yet emigrated.

---

### Land & Tax Records
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Cover the heart of the 1830s. First place to look for a household.
- **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s):** Immediately follows the 1840s target period.

---

### Probate & Court Records
- Many wills and probate records were **destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire**.
- Some surviving abstracts and transcriptions exist at the National Archives of Ireland.
- An empty probate search is a coverage gap, not proof the ancestor left nothing.

---

### Emigration Records *(Especially relevant for Famine-era emigrants)*
- **Port:** Cobh (Queenstown), County Cork
- **Record type:** Passenger manifests (departure and arrival)
- **Where held:** Arrival manifests in destination countries (USA, Canada, Australia)
- **Important:** Cork port manifests list complete family groups, including infants traveling with parents — search the full manifest for siblings and parents traveling together.

---

### Military Records
- County Cork men could have served in the British Army during this period.
- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) holds British Army service and pension records.

---

### Cemetery Records
- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) — free online resource.

---

### Newspapers
- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical papers.
- Useful for: obituaries, marriage notices, estate/probate notices, shipping news.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland | Catholic parish registers (free digital images to 1880) | Free online — see [Ireland Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy) for link |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers | In-person or consult FamilySearch Wiki |
| National Archives of Ireland | Surviving probate abstracts, government records | In-person in Dublin |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Fold3 | British military records | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Cork newspapers | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |

---

## Known Record Losses
The **1922 Four Courts fire** destroyed:
- All 1841 and 1851 census returns
- A large portion of Irish will and probate records

Church registers and land records held outside the Four Courts **survived** and are the primary substitutes.

---

## Recommended Research Sequence
1. **Identify the townland and parish** — this unlocks the right church register series.
2. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** — confirms presence in a specific townland during the 1830s.
3. **Search Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s)** — the main census substitute; captures families that had not yet emigrated.
4. **Search Catholic or Church of Ireland parish registers** at the National Library of Ireland / Representative Church Body Library for baptisms and marriages.
5. **If your ancestor emigrated during the Famine (post-1845)**, search arrival manifests in the destination country and examine the full passenger list for the whole family group.
6. For surviving probate, consult the National Archives of Ireland for abstracts.

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s-1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** County Cork was established as a county in 1606 (from place_search_all). It falls within the Province of Munster.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Cork City
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Munster, Ireland; in the 1830s-1840s administered as part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the place_population tool for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural; Cork City and Cobh (Queenstown) served as major Atlantic ports, relevant to both trade and emigration
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Gaelic Irish Catholic; a Protestant Anglo-Irish landlord class present throughout the county
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic; Church of Ireland (Anglican) present; smaller Presbyterian and nonconformist communities
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine began in 1845, transforming the county through death and emigration; Cobh (Queenstown) became the primary Famine-era emigration port for the entire island

## Boundary changes
- County Cork was formed in 1606. No boundary changes within or immediately adjacent to the 1830s-1840s target period were returned by the place tools. The county boundaries appear stable through this period.

## Available record types

For this period, civil registration had not yet begun for most record types. Church records and land/tax records carry the full weight of vital evidence. The specific sub-pages of the FamilySearch Wiki covering each record type for Ireland (Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Land and Property, Probate, Military, Naming Customs) were not available through the wiki tool during this survey — all resolved to the same generic Ireland Genealogy overview page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy. The findings below are grounded in that page's content.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** State registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages began on 1 January 1864 (national level). Non-Catholic marriages were registered from 1845 (national level). Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- **What exists for 1830s-1840s:** None. The FamilySearch Wiki states explicitly: "No civil vital records exist for the 1830s-1840s — use church registers instead." There is no county-courthouse vital-record system as in the United States.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire target decade falls before civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Roman Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers are the only substitute (see Church Records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (the majority); Church of Ireland (Anglican). The FamilySearch Wiki states that survival varies widely by parish and that many Cork parishes' registers begin in the 1810s-1830s — meaning some parishes have registers that reach into the target period and some do not. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Record types:** Baptisms and marriages (Catholic); baptisms, marriages, and burials (Church of Ireland)
- **Where held:**
  - Roman Catholic registers: The National Library of Ireland holds microfilm and digital images of Catholic registers up to 1880, available free online. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
  - Church of Ireland registers: The Representative Church Body Library (Dublin) and local custody. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Gaps:** Which specific Cork parishes have registers surviving from the 1830s-1840s, and what date ranges they cover, was not confirmed by this survey — the specific County Cork Genealogy and Ireland Church Records wiki pages were not accessible (both returned the generic overview page). Survival of registers before the 1830s varies by parish; some have no records at all from this period.
- **Language:** Generally English; occasional Latin in Catholic registers for some entries
- **Important note:** The specific Roman Catholic civil parish your ancestor belonged to determines which parish register to search. The Parish Register Project at the National Library of Ireland is the access point for Catholic registers; the Representative Church Body Library is the equivalent for Church of Ireland. No URL for either institution was returned by this survey's tools — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for access links.

### Census records
- **National census:** Ireland conducted national censuses in 1841 and 1851, both of which cover the target period. However, the returns for 1841 and 1851 were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire in Dublin. The FamilySearch Wiki states: "The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most pre-1901 census returns." Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- **State or provincial census:** None confirmed by tool results for this period.
- **Census substitutes (confirmed by tool results):**
  - Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837): List occupiers of tithe-liable land — a key census substitute for the 1830s. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
  - Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork in the early 1850s): Lists every householder and is described by the FamilySearch Wiki as the major substitute for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Access:** The digitization level (indexed vs. browse-only) of these census substitutes was not confirmed by this survey — collections_search and volume_search tools were not available.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration
- **Date range:** Probate records existed for County Cork before and during the 1830s-1840s.
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch Wiki states that many wills and government records were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy). The specific repositories holding surviving Cork probate records (including the National Archives of Ireland, which holds some surviving abstracts and transcriptions) were not confirmed by tool results — the Ireland Probate Records wiki page returned only the generic overview.
- **Access:** Not confirmed — catalog_search was not available during this survey run.

### Land records
- **Types (confirmed by tool results):**
  - Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837): Cover the core of the 1830s target period. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
  - Griffith's Valuation (Cork, early 1850s): Immediately follows the 1840s target period and captures families who had not yet emigrated. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Survey system:** The specific Irish land survey system and land-distribution jurisdiction were not confirmed by tool results — the Ireland Land and Property wiki page returned only the generic overview page.
- **Date range:** Tithe Applotment Books: 1823-1837. Griffith's Valuation for Cork: early 1850s.
- **Where held:** Specific holding repositories and online access points beyond the NLI reference in the wiki were not confirmed by tool results.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1830s-1840s in County Cork fell under British administration. Men from County Cork could have served in the British Army.
- **Record types:** British Army service records, pension records
- **Where held:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) was returned by the external_links_search tool as a resource for military records. The specific Cork collections available there and what date ranges they cover were not confirmed by this survey's tool results — the Ireland Military Records wiki page returned only the generic overview.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not confirmed by tool results.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) was returned by the external_links_search tool as an online cemetery resource.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers — specific holdings not confirmed by tool results.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Specific Cork newspaper titles, their date ranges, and survival were not confirmed by tool results (all specific sub-pages returned the generic overview page).
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) was returned by the external_links_search tool. Coverage of Cork papers in the 1830s-1840s specifically was not confirmed.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate and probate notices, shipping news relevant to emigration

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Cobh (then called Queenstown), County Cork. The FamilySearch Wiki states: "Famine-era emigration from Cork ports (Cobh/Queenstown) generated passenger manifests." Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Record types:** Passenger departure lists; arrival manifests in destination countries (United States, Canada, Australia)
- **Where held:** Destination countries' national archives hold arrival manifests. Specific repositories and online databases covering Cork departures were not confirmed beyond the wiki reference.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. The FamilySearch Wiki specifically notes that Cork port manifests "list complete family groups including young children traveling with parents." When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members — children as young as newborns are listed. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)

### Tax records
- **Types:** The Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837) function as both land and tax records, listing occupiers of tithe-liable land. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Date range:** 1823-1837
- **Substitute value:** Directly substitutes for a missing 1830s census; covers many of the same households a census would capture.

### Other record types
- **Poor Law records:** County Cork came under Poor Law administration from 1838, which generated workhouse registers and Board of Guardian records naming paupers and relief recipients. Specific holdings and access were not confirmed by tool results.
- **Estate papers:** Landlord estate papers survive for many Cork properties and can name tenants by name. Specific repositories and collections were not confirmed by tool results.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland (via FamilySearch Wiki reference) | Catholic parish registers, free digital images to 1880 | Entire vital records gap before 1864 civil registration | Free (URL not returned by tools — see [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Cemetery records not otherwise online for this period | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military records | British Army service for County Cork men | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Local Cork news, obituaries, marriage notices | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The collections_search, volume_search, and catalog_search tools were not available during this survey. The digitization level, indexed vs. browse-only status, and specific collection counts for County Cork record sets could not be confirmed from tool results. Additionally, all specific FamilySearch Wiki sub-pages attempted for Ireland (Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Land and Property, Probate, Military, Naming Customs, and County Cork Genealogy) resolved to the same generic Ireland Genealogy overview page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy — no additional record-type detail was accessible. The curated external links tool returned only generic resources not specific to County Cork. Direct consultation of the FamilySearch Catalog and the FamilySearch Wiki is strongly recommended to fill these gaps before planning searches.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland | Catholic parish registers (microfilm and digital) to 1880 | In-person in Dublin; also digitized free online per FamilySearch Wiki |
| Representative Church Body Library | Church of Ireland registers | In-person in Dublin; per FamilySearch Wiki |

## Records NOT online
- Church records for parishes whose registers begin after 1830 or exist only in fragile physical form
- Surviving probate records (after the 1922 fire destroyed much of the series)
- Poor Law workhouse and Board of Guardian records
- Landlord estate papers for Cork properties
- Specific Cork departure passenger lists from Cobh/Queenstown (access depends on the destination country's holdings)
- Most Cork record types not digitized: the specific extent of online coverage was not confirmed because collections_search and volume_search were unavailable

## Known record losses
- The 1922 Four Courts fire in Dublin destroyed most pre-1901 census returns — including the 1841 and 1851 returns most directly relevant to this period — and a large portion of Irish will and probate records. Per the FamilySearch Wiki: "The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most pre-1901 census returns and many wills and government records." Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy). Church records and land records held outside the Four Courts were unaffected and are the primary surviving substitutes. An empty search result for census or probate is a coverage gap caused by this destruction, not evidence the person left no records.

## Research tips
- For the 1830s-1840s, there are no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for Roman Catholics — parish registers are the only vital record source. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- Work the Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837) first for a 1830s household — they function as the census for this decade and confirm the ancestor's presence and landholding in a specific townland. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- Griffith's Valuation (Cork, early 1850s) is the major substitute for the lost 1841 and 1851 censuses; it names every householder and is essential even though it falls slightly outside the target window. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- If the ancestor emigrated during the Famine (from 1845 onward) via Cobh (Queenstown), search arrival manifests in the destination country carefully — Cork departure manifests list whole families including infants, so siblings and parents traveling together appear on the same manifest page. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- The 1922 fire means a negative probate or census result cannot be taken as evidence the person left no record — check church and land records as the surviving alternatives. Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)
- Naming customs for Ireland were not confirmed by this survey — the specific Ireland Naming Customs wiki page was not accessible (returned the generic overview page). Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Irish naming patterns before drawing conclusions from given names.

---

County Cork in the 1830s and 1840s is a period where church records and two land surveys — the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation — do most of the genealogical work, because civil registration had not yet begun and the 1922 fire took the census returns. The National Library of Ireland holds Catholic parish registers for free online access, and the Representative Church Body Library holds the Church of Ireland equivalents; together they are the main vital-record resource for this period. The single most important warning is that a failed search for a birth, marriage, or death certificate for this period is expected — not a problem — because those documents simply do not exist for the 1830s-1840s.

The natural next step is to identify the specific townland and civil/Catholic parish your ancestor came from — that will determine which parish register series to target — and then to run searches in the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation to confirm their presence and narrow the parish.

# Locality Guide: Javorje, Škofja Loka, Slovenia (1812)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Javorje is a small settlement within the Škofja Loka area (historically **Bischoflack** in German; also *Lack* or *Altenmarkt* in older records), which was part of **Krain (Carniola)**, a Habsburg crown land. In 1812, the area was nominally under the **French Illyrian Provinces** (1809–1813), but Catholic parish administration continued uninterrupted. After Napoleon's defeat in 1813, Habsburg Austrian administration resumed.

The area falls within the **Archdiocese of Ljubljana** (Labacensis) for church records purposes.

---

## The Short Answer

An 1812 marriage in Javorje will be found — if it survives — in a **Catholic parish marriage register** (*knjiga porok* / *Liber matrimoniorum*), held at the **Archdiocesan Archive in Ljubljana**. There is no civil registration for 1812 in this area; that did not begin until 1829–1835.

---

## Why There Is No Civil Registration for 1812

Austria required parishes to submit duplicate registers to civil authorities starting in **1835** (Catholic) and **1829** (Evangelical). For 1812, only the parish original exists. The brief French Illyrian Provinces administration did not create a parallel civil registration system that survived.

---

## Primary Repository

**Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana** (Archdiocesan Archive)
Krekov trg 1, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia
📧 arhiv.lj@rkc.si

Pre-1880s originals and transcripts of Catholic parish registers for the Archdiocese of Ljubljana — which covers the Škofja Loka area — are held here, not at the parish itself or any civil registry.

---

## Critical First Step: Identify the Serving Parish

No tool result in this survey identifies which specific parish held jurisdiction over Javorje in 1812. Before anything else:

1. **Contact the Nadškofijski arhiv** (arhiv.lj@rkc.si) to identify the correct parish and confirm whether the 1812 marriage register survives.
2. **Consult the 1972–1974 published inventory of Slovenian parish registers**, which covers all parishes and is noted on the [FamilySearch Wiki: Slovenia Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Slovenia_Church_Records).

---

## Online Access

| Resource | What It Offers | URL |
|---|---|---|
| **Matricula Online** | Images of Slovenian Catholic church registers | https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/ |
| **FamilySearch Wiki** | Research guidance and links | FamilySearch Wiki: Slovenia Church Records |

**Matricula Online is your best online starting point.** Browse the Slovenia section to see which parishes' registers have been digitized and what years they cover. No name index is implied — records may require browsing image-by-image.

**FamilySearch's digitized holdings** do not currently include confirmed parish marriage register volumes for the Škofja Loka area covering 1812. This is a digitization gap, not a confirmed loss.

---

## Language and Name Forms

Records from 1812 are written in **Latin** (formal register entries) with **German** marginal notes and place names:
- Škofja Loka → **Bischoflack**, **Lack**, or **Altenmarkt**
- Javorje may appear under a Germanized or Latinized variant

Search archive finding aids under these German/Latin forms, not only the modern Slovenian names.

| Record Type | Where Held | Notes |

| Habsburg military records | Österreichisches Staatsarchiv (Kriegsarchiv), Vienna | For men from Krain during the Napoleonic wars |

---

## Known Record Losses

No source in this survey states that parish registers for the Škofja Loka area were destroyed or lost. The absence from FamilySearch indexes is a coverage gap. The archdiocesan archive is the authoritative repository for confirming what survives.

---

## Your Next Step

**Email the Nadškofijski arhiv in Ljubljana** (arhiv.lj@rkc.si) to:
1. Identify which parish served Javorje in 1812.
2. Confirm whether that parish's marriage register for 1812 has survived.

# Locality Guide: Kolonica, Zemplén County (Kingdom of Hungary) / Snina District (Slovakia) (1700–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Historical identity (target period):** During 1700–1890, Kolonica was a village in Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary, under Habsburg and later Austro-Hungarian administration. The FamilySearch catalog confirms this: the surviving register is described as "Greek Catholic parish registers of baptisms, marriages and deaths for Kolonica, Slovakia, formerly Kolonica, Zemplén, Hungary."
- **Post-1920:** After the Treaty of Trianon, Kolonica became part of Czechoslovakia. Modern administrative placement: Snina District, Slovakia (from 1993).
- **County seat:** Zemplén County was administered from Sátoraljaújhely (now in Hungary).
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by any tool for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural village in an upland Carpathian region.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Rusyn (Ruthenian) population, confirmed by the Greek Catholic religious affiliation of the parish.
- **Religious denominations:** Greek Catholic (Uniate) confirmed as the parish denomination by catalog entry koha:727653. Other denominations may have been present but are not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.
- **Key historical events:** Austro-Hungarian dual monarchy established 1867; World War I ended Hungarian rule; Czechoslovakia formed 1918.

## Boundary changes
- **1700–1918:** Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary (Habsburg Empire, then Austro-Hungarian Empire after 1867). Records created in this era are labeled under Hungary.
- **1918–1922:** Transition period; became part of Czechoslovakia under the Treaty of Trianon (1920).
- **1922–1960:** Snina district, Czechoslovakia.
- **1960–1993:** Humenné district, Czechoslovakia, then briefly Slovak Republic.
- **1993–present:** Snina District, Slovakia.
- **Researcher implication:** Any index or archive entry for 1700–1890 will use "Kolonica, Zemplén, Hungary" — not modern Slovak place names.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Slovakia and Hungary vital records pages; no specific civil registration start year for this jurisdiction was confirmed by any tool result. Civil vital registration in the Kingdom of Hungary was generally introduced in 1895, but this survey cannot confirm the precise start date or registration level for Zemplén County.
- **What exists:** No civil vital registration records for Kolonica in the 1700–1890 target period were found in any indexed collection or digitized volume by this survey. Church registers are the primary source for the entire period.
- **Where held:** Hungarian-era civil registers (post-1895) would be held at the Slovak state archives. No confirmed online collection was identified.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Greek Catholic parish registers are the primary source (see Church records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations confirmed:** Greek Catholic (Grécko-katolícka cirkev), parish office Kolonica (Snina). No other denomination confirmed by any tool result.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (krsty), marriages (manželstvá), deaths (úmrtia).
- **Surviving register confirmed:** Catalog entry koha:727653, titled "Cirkevná matrika, 1824–1924", created by the Greek Catholic Parish Office Kolonica (Snina).
  - **Film 1792766** (image group 4406755, indexed): Inv. č. 460 — Baptisms 1824–1833, Marriages 1825–1833, Deaths 1824–1833; Inv. č. 461 — Baptisms 1890–1922.
  - **Film 1792767** (image group 4405907, indexed): Inv. č. 461 (continued) — Baptisms 1922–1924, Marriages 1890–1924, Deaths 1890–1924.
  - **Film 1793684:** Listed in catalog notes but stated as having no images available online. This film likely covers the 1834–1889 period that is absent from the two accessible films above.
- **Digitization level:** The two available films are name-indexed and available online via FamilySearch collection 1554443 (Slovakia Church and Synagogue Books) at https://familysearch.org/search/collection/1554443.
- **Where originals are held:** State Regional Archive in Levoča, Slovakia (Štátny oblastný archív v Levoči), confirmed by catalog note: "Pôvodné dokumenty boli mikrofilmované v Štátnom oblastnom archíve v Levoči."
- **Language:** Latin and Hungarian. Researchers must be able to read these languages or use translation assistance.
- **Gap — 1700 to 1823:** No church records for Kolonica before 1824 were confirmed by any tool result. Whether earlier registers exist and survive is unknown from this survey. If they exist, they would be held at the State Regional Archive in Levoča or the Greek Catholic eparchy archive.
- **Gap — 1834 to 1889:** Film 1793684 is cited but its images are not available online. The 1834–1889 period is not accessible digitally without obtaining that film through FamilySearch Library or contacting the Levoča archive directly.

### Census records
- **Hungarian-era censuses:** The Kingdom of Hungary conducted various enumerations. No specific census collection for Kolonica was returned by any tool in this survey.
- **Access:** No indexed or digitized census collection for this place was found in collections_search or volume_search.
- **Tax lists as substitutes:** Hungarian conscription and tax records may name heads of household and can partially substitute for missing census years; no specific collection confirmed here.

### Probate and court records
- **Jurisdiction:** Probate and court records for 1700–1890 would have been filed at the Zemplén County level under Hungarian administration.
- **Where held:** Slovak state archives (the successor institutions to Hungarian county offices). No digitized collection confirmed by any tool result.
- **Access:** Physical or written inquiry to the Slovak state archives is required.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Hungarian land tenure system; urbarial (serf land) records and estate records were kept by the noble landowners and county administration.
- **Types:** Urbarial registers, land surveys, tax rolls.
- **Where held:** Slovak state archives and the Hungarian National Archives (Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár) for central records. No specific collection for Kolonica confirmed.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Napoleonic Wars, Austro-Prussian War (1866), Austro-Hungarian military service.
- **Record types:** Habsburg/Austro-Hungarian military conscription and service records. Men from Zemplén County served in Imperial regiments.
- **Where held:** Austrian State Archives (Österreichisches Staatsarchiv), Vienna, for Habsburg military records. No specific Kolonica collection confirmed.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** No FindAGrave or BillionGraves results were confirmed for Kolonica by any tool. Researchers may check https://www.findagrave.com/ directly.
- **Physical records:** Greek Catholic burial registers are part of the confirmed parish register (see Church records above).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No local newspaper for Kolonica-area or Zemplén County was confirmed by any tool result for the target period.
- **Hungarian-language papers:** Zemplén County would have had Hungarian-language papers. Digitized Hungarian press may be accessible through the Hungarian National Library (Országos Széchényi Könyvtár).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Emigration from Zemplén County (and Rusyn villages like Kolonica) to the United States surged from the 1880s onward.
- **Relevant ports:** Hamburg (Germany), Bremen (Germany), and Liverpool (UK) for European departure; Ellis Island / Castle Garden (New York) for arrival.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests, indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry), naturalization records filed in U.S. courts, and Hungarian emigration papers.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest page for all family members when researching an emigrating family.
- **Where held:** NARA for U.S. arrival records; FamilySearch and Ancestry for indexed manifests. Departure records (Hamburg lists) are online through Ancestry.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Hungarian county tax (dicalis) rolls and urbarial records.
- **Date range:** These records predate the target period and run through it; they can serve as a census substitute.
- **Where held:** Slovak state archives; some may be at the Hungarian National Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1554443 — Slovakia Church and Synagogue Books) | Greek Catholic parish register, Kolonica, 1824–1833 and 1890–1924 (baptisms, marriages, deaths); name-indexed | Only surviving online church records for this parish | Free — https://familysearch.org/search/collection/1554443 |

**Coverage of this survey:** The two available films (1792766 and 1792767) together cover baptisms, marriages, and deaths for 1824–1833 and 1890–1924. Film 1793684, covering approximately 1834–1889, was cited in the catalog but has no online images. No other digitized collection or indexed volume was returned for Kolonica or for Slovakia by collections_search or volume_search.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Štátny oblastný archív v Levoči (State Regional Archive, Levoča, Slovakia) | Original Greek Catholic parish registers for Kolonica, confirmed as the filming source | In-person or written inquiry; website: www.archivsr.sk |
| Österreichisches Staatsarchiv (Austrian State Archives, Vienna) | Habsburg / Austro-Hungarian military and administrative records | In-person or online request: www.oesta.gv.at |
| Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár (Hungarian National Archives, Budapest) | Hungarian county records for Zemplén County, pre-1920 | In-person or online request: www.mnl.gov.hu |
| FamilySearch Library (Salt Lake City) | Microfilm copies of films 1792766 and 1792767; film 1793684 also held but images not online | Request through FamilySearch catalog: www.familysearch.org/catalog |

## Records NOT online
- Greek Catholic parish register for Kolonica, 1834–1889 (film 1793684 — images not available online as of this survey)
- Any Greek Catholic registers predating 1824, if they survive
- Hungarian-era civil vital records (post-1895)
- Zemplén County probate, court, and land records
- Military records (held in Vienna and Budapest)
- Tax and urbarial records

## Known record losses
No tool result stated that any specific Kolonica record set was destroyed. The absence of a confirmed register before 1824 is a gap in this survey — it may reflect a loss, records not yet microfilmed, or records held in a repository not yet checked. The State Regional Archive in Levoča should be contacted to determine whether pre-1824 registers survive.

## Research tips
- The key online starting point is FamilySearch collection 1554443 (Slovakia Church and Synagogue Books), which contains the name-indexed Greek Catholic register for Kolonica covering 1824–1833 and 1890–1924.
- For the 1834–1889 gap, request film 1793684 through the FamilySearch Library (catalog entry koha:727653) or contact the State Regional Archive in Levoča directly.
- All records in the confirmed register are in Latin and Hungarian — plan for translation before or during research.
- Always search under "Kolonica, Zemplén, Hungary" when using Hungarian-era indexes, not the modern Slovak place name.
- For ancestors who emigrated to the United States from the 1880s onward, U.S. arrival manifests on FamilySearch and Ancestry often name the specific village of origin, which can bridge back to the parish register.
- The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for all Slovakia- and Hungary-specific research pages during this survey. Before planning further research, re-run the locality guide or consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Slovakia and Hungary guidance.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **Established:** 1761; boundaries were stable throughout the 1820–1850 period
- **Borders:** New York to the west (Columbia and Rensselaer Counties) and Vermont to the north (Bennington County)
- **Economy:** Agriculture, iron foundries, paper mills, marble quarrying, early textile manufacturing
- **Dominant religion:** Congregational; also Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

### Pre-1841: Town-Level Only
Massachusetts had **no statewide registration system** before 1841. All births, marriages, and deaths were recorded solely at the **town clerk's office** in the town where the event occurred. You must know which Berkshire County town your family lived in before you can find these records.

- **Marriage intentions** may appear in both the bride's and groom's home towns — check both.
- **Published transcriptions:** The *"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"* series covers over 200 Massachusetts towns, including Berkshire County towns. These compiled abstracts are a logical first stop. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)

### 1841–1850: Town + State Copies
From 1841 onward, the state began collecting copies from each town. Both the town original and the state copy exist for this window.

### Key Online Collection
**FamilySearch collection 2061550 — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** covers the target period. Additionally, FamilySearch has digitized a **Berkshire County town clerk vital records volume** (image group 004500891, 512 images, 1761–1850) — but this volume is **browse-only**: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. It must be browsed page by page.

---

## Church Records
Church baptisms are **essential substitutes for pre-1841 civil birth registration**.

- **Denominations:** Congregational (most extensive registers), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and sometimes confirmation records
- **FamilySearch collection 1921657 — "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** covers the target period statewide.
- FamilySearch also has a digitized **Pittsfield Congregational Church volume** (image group 004500892, 274 images, 1791–1850) — also **browse-only**, 0% name-indexed.
- For other Berkshire County churches, contact individual church archives or the New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS).

---

## Census Records

| Year | Coverage | Note |
|------|----------|-------|
| 1820, 1830, 1840 | Head of household only; others tallied by age/sex | Useful for locating the family |
| **1850** | **Every person named**, with age, birthplace, occupation | Critical — the first to list all family members |

The **1850 mortality schedule** lists persons who died June 1849–June 1850 and can substitute for missing death records.

---

## Probate Records
- **FamilySearch collection 1678901 — "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"**
- Originals held at: **Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield**
- Includes wills (testate) and administration/inventory records (intestate), guardianships, and bonds.

---

## Land Records
- Massachusetts is an original colony (metes and bounds system; no federal land patents)
- **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield** holds deeds and mortgages from 1761
- Town-level **tax valuation lists** (held by town clerks and the Massachusetts Archives) can substitute for missing census or vital records

---

## Military Records
- **War of 1812 veterans** would have been alive throughout this period and may have filed **pension claims** (search NARA and Fold3)
- **Mexican-American War (1846–1848):** Service records and bounty land warrants at NARA
- Massachusetts militia rolls are at the **Massachusetts Archives, Boston**

---

## Cemetery & Newspaper Records
- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) has photographed and transcribed many Berkshire County cemeteries (volunteer-driven; coverage is incomplete)
- **Newspapers.com** and the **Massachusetts Digital Commonwealth** (digitalcommonwealth.org) hold historical Berkshire newspapers — obituaries and marriage notices can fill pre-1841 vital record gaps

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620–1890; Church Records; Probate Records; Naturalization Records; browse-only Berkshire volumes | Free — familysearch.org |
| Ancestry | Federal Census 1820–1850 (name-indexed) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | War of 1812 and Mexican-American War records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA | Passenger lists, military pension files | In-person / some online — archives.gov |

### Physical / Regional
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Berkshire County town clerk offices | Original vital records, town meeting records, tax lists |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Land records from 1761 |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Wills, inventories, guardianships from 1761 |
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony/state records, militia rolls, tax valuations |
| **NEHGS, Boston** (americanancestors.org) | Largest regional genealogical library; transcribed vital records, church records, manuscripts — the essential complement to FamilySearch for western MA |
| Berkshire County Historical Society, Pittsfield | Local histories, manuscripts — berkshirehistory.org |

---

## Cross-Border Research (Critical for This Family)

Because the family lived near both the New York and Vermont lines, **records may exist on either side of the border**:

- **Columbia and Rensselaer Counties, NY (west):** New York had no statewide vital registration in this period either, but county deed and probate courts, church registers, and census records may document relatives or property just across the line.
- **Bennington County, VT (north):** Vermont recorded vital events at the town level; church records and probate courts there are worth checking too.

Search the adjoining county deed and probate records alongside the Massachusetts ones, especially if the family owned land or had relatives across the border.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Know the town first.** Vital records are recorded by town, not county — identifying the specific Berkshire town is the essential first step before any search.
2. **Start with the published "Vital Records to 1850" transcriptions** — available at NEHGS, FamilySearch, and many public libraries.
3. **Budget time for image browsing.** Both FamilySearch Berkshire volumes are non-indexed; systematic page-by-page browsing is the only way in.
4. **The 1850 census is your best single snapshot** — it names every household member, with ages and birthplaces that help reconstruct births and origins from the whole 1820–1850 window.
5. **Church baptisms fill pre-1841 birth gaps** — prioritize finding which denomination served your family's specific town.
6. **NEHGS is essential** — many Massachusetts genealogical records not on FamilySearch are held or transcribed there.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1761 (Berkshire County established by the Massachusetts General Court)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsfield
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts (Commonwealth)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tool for this county; consult published census tabulations (1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 federal censuses)

- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (the dominant early church), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker — present throughout the county
- **Key historical events:** War of 1812 service (veterans active throughout the period), Mexican-American War (1846–1848), and expansion of mill industries drawing migration from the border states

## Boundary changes

- Berkshire County boundaries were established in 1761 and were stable throughout the 1820–1850 target period.
- The county borders New York to the west (Columbia County, formed 1786; Rensselaer County, formed 1791) and Vermont to the north (Bennington County, formed 1779).
- No subdivision of Berkshire County occurred during the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start dates:** Town-level registration was mandated by the Massachusetts government as early as 1639, though not all towns complied consistently. Massachusetts was the first U.S. state to establish a permanent statewide recording system; that began in **1841** (state level). Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)
- **Practical split for 1820–1850:**

  - 1841–1850: The state began collecting copies from each town. Both the town original and the state copy exist for this window.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by the town clerk. Marriage intentions were additionally recorded in the bride's home town; duplicates may appear in the groom's home town and their current residence.
- **Published compilations:** The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series covers over 200 Massachusetts towns, including Berkshire County towns, per the FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts Genealogy article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial). These are transcribed compilations, not originals.
- **Where held:** Originals are with each town clerk's office. FamilySearch indexes this statewide series as collection **2061550 — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890"** (3,456,789 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550).
- **Digitized Berkshire volume:** FamilySearch has digitized one Berkshire County volume of town clerk vital and town records (imageGroupNumber 004500891, 512 images, covering 1761–1850). This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be browsed image by image.
- **Gaps:** Compliance with the 1639 mandate varied by town. Some early entries are missing; check the published compilations as a cross-reference.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational (the most extensive early registers), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker
- **Record types:** Baptisms (which often substitute for birth records before 1841), marriages, burials, and in some churches, confirmation records

Separately, FamilySearch has a digitized Berkshire-specific volume: Congregational church records for Pittsfield (imageGroupNumber 004500892, 274 images, 1791–1850). This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives for originals; FamilySearch microfilm for copies. The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) holds the largest regional genealogical library and may hold transcripts or microfilm not on FamilySearch.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Important note:** No tool result in this survey confirmed which specific Berkshire County towns were served by which Congregational or other parishes; do not assume a town's church affiliation from county placement alone. Verify the parish that served a specific town at the research date through the NEHGS or the county historical society.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1820, 1830, and 1840 enumerate heads of household only; other household members appear as tallies by age and sex. The **1850** census is the first to list every household member by name, age, birthplace, and occupation — it falls within the target period and is a critical source.
- **State/provincial census:** This survey did not confirm a Massachusetts state census for the 1820–1850 window. The FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts-specific census page returned only generic content in this survey.
