entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, circa 1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Jurisdiction in 1800:** Mississippi Territory (formed 1798, encompassing present-day Mississippi and Alabama)
- **Alabama Territory formed:** 1817, from the eastern portion of Mississippi Territory
- **Alabama statehood:** December 14, 1819
- **Administrative center:** Natchez was the Mississippi Territory seat; Washington County (formed 1800) was among the earliest organized counties in present-day Alabama
- **Population during period:** Population figures for the Alabama portion of Mississippi Territory could not be confirmed from tool results for this period
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, fur trade; Mobile was an active Spanish colonial port
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers (arriving from Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia, especially after the Creek War of 1813-1814), Creek and Cherokee nations, French Creole and Spanish colonial populations around Mobile, enslaved African Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (especially Mobile area, with French and Spanish colonial roots), Methodist and Baptist circuits expanding across the territory from the early 1800s, Presbyterian
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813-1814 opened much of present-day Alabama to Anglo-American settlement; Mobile transferred from Spain to the U.S. in 1813

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: Present-day Alabama partly claimed by Spain and Georgia; Mobile area under active Spanish colonial administration (1780-1813)
- 1798: Mississippi Territory formed, covering present-day Mississippi and Alabama (Mobile District remained Spanish)
- 1813: Spain ceded Mobile to the United States; Mobile District incorporated into Mississippi Territory
- 1817: Eastern portion of Mississippi Territory separated as Alabama Territory
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood
- **Research implication:** Records for a person in present-day Alabama around 1800 may be catalogued under Mississippi Territory (not Alabama), and for anyone near Mobile under Spanish or British colonial records. Work all three trail segments together as one continuous research trail.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the Alabama region around 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Vital Records page could not be retrieved during this survey, so no registration start date for any level (county, statewide) can be stated from tool results.
- **What exists:** No indexed vital record collections on FamilySearch predate 1803 for this area.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for 1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; territorial census enumerations; estate inventories naming surviving family members.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (especially Mobile, continuous registers from the French colonial period); Methodist and Baptist circuits from the early 1800s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1986396 "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" covers records from 1803 (156,789 records; 78,394 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396). For pre-1803 Catholic records in the Mobile area: original French colonial records at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France), with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives; original Spanish colonial records at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain), with copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Gaps:** Church records before 1803 are not in the FamilySearch indexed collection; Mobile-area colonial Catholic records require contact with the archives named above.
- **Language:** Pre-1813 Mobile-area records may be in French or Spanish.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1800 federal census did not enumerate present-day Alabama. The first to include the Alabama portion was the 1810 census (under Mississippi Territory). FamilySearch collection 2016756 "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (287,634 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756) covers from 1810.
- **Territorial enumerations:** Territorial censuses for 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery, Alabama) and are not available as indexed online collections. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Access:** 1810 federal census and later are searchable via Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/). Territorial censuses 1801-1808 require a written inquiry or in-person visit to the Alabama Department of Archives and History.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, inventories, guardianships, territorial court proceedings.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1537764 "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (438,210 records; 219,105 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) begins in 1809. FamilySearch browse-only volume image group 004512890 covers Washington County, Alabama deed and probate records 1803-1820 (96 images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** County courthouses (Washington County organized 1800, among the earliest in present-day Alabama); Alabama Department of Archives and History for older records. Territorial-era court records may be catalogued under Mississippi Territory.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Public-land (federal) state — rectangular survey system administered by the General Land Office.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government through the General Land Office. Original land patents are searchable free at the BLM General Land Office website (https://glorecords.blm.gov). For the Mobile District pre-1813, Spanish land grants are held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville); copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Types:** Federal land patents/grants, county deed books, Spanish land grants (Mobile area pre-1813), territorial tax and land court records.
- **Digitized volumes (browse-only):** FamilySearch image group 004512889: 214 images, Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808-1819 (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). FamilySearch image group 004498712 (Mississippi Territory): 143 images, territorial land and court records, 1799-1817 (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Date range:** Federal land sales in Alabama began in earnest after the Creek Cession of 1814; territorial land records begin with the organization of Mississippi Territory (1798).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812; Creek War of 1813-1814; Mississippi Territory militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA; https://www.archives.gov/). Fold3.com (https://www.fold3.com/) hosts many military records (subscription).

- **Alabama statehood:** December 14, 1819
- **Administrative center:** Natchez was the Mississippi Territory seat; Washington County (formed 1800) was among the earliest organized counties in present-day Alabama
- **Population during period:** Population figures for the Alabama portion of Mississippi Territory could not be confirmed from tool results for this period
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, fur trade; Mobile was an active Spanish colonial port
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers (arriving from Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia, especially after the Creek War of 1813-1814), Creek and Cherokee nations, French Creole and Spanish colonial populations around Mobile, enslaved African Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (especially Mobile area, with French and Spanish colonial roots), Methodist and Baptist circuits expanding across the territory from the early 1800s, Presbyterian
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813-1814 opened much of present-day Alabama to Anglo-American settlement; Mobile transferred from Spain to the U.S. in 1813

- 1798: Mississippi Territory formed, covering present-day Mississippi and Alabama (Mobile District remained Spanish)
- 1813: Spain ceded Mobile to the United States; Mobile District incorporated into Mississippi Territory
- 1817: Eastern portion of Mississippi Territory separated as Alabama Territory
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood

---

## Arkansas Region Before 1800 — Colonial Records & Repositories

The Arkansas region before 1800 was a sparsely settled colonial outpost — first French from 1686, then Spanish from 1763 — centered almost entirely at **Arkansas Post (Puesto de los Arcos)**, the only significant European presence.

### Record Types & What Survives

No civil vital registration existed in this period. The **Catholic Church** was the sole record-keeper for births (baptisms), marriages, and burials.

**What's available online:**
- A **64-image FamilySearch volume** of Spanish colonial sacramental registers, 1763–1800, written in Spanish, with **no name index** — every page must be browsed individually by a researcher who can read 18th-century Spanish ecclesiastical handwriting.

**Records that exist only in physical repositories:**
- Spanish colonial household censuses (*padrones*)
- Land concessions
- Military muster rolls
- French-period church registers (pre-1763)

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) | Surviving colonial records for Arkansas |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Diocesan church records |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Principal archive for all Spanish Louisiana colonial documentation |
| **Library of Congress** (Washington, D.C.) | Partial microfilm copies of Archivo General de Indias holdings |

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission** to identify which surviving colonial records pertain to your specific ancestor and time window.
2. Work outward to the **Archivo General de Indias** and Library of Congress microfilm for original Spanish colonial documentation.
3. For the most current guidance on what has been digitized, consult the [FamilySearch Arkansas Genealogy Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy) directly.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Spanish Colonial Period, 1686–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French colony from 1686 (Arkansas Post, the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley); ceded to Spain by the Treaty of Paris in 1763; secretly returned to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1800; transferred to the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Poste aux Arkansas / Puesto de los Arcos; near present-day Gillett, Arkansas County)
- **Parent jurisdiction during target period:** Spanish Louisiana, administered under the Captaincy General of Cuba (1763–1800); before 1763, Province of Louisiana under France
- **Population during period:** Sparse European and Creole settlement at and near Arkansas Post; a small Spanish military garrison; enslaved Africans; surrounding Quapaw, Osage, and other Native American nations. No reliable population figures were returned by the population tool.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence farming, Spanish military garrison supply
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish colonial officials and soldiers, enslaved Africans, Quapaw and other Native Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the only officially recognized denomination under Spanish colonial law; French Recollect and later Jesuit/Capuchin missionaries served the post from the early 1700s)
- **Key historical events:** Transfer of Louisiana from France to Spain in 1763; Spanish reorganization of the colonial administration; return of the territory to France in 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1763:** Part of French Louisiana (Province of Louisiana, France)
- **1763–1800:** Spanish Louisiana (Luisiana Española), administered through the Captaincy General of Cuba under the Governor of Louisiana at New Orleans
- **1800:** Returned to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso (French control was nominal and brief)
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — region became U.S. territory
- **1812:** Included in Missouri Territory
- **1819:** Arkansas Territory established
- **1836:** Arkansas admitted to statehood (standardPlace date range: +1836/)

Note: All records predating 1803 were created under French or Spanish colonial authority, not U.S. jurisdiction. Researchers working this period are tracing colonial-era documentation, not American-era county or state records.

## Available record types

For each record type, the jurisdictional level is the colonial post or its governor at New Orleans — there were no counties or townships in this period.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the Arkansas region before 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki did not load an Arkansas-specific Vital Records page during this survey; no registration start date can be stated. Under Spanish colonial law, the Catholic Church held sole responsibility for recording births (via baptism), marriages, and deaths (via burial).
- **What exists:** No civil registration for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (see Church Records below)
- **Gaps:** Complete gap in civil vital records for the entire colonial period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic — French Recollect missionaries from the early 1700s; Capuchin and other clergy during the Spanish period
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (and occasional confirmations when a bishop visited)
- **Where held:**
  - **FamilySearch (browse-only images):** 1 digitized volume, image group 008814402, 64 images, covering 1763–1800. Record type: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), place: Arkansas Post, Arkansas County. Records are in Spanish. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image. No name search is possible. Access is free at FamilySearch.
  - **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock:** Holds original sacramental registers from the French missionary period (early 1700s), per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records).
  - **Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock:** Holds transcribed versions of surviving sacramental registers, per the same wiki source.
- **Gaps:** The French-period registers (pre-1763) are not represented in the FamilySearch digitized volume. Coverage overall is sparse, reflecting the small and transient population of Arkansas Post.
- **Language:** Spanish (1763–1800) and French (pre-1763); 18th-century ecclesiastical paleography is required to read the originals.

### Census records
- **Spanish colonial padrones:** The Spanish administration conducted periodic household censuses (padrones) of Arkansas Post. Surviving padrones are held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Arkansas was 1820 (Arkansas Territory). No federal census coverage exists for the pre-1800 period.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish military muster rolls (see Military Records) function as partial population listings.
- **Access:** Physical repositories only — no confirmed online index for colonial padrones.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate and civil proceedings existed at the military/civil post level under Spanish colonial administration; surviving records are fragmentary.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Library of Congress microfilm of colonial records.
- **Access:** Physical or microfilm; no confirmed online access.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land grants (concessions) used metes-and-bounds descriptions referencing local landmarks and waterways.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish colonial authorities at Arkansas Post (and confirmed by the Governor of Louisiana in New Orleans) issued concessions. The Archivo General de Indias in Seville is the principal original archive for these grants, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Types:** Land concessions (concesiones de tierra)
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville (originals); Arkansas History Commission (surviving records and transcriptions); Library of Congress (microfilm)
- **Post-1803 research trail:** Spanish land grants issued before 1803 were honored under the Louisiana Purchase and many were submitted for confirmation through U.S. territorial courts after 1803. Searching Arkansas territorial and early statehood land records for Spanish-era grant confirmations can yield names and property descriptions originating in the colonial period.
- **Access:** Physical repositories and Library of Congress microfilm; FamilySearch's Arkansas land collection (collection 2085124 covers Census Substitutes 1819-1870, not colonial land).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish garrison records for the Puesto de los Arcos (Arkansas Post)
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, service records, payroll lists for the Spanish colonial garrison
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville (originals); Arkansas History Commission; Library of Congress microfilm
- **Access:** Physical repositories; no confirmed online access for this period.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Arkansas Post (Catholic cemetery, now within Arkansas Post National Memorial)
- **Online coverage:** No confirmed online coverage for burials predating 1800 from tool results. FindAGrave (findagrave.com) is a general resource but was not confirmed to hold pre-1800 entries for this location.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers fold into the sacramental registers (see Church Records above).

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers existed in the Arkansas region before 1800. This record type does not apply to this period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- No formal immigration records existed under Spanish colonial administration. Settlers arrived under land concessions, military assignments, or by permission of the colonial governor. Relevant documentation would appear in the land concession records and military muster rolls (see above).
- Naturalization as an American-era concept did not apply before 1803.

### Tax records
- Spanish colonial tax and tribute records may exist within the Archivo General de Indias and Arkansas History Commission holdings alongside the padrones and land records.
- **Access:** Physical repositories; no confirmed online access.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** Spanish colonial notarial acts (contracts, wills, powers of attorney) were generated through the colonial post's civil administration. These are held at the Archivo General de Indias and possibly in surviving Arkansas History Commission collections.
- **Native American records:** The Quapaw and neighboring nations are mentioned in French and Spanish colonial documents. The Arkansas History Commission and academic publications are the best avenue for these records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | 1 browse-only volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) 1763–1800, Arkansas Post, 64 images (image group 008814402); also indexed post-1800 collections (County Marriages 1837-1957, Census Substitutes 1819-1870) | Only online source of pre-1800 church records (browse-only, Spanish-language) | Free |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | May hold post-1803 territorial records including Spanish land grant confirmations | Post-Louisiana-Purchase territorial records bridging colonial-era land claims | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching the place and period (1700–1800); that complete result set of 1 volume is detailed above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR | Surviving Spanish colonial records (padrones, land concessions, military records); transcriptions of sacramental registers | In-person; written inquiry |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French-period sacramental registers (pre-1763) | Contact diocese directly |
| Archivo General de Indias, Avenida de la Constitución 3, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for Louisiana: padrones, land concessions, military muster rolls, court and notarial records | In-person in Seville; partial microfilm holdings at the Library of Congress |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Microfilm copies of select Spanish colonial records from the Archivo General de Indias | In-person at the Library of Congress; some material accessible via written request |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial padrones (censuses): physical repositories only (Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias)
- Spanish land concessions and grant records: physical / Library of Congress microfilm only
- Spanish military garrison muster rolls and payroll records: physical / Library of Congress microfilm only
- French-period Catholic sacramental registers (pre-1763): Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission only
- Spanish colonial notarial and court records: physical repositories only

## Known record losses
No specific record losses were confirmed by tool results for this period and place. The surviving record volume is inherently limited by the small population and remote location of Arkansas Post. The Arkansas History Commission is the recommended first contact to determine which colonial records have survived.

## Research tips
- The sacramental registers covering 1763–1800 are digitized at FamilySearch as image group 008814402 (64 browse-only images, in Spanish) and must be read image by image with no name index. A working knowledge of 18th-century Spanish ecclesiastical handwriting (letra procesal or similar) is required.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's Arkansas Genealogy article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) identifies the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, and Library of Congress microfilm as the repositories holding surviving civil and military colonial records.
- French Catholic missionaries maintained registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s; these pre-1763 registers are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records.
- Spanish land grants issued before 1803 were honored under the Louisiana Purchase. Searching Arkansas territorial records (post-1819) for Spanish-era land grant confirmation petitions is an effective strategy for identifying colonial-era settlers.
- The indexed FamilySearch collections for Arkansas (County Marriages 1837-1957; Census Substitutes 1819-1870) all postdate the colonial period and will not directly document pre-1800 ancestors, but they may name descendants who can confirm the family line.
- All records from this period are in French or Spanish; a working knowledge of both colonial Latin (for church records) and 18th-century French/Spanish is needed to read originals accurately.
- Because civil infrastructure was absent in this era, a negative result in any online database should not be read as evidence the person did not exist — the records are simply not indexed or not digitized.

Surviving padrones are held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Arkansas was 1820 (Arkansas Territory). No federal census coverage exists for the pre-1800 period.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish military muster rolls (see Military Records) function as partial population listings.
- **Access:** Physical repositories only — no confirmed online index for colonial padrones.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate and civil proceedings existed at the military/civil post level under Spanish colonial administration; surviving records are fragmentary.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Library of Congress microfilm of colonial records.
- **Access:** Physical or microfilm; no confirmed online access.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land grants (concessions) used metes-and-bounds descriptions referencing local landmarks and waterways.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish colonial authorities at Arkansas Post (and confirmed by the Governor of Louisiana in New Orleans) issued concessions. The Archivo General de Indias in Seville is the principal original archive for these grants, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Types:** Land concessions (concesiones de tierra)
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville (originals); Arkansas History Commission (surviving records and transcriptions); Library of Congress (microfilm)
- **Post-1803 research trail:** Spanish land grants issued before 1803 were honored under the Louisiana Purchase and many were submitted for confirmation through U.S. territorial courts after 1803. Searching Arkansas territorial and early statehood land records for Spanish-era grant confirmations can yield names and property descriptions originating in the colonial period.
- **Access:** Physical repositories and Library of Congress microfilm; FamilySearch's Arkansas land collection (collection 2085124 covers Census Substitutes 1819-1870, not colonial land).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish garrison records for the Puesto de los Arcos (Arkansas Post)
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, service records, payroll lists for the Spanish colonial garrison
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville (originals); Arkansas History Commission; Library of Congress microfilm
- **Access:** Physical repositories; no confirmed online access for this period.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Arkansas Post (Catholic cemetery, now within Arkansas Post National Memorial)
- **Online coverage:** No confirmed online coverage for burials predating 1800 from tool results. FindAGrave (findagrave.com) is a general resource but was not confirmed to hold pre-1800 entries for this location.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers fold into the sacramental registers (see Church Records above).

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers existed in the Arkansas region before 1800. This record type does not apply to this period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- No formal immigration records existed under Spanish colonial administration. Settlers arrived under land concessions, military assignments, or by permission of the colonial governor. Relevant documentation would appear in the land concession records and military muster rolls (see above).
- Naturalization as an American-era concept did not apply before 1803.

### Tax records
- Spanish colonial tax and tribute records may exist within the Archivo General de Indias and Arkansas History Commission holdings alongside the padrones and land records.
- **Access:** Physical repositories; no confirmed online access.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** Spanish colonial notarial acts (contracts, wills, powers of attorney) were generated through the colonial post's civil administration. These are held at the Archivo General de Indias and possibly in surviving Arkansas History Commission collections.
- **Native American records:** The Quapaw and neighboring nations are mentioned in French and Spanish colonial documents. The Arkansas History Commission and academic publications are the best avenue for these records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | 1 browse-only volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) 1763–1800, Arkansas Post, 64 images (image group 008814402); also indexed post-1800 collections (County Marriages 1837-1957, Census Substitutes 1819-1870) | Only online source of pre-1800 church records (browse-only, Spanish-language) | Free |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | May hold post-1803 territorial records including Spanish land grant confirmations | Post-Louisiana-Purchase territorial records bridging colonial-era land claims | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching the place and period (1700–1800); that complete result set of 1 volume is detailed above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR | Surviving Spanish colonial records (padrones, land concessions, military records); transcriptions of sacramental registers | In-person; written inquiry |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French-period sacramental registers (pre-1763) | Contact diocese directly |
| Archivo General de Indias, Avenida de la Constitución 3, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for Louisiana: padrones, land concessions, military muster rolls, court and notarial records | In-person in Seville; partial microfilm holdings at the Library of Congress |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Microfilm copies of select Spanish colonial records from the Archivo General de Indias | In-person at the Library of Congress; some material accessible via written request |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial padrones (censuses): physical repositories only (Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias)
- Spanish land concessions and grant records: physical / Library of Congress microfilm only
- Spanish military garrison muster rolls and payroll records: physical / Library of Congress microfilm only
- French-period Catholic sacramental registers (pre-1763): Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission only
- Spanish colonial notarial and court records: physical repositories only

## Known record losses
No specific record losses were confirmed by tool results for this period and place. The surviving record volume is inherently limited by the small population and remote location of Arkansas Post. The Arkansas History Commission is the recommended first contact to determine which colonial records have survived.

## Research tips
- The sacramental registers covering 1763–1800 are digitized at FamilySearch as image group 008814402 (64 browse-only images, in Spanish) and must be read image by image with no name index. A working knowledge of 18th-century Spanish ecclesiastical handwriting (letra procesal or similar) is required.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's Arkansas Genealogy article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) identifies the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, and Library of Congress microfilm as the repositories holding surviving civil and military colonial records.
- French Catholic missionaries maintained registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s; these pre-1763 registers are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records.
- Spanish land grants issued before 1803 were honored under the Louisiana Purchase. Searching Arkansas territorial records (post-1819) for Spanish-era land grant confirmation petitions is an effective strategy for identifying colonial-era settlers.
- The indexed FamilySearch collections for Arkansas (County Marriages 1837-1957; Census Substitutes 1819-1870) all postdate the colonial period and will not directly document pre-1800 ancestors, but they may name descendants who can confirm the family line.
- All records from this period are in French or Spanish; a working knowledge of both colonial Latin (for church records) and 18th-century French/Spanish is needed to read originals accurately.
- Because civil infrastructure was absent in this era, a negative result in any online database should not be read as evidence the person did not exist — the records are simply not indexed or not digitized.

---

**Ohio ca. 1790: Pre-Statehood Boundary Changes and Record Availability**

Researching in Ohio around 1790 means working entirely within the **Northwest Territory**, not the state of Ohio, which did not exist until **March 1803**. The key points from the locality guide are:

### Boundary Changes
- In 1790, the territory had only **two organized counties**:
  - **Washington County** (formed 1788) — covered most of the region
  - **Hamilton County** (carved from Washington in 1790) — covered the southwest
- County lines shifted frequently through statehood, so every record is filed under whichever county held a given township on the **precise date of the event**
- **Critical first step:** Identify the exact county that held your ancestor's township in 1790 before searching any repository — filing under the wrong county will return nothing

### Records Available Despite Early Gaps

| Record Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Civil vital records** | None existed — no civil birth or death registration at all |
| **Church records** | The only proxy for vital events (baptisms, burials, circuit-rider minutes); FamilySearch holds a digitized collection starting in 1787 |
| **Marriage records** | Kept at the county level from **1789** |
| **Land records** | Most consequential source for this period; split across **three separate survey systems**: Virginia Military District warrants (held at the Virginia State Library, Richmond), Connecticut Western Reserve records (Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland), and general Land Office records |
| **Tax lists** | Beginning late 1790s — the best substitute for the sparse 1790 census |
| **Early territorial volumes on FamilySearch** | Digitized but browse-only (image by image, no name search) |

### Key Takeaway
The guide was saved to your project as **loc_001**. Your next step is to confirm whether your ancestor's location fell within **Washington County or Hamilton County** in 1790, then search county-level marriages, land records, and tax lists on FamilySearch — keeping in mind that land records for some areas must be sought outside Ohio entirely (Virginia and Connecticut repositories).

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (ca. 1785–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Northwest Territory organized 1787 by the Northwest Ordinance; Washington County (first Ohio county) organized 1788; Hamilton County organized 1790 from Washington County.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Marietta (Washington County); Cincinnati (Hamilton County).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (the region did not become the state of Ohio until March 1, 1803).
- **Population during period:** FamilySearch returned no population figures for Ohio in this period. Settlement was extremely sparse in 1790 — most European-American migrants had arrived only within the preceding two or three years.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, military garrisons.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American migrants from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England; some German settlers; Indigenous peoples held much of the territory throughout this period.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist and Baptist circuit-riders, Presbyterian congregations, small Catholic communities; Lutheran and German Reformed congregations among German settlers.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787), Northwest Indian War and Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794), Jay's Treaty (1795), Ohio statehood (March 1, 1803).

## Boundary changes
- In 1790, Ohio did not exist — the entire region was **Northwest Territory**, organized by Congress under the Ordinance of 1787.
- **Washington County** (est. 1788) was the first organized county and covered most of the territory initially.
- **Hamilton County** was carved from Washington County in 1790, covering the southwestern portion.
- County boundaries changed repeatedly between 1788 and 1803 as new counties were created from the original two. Any record from 1790 is filed under whichever county held that township at the precise moment — the researcher must determine the correct county for the date and location of every event.
- Ohio achieved statehood on March 1, 1803. Records created before that date are territorial; those after are state records. These form one continuous research trail and must be searched together despite the jurisdictional label change.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil vital registration existed in 1790 or at statehood. The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Vital Records page did not return Ohio-specific content during this survey; accordingly, no state registration date is stated here.
- **What exists:** No government birth or death records for 1790. Marriage records were created at the county level beginning in the territorial period. FamilySearch holds **Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013** (collection 1803785; 1,523,678 records; 3,047,356 persons; images available; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785).
- **Where held:** County courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1803785 for marriages.
- **Gaps:** Civil birth and death registration did not occur in 1790. Only marriages were formally recorded at the county level. No Ohio-specific start date for statewide birth/death registration was confirmed by any tool result in this survey.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; family Bible records; tombstone inscriptions; estate inventories naming heirs.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, German Reformed, Lutheran (frontier circuit-riders and small congregations).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some confirmation registers and class meeting lists.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds **Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950** (collection 2246917; 678,234 records; images available; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917). Denominational archives at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus.
- **Gaps:** Coverage for 1790 is thin — most congregations on the Ohio frontier were newly formed or itinerant, and earliest registers often did not survive.
- **Language:** English; some German-language registers for German Reformed and Lutheran congregations.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census (1790) enumerated the Northwest Territory, but Ohio settlement was extremely sparse and coverage incomplete. The 1800 federal census is the first with reasonable Ohio coverage. Both enumerations named heads of household only.
- **State/provincial census:** No territorial or state census for the 1785–1803 period was confirmed by tool results.
- **Other enumerations:** Territorial and county tax lists serve as the primary census substitute for the 1790s (see Tax records).
- **Access:** FamilySearch has the 1800 and later federal censuses indexed. 1790 Northwest Territory enumeration data is browse-only.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianships, letters of administration; territorial court minutes recording land disputes, debt suits, and local appointments.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush).
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the dominant commercial and port city.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (federal)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 migrants arrived from across the United States and abroad between 1848 and 1855 (Wikipedia). The place_population tool returned no data for this period.
- **Economy:** Gold mining, commerce, and port trade dominated the period 1848–1860.
- **Ethnic composition:** Diverse — migrants from the eastern United States, Latin America, Europe, China, and Australia (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Franciscan mission network documented the Catholic population through 1850; various Protestant and Catholic congregations formed in mining camps and cities after statehood. No tool result names specific denominations for this period beyond the Franciscan mission records.
- **Key historical events:** The Gold Rush began January 24, 1848, when James Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill; it drew an estimated 300,000 people to California by 1855 and precipitated statehood in 1850 (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
- California was admitted to the Union in 1850 as a state, with no prior territorial civil record series.
- Counties were created rapidly throughout the 1850s as mining camps became permanent communities. The operative record-keeping unit is the county, not the state.
- place_search_all returned no historical jurisdiction data beyond the state entry dated from 1850.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds a collection titled "California, County Births, 1850-1919" (collection 2017276, 789,456 records) and "California, County Marriages, 1850-1952" (collection 1452832, 567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons), both beginning in 1850 — indicating county-level registration was operative from statehood.
- **Registration level and start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; the specific statewide registration requirement date cannot be confirmed from any tool result. Research the specific county for its earliest records.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and FamilySearch collections 2017276 and 1452832.
- **Gaps:** No death-record collection appears in the collections_search results for this period. Deaths in mining camps were often unrecorded in formal civil registers; substitute sources include church burial registers, cemetery records, newspaper death notices, and probate files.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Franciscan Mission Records, 1769-1850 (FamilySearch collection 1804372, 98,765 records) cover baptisms, marriages, and burials for the Catholic Mission network — primarily relevant for California-born individuals or those connected to the missions before the Gold Rush.

### Church records
- **Denominations documented:** Franciscan mission records (1769–1850) are the main pre-Gold Rush church series. Post-statehood denominations included various Catholic parishes and Protestant congregations in mining towns. No tool result names specific post-1850 congregations for this period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (mission era); post-1850 church records vary by congregation.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1804372 for mission records; individual parish and denominational archives for post-1850 congregations.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Spanish and Latin.
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Church Records page returned only generic content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Church_Records directly for holdings by denomination.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1850 federal census is the first taken in California after statehood, but it is partially destroyed — some county returns are missing (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). Use as a starting point, but expect gaps.
- **State census:** The California state census of 1852 covers the same population and partially compensates for the damaged 1850 returns. FamilySearch holds a digitized volume (image group 006601001, 1850-1852, 522 images) that is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable — indexed + images.
- **Other enumerations:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Census page returned only generic content; no additional state or special enumerations could be confirmed from tool results.
- **Access:** 1852 state census: indexed + images (88%, full-text). 1850 federal census: check Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) for indexed access.

### Mining claim records
- **Types:** Mining Claim Registers recording individual claims by name, location, and date.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds a digitized volume of Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, 1849–1855 (image group 006601002, 340 images). It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. It must be searched image by image with no name search.
- **Where held:** County recorders' offices held mining claim records (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Physical records remain at county courthouses.
- **Note:** Mining claims are among the most direct sources for documenting a Gold Rush miner's presence and location. Always identify the county of operation.

### Immigration and arrival records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary sea entry point; Sacramento was a major inland arrival hub.
- **Ship passenger manifests:** Held at NARA San Bruno (National Archives, Pacific Sierra Region) for San Francisco arrivals (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Access via archives.gov (https://www.archives.gov/).
- **Port Arrival Registers:** FamilySearch holds a digitized volume for Sacramento, 1849–1858 (image group 006601003, 298 images). It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.
- **Overland arrivals:** Overland trail diaries and journals exist at the California State Library and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — county, state, or federal. No specific California naturalization collection appeared in collections_search for this period.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Voter registration (Great Registers)
- **What exists:** "California, Great Registers, 1866-1910" (FamilySearch collection 1923340, 1,345,678 records). These are the voter registration rolls for adult male citizens.
- **Important limitation:** Great Registers begin in 1866 — they do not cover the main Gold Rush decade (1848–1860). They are valuable for identifying where a miner settled after the rush but cannot document arrival or presence in the 1850s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1923340 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a public land (federal) state; federal land patents are the primary source for land grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Land and Property page returned only generic content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Land_and_Property for specific repositories.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents; county deed books at county courthouses; federal patents at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website.
- **Date range:** From statehood (1850).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions; also naturalizations (pre-1906 filed in any court of record).
- **Where held:** County courthouses and state archives. The FamilySearch Wiki California Probate Records page returned only generic content — consult the wiki directly.
- **Note:** Probate files for miners who died intestate (without a will) often name heirs and establish family relationships — a critical source when vital records are absent.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Mexican-American War (ended 1848) immediately preceded the Gold Rush; some migrants were veterans. The Civil War (1861–1865) falls just after the target period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, and draft registrations at the National Archives (archives.gov, https://www.archives.gov/). Military records for this period are accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Where held:** NARA; state adjutant general records may be at the California State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mining camps had their own burial grounds, many now unmarked or relocated. No specific cemetery names were returned by tool results for this period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed cemetery records for California.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are at county or municipal level.

### Newspaper records
- **What exists:** San Francisco had newspapers from the Gold Rush era. Historical newspapers are searchable via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate sales, mining claim disputes), and ship arrival lists published in newspapers supplement formal records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property and personal property tax records.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and state archives.
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax lists can substitute for census years and place a person at a specific county location year by year.

### Other record types
- **Manuscript collections:** The California State Library and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections including overland trail diaries and journals (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- **Mining company records:** Some larger mining companies maintained employment records; check county historical societies for surviving business records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850-1919 (2017276); County Marriages 1850-1952 (1452832); Great Registers 1866-1910 (1923340); Mission Records 1769-1850 (1804372); 1852 State Census (browse 006601001); Mining Claims San Francisco 1849-1855 (browse 006601002); Port Arrivals Sacramento 1849-1858 (browse 006601003) | Primary indexed and browse-only records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1850 federal census (partially destroyed) | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records | Deaths not in civil registers or newspapers | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, ship arrivals, legal notices | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Fold3 | Military Records | Veterans of Mexican-American War and later conflicts | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Ship passenger manifests (NARA San Bruno); naturalization records | Sea arrivals at San Francisco; pre-1906 naturalizations | Free / in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for the period 1848–1860 in FamilySearch volume_search. Only 3 volumes were detailed above (the first page of results). The remaining 11 were not examined in this survey — query FamilySearch directly for the full set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| County courthouses (California) | Deeds, probate, court records, mining claim registers, early vital records | In-person / mail |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State-level records, court records, state census | In-person / online request |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Manuscript collections, overland diaries, Gold Rush materials | In-person / online catalog |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush-era manuscript collections, diaries, journals | In-person / appointment |
| NARA Pacific Sierra Region, San Bruno | Ship passenger manifests, federal court naturalizations | In-person / research request |

## Records NOT online
- Mining claim registers held at individual county recorders' offices (physical records; the FamilySearch volume covers San Francisco only, browse-only)
- County-level death records for the 1850s (no death collection for this period appeared in collections_search)
- Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in state and local courts (location varies by court; not consolidated online)
- Manuscript and diary collections at the California State Library and Bancroft Library
- Most church congregation records from post-1850 denominations

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census for California is partially destroyed — some county returns are missing (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1852 California state census (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 88% indexed) partially compensates.
- No other specific record losses were stated by tool results. An empty search result for a county is a coverage gap, not evidence of destruction.

## Research tips
- Begin by identifying the specific California county where the ancestor mined or settled; nearly all 1850s records were created and held at the county level, not statewide. County boundaries shifted rapidly in the 1850s — confirm the county that governed the target location at the specific year. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- Search the 1852 California state census (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed) as a primary document; it was specifically designed to capture the Gold Rush population and partially compensates for the damaged 1850 federal census. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- Mining claim registers at county recorders' offices are among the most direct sources for documenting a miner's presence; San Francisco's are online (browse-only, volume 006601002) and others remain physical at county courthouses. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- Ship passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno document sea arrivals at San Francisco — a primary route for migrants from the eastern United States. The Sacramento port arrival registers (volume 006601003) cover inland arrivals but are browse-only. For overland migrants, check the manuscript collections at the California State Library and the Bancroft Library. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- A negative online result is not absence: 11 of the 14 digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period were not examined in this survey, and many county records are undigitized and held only at county courthouses or state archives.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush).
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the dominant commercial and port city.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (federal)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 migrants arrived from across the United States and abroad between 1848 and 1855 (Wikipedia). The place_population tool returned no data for this period.
- **Economy:** Gold mining, commerce, and port trade dominated the period 1848–1860.
- **Ethnic composition:** Diverse — migrants from the eastern United States, Latin America, Europe, China, and Australia (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Franciscan mission network documented the Catholic population through 1850; various Protestant and Catholic congregations formed in mining camps and cities after statehood. No tool result names specific denominations for this period beyond the Franciscan mission records.
- **Key historical events:** The Gold Rush began January 24, 1848, when James Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill; it drew an estimated 300,000 people to California by 1855 and precipitated statehood in 1850 (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
- California was admitted to the Union in 1850 as a state, with no prior territorial civil record series.
- Counties were created rapidly throughout the 1850s as mining camps became permanent communities. The operative record-keeping unit is the county, not the state.
- place_search_all returned no historical jurisdiction data beyond the state entry dated from 1850.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds a collection titled "California, County Births, 1850-1919" (collection 2017276, 789,456 records) and "California, County Marriages, 1850-1952" (collection 1452832, 567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons), both beginning in 1850 — indicating county-level registration was operative from statehood.
- **Registration level and start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; the specific statewide registration requirement date cannot be confirmed from any tool result. Research the specific county for its earliest records.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and FamilySearch collections 2017276 and 1452832.
- **Gaps:** No death-record collection appears in the collections_search results for this period. Deaths in mining camps were often unrecorded in formal civil registers; substitute sources include church burial registers, cemetery records, newspaper death notices, and probate files.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Franciscan Mission Records, 1769-1850 (FamilySearch collection 1804372, 98,765 records) cover baptisms, marriages, and burials for the Catholic Mission network — primarily relevant for California-born individuals or those connected to the missions before the Gold Rush.

### Church records
- **Denominations documented:** Franciscan mission records (1769–1850) are the main pre-Gold Rush church series. Post-statehood denominations included various Catholic parishes and Protestant congregations in mining towns. No tool result names specific post-1850 congregations for this period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (mission era); post-1850 church records vary by congregation.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1804372 for mission records; individual parish and denominational archives for post-1850 congregations.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Spanish and Latin.
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Church Records page returned only generic content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Church_Records directly for holdings by denomination.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1850 federal census is the first taken in California after statehood, but it is partially destroyed — some county returns are missing (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). Use as a starting point, but expect gaps.
- **State census:** The California state census of 1852 covers the same population and partially compensates for the damaged 1850 returns. FamilySearch holds a digitized volume (image group 006601001, 1850-1852, 522 images) that is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable — indexed + images.
- **Other enumerations:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Census page returned only generic content; no additional state or special enumerations could be confirmed from tool results.
- **Access:** 1852 state census: indexed + images (88%, full-text). 1850 federal census: check Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) for indexed access.

### Mining claim records
- **Types:** Mining Claim Registers recording individual claims by name, location, and date.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds a digitized volume of Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, 1849–1855 (image group 006601002, 340 images). It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. It must be searched image by image with no name search.
- **Where held:** County recorders' offices held mining claim records (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Physical records remain at county courthouses.
- **Note:** Mining claims are among the most direct sources for documenting a Gold Rush miner's presence and location. Always identify the county of operation.

### Immigration and arrival records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary sea entry point; Sacramento was a major inland arrival hub.
- **Ship passenger manifests:** Held at NARA San Bruno (National Archives, Pacific Sierra Region) for San Francisco arrivals (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Access via archives.gov (https://www.archives.gov/).
- **Port Arrival Registers:** FamilySearch holds a digitized volume for Sacramento, 1849–1858 (image group 006601003, 298 images). It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.
- **Overland arrivals:** Overland trail diaries and journals exist at the California State Library and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — county, state, or federal. No specific California naturalization collection appeared in collections_search for this period.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Voter registration (Great Registers)
- **What exists:** "California, Great Registers, 1866-1910" (FamilySearch collection 1923340, 1,345,678 records). These are the voter registration rolls for adult male citizens.
- **Important limitation:** Great Registers begin in 1866 — they do not cover the main Gold Rush decade (1848–1860). They are valuable for identifying where a miner settled after the rush but cannot document arrival or presence in the 1850s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1923340 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a public land (federal) state; federal land patents are the primary source for land grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Land and Property page returned only generic content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Land_and_Property for specific repositories.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents; county deed books at county courthouses; federal patents at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website.
- **Date range:** From statehood (1850).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions; also naturalizations (pre-1906 filed in any court of record).
- **Where held:** County courthouses and state archives. The FamilySearch Wiki California Probate Records page returned only generic content — consult the wiki directly.
- **Note:** Probate files for miners who died intestate (without a will) often name heirs and establish family relationships — a critical source when vital records are absent.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Mexican-American War (ended 1848) immediately preceded the Gold Rush; some migrants were veterans. The Civil War (1861–1865) falls just after the target period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, and draft registrations at the National Archives (archives.gov, https://www.archives.gov/). Military records for this period are accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Where held:** NARA; state adjutant general records may be at the California State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mining camps had their own burial grounds, many now unmarked or relocated. No specific cemetery names were returned by tool results for this period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed cemetery records for California.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are at county or municipal level.

### Newspaper records
- **What exists:** San Francisco had newspapers from the Gold Rush era. Historical newspapers are searchable via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate sales, mining claim disputes), and ship arrival lists published in newspapers supplement formal records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property and personal property tax records.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and state archives.
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax lists can substitute for census years and place a person at a specific county location year by year.

### Other record types
- **Manuscript collections:** The California State Library and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections including overland trail diaries and journals (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- **Mining company records:** Some larger mining companies maintained employment records; check county historical societies for surviving business records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850-1919 (2017276); County Marriages 1850-1952 (1452832); Great Registers 1866-1910 (1923340); Mission Records 1769-1850 (1804372); 1852 State Census (browse 006601001); Mining Claims San Francisco 1849-1855 (browse 006601002); Port Arrivals Sacramento 1849-1858 (browse 006601003) | Primary indexed and browse-only records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1850 federal census (partially destroyed) | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records | Deaths not in civil registers or newspapers | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, ship arrivals, legal notices | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Fold3 | Military Records | Veterans of Mexican-American War and later conflicts | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Ship passenger manifests (NARA San Bruno); naturalization records | Sea arrivals at San Francisco; pre-1906 naturalizations | Free / in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for the period 1848–1860 in FamilySearch volume_search. Only 3 volumes were detailed above (the first page of results). The remaining 11 were not examined in this survey — query FamilySearch directly for the full set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| County courthouses (California) | Deeds, probate, court records, mining claim registers, early vital records | In-person / mail |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State-level records, court records, state census | In-person / online request |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Manuscript collections, overland diaries, Gold Rush materials | In-person / online catalog |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush-era manuscript collections, diaries, journals | In-person / appointment |
| NARA Pacific Sierra Region, San Bruno | Ship passenger manifests, federal court naturalizations | In-person / research request |

## Records NOT online
- Mining claim registers held at individual county recorders' offices (physical records; the FamilySearch volume covers San Francisco only, browse-only)
- County-level death records for the 1850s (no death collection for this period appeared in collections_search)
- Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in state and local courts (location varies by court; not consolidated online)
- Manuscript and diary collections at the California State Library and Bancroft Library
- Most church congregation records from post-1850 denominations

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census for California is partially destroyed — some county returns are missing (FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1852 California state census (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 88% indexed) partially compensates.
- No other specific record losses were stated by tool results. An empty search result for a county is a coverage gap, not evidence of destruction.

## Research tips
- Begin by identifying the specific California county where the ancestor mined or settled; nearly all 1850s records were created and held at the county level, not statewide. County boundaries shifted rapidly in the 1850s — confirm the county that governed the target location at the specific year. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- Search the 1852 California state census (FamilySearch volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed) as a primary document; it was specifically designed to capture the Gold Rush population and partially compensates for the damaged 1850 federal census. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- Mining claim registers at county recorders' offices are among the most direct sources for documenting a miner's presence; San Francisco's are online (browse-only, volume 006601002) and others remain physical at county courthouses. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- Ship passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno document sea arrivals at San Francisco — a primary route for migrants from the eastern United States. The Sacramento port arrival registers (volume 006601003) cover inland arrivals but are browse-only. For overland migrants, check the manuscript collections at the California State Library and the Bancroft Library. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- A negative online result is not absence: 11 of the 14 digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period were not examined in this survey, and many county records are undigitized and held only at county courthouses or state archives.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Originally settled as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York City. Throughout the 1700s the city was the principal settlement of the Province of New York under British colonial rule.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan, New York County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial, until 1783); thereafter State of New York
- **Population during period:** Population retrieval tools returned no data for this period and place. Historical sources note the city grew substantially during the colonial era as a major commercial port.
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and colonial administrative center (Wikipedia)
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch and English families prominent; also French Huguenot, German, Jewish, and African populations
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran
- **Key historical events:** British colonial rule throughout the century; American Revolution 1775-1783; British occupation of New York City 1776-1783

## Boundary changes
- During the 1700s, New York City consisted primarily of Manhattan (New York County). The surrounding boroughs were separate communities.
- The colonial period (1700-1783) placed the city under the Province of New York. After American independence (1783) records fall under New York State jurisdiction.
- place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions for this place during this survey.

One digitized volume specifically for New York City is confirmed by volume_search: Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776 (image group 007733180, 211 images). - **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate and legal notices, ship arrivals

- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the principal port of entry and departure throughout the 1700s
- **Record types:** Colonial-era passenger lists (pre-federal); naturalization proceedings (before 1906, any court of record could naturalize, including the Mayor's Court)

- **Date range:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of colonial New York City (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). - **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Held at the New York State Archives; named in the FamilySearch Wiki as a key source for 1700s research (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
