- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the principal port of entry and departure throughout the 1700s
- **Record types:** Colonial-era passenger lists (pre-federal); naturalization proceedings (before 1906, any court of record could naturalize, including the Mayor's Court)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal-era passenger records; colonial-era passenger records may be at the New York State Archives or the NYGBS
- **Content note:** Examine full passenger manifests for all family members, including infants and children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Ward tax assessment lists (property and personal estates)
- **Date range:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of colonial New York City (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records). FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (collection id 1678432, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) covers 1799-1804, at the very edge of the target period.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives for most colonial-era tax lists; FamilySearch for the 1799-1804 collection
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census years and confirm residence and economic status

### Other record types
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Held at the New York State Archives; named in the FamilySearch Wiki as a key source for 1700s research (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Abstracts of Wills series:** Published by the New-York Historical Society; indexes wills proved before the colonial Prerogative Court of New York
- **NYGBS and NYHS collections:** The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society both hold extensive colonial-era manuscript and printed collections

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) | New York, Church Records, 1640-1940 (id 1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (id 2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (id 1542780); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (id 1678432) | Church/land/probate/tax records with no civil registration in this period | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal military pension files; federal-era passenger lists | Revolutionary War service, pension, and immigration records | Free (online via NARA) |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery transcriptions | Colonial-era burial information not available online elsewhere | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices not in other record types | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches New York City specifically for 1700-1800 (Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776, image group 007733180). This is the complete set returned by volume_search at the city level. The state-level collections_search returned 5 collections spanning the colonial period; these are broader NY state collections that may contain NYC records within them.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives | New York Colonial Manuscripts; colonial militia rolls; colonial land patents; provincial census records | In-person / online request |
| New-York Historical Society | Abstracts of Wills series; colonial church collections; manuscript collections | In-person; some digitized |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Extensive colonial-era collections | In-person; member access |
| New York County Clerk / Surrogate's Court | Land deed books; colonial probate records | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial ward tax assessment lists (most years, most wards) for the 1700s
- Anglican (Trinity Church) and Presbyterian church registers for the 1700s — not confirmed as digitized at the city level in this survey
- New York Colonial Manuscripts held at the New York State Archives
- Mayor's Court records of New York City
- Most colonial militia rolls

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states a specific destruction of colonial New York City records. Absence of digitized online results for a record type is a coverage gap, not confirmed evidence of destruction. The British occupation of the city (1776-1783) may have created disruptions; researchers should check for gaps in church registers during this span.

## Research tips
- Church records are the only source for vital events (baptisms, marriages, burials) in 1700s New York City — no civil registration existed. Begin every family search with the denomination most likely to have served the family, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- Dutch Reformed registers 1700-1776 (image group 007733180 on FamilySearch) are in Dutch and must be browsed image by image with no name index — the researcher must read Dutch or use translated finding aids and published extracts.
- Wills proved in the colonial Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in the "Abstracts of Wills" series from the New-York Historical Society — consult this index before searching original probate records (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- Colonial militia rolls name men of military age and serve as a partial substitute for census records for the 1700s (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- The FamilySearch Wiki specific pages for New York (Vital Records, Church Records, Land, Probate, Census, City Genealogy) all returned only generic content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy directly in a browser for additional guidance.
- The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and the New-York Historical Society are the two premier repositories for colonial-era NYC research; contact both when FamilySearch and NARA collections are exhausted.

The guide has been saved as **loc_001** in your project. Here is the full report from the locality guide agent:

---

Researching Virginia families during the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) puts you in one of the best-documented periods in American genealogy. Because no statewide civil registration existed yet, the most important records fall into these categories:

**Military Records**
- **National Archives (NARA):** Service records, muster rolls, and pension applications for veterans and their widows. This is the premier resource for military service documentation.
- **Library of Virginia (Richmond):** Virginia militia records.

**Population Substitutes**
- **County personal property tax lists beginning in 1782** — these are the standard substitute for the largely destroyed 1790 Virginia census and provide a first population snapshot for most families.

**FamilySearch Collections (5 indexed collections covering this period):**
1. Military records
2. Church records
3. Land and will records
4. Tax records
5. County court records

**Two Critical Caveats**
1. **Virginia Military District (Ohio):** Bounty land that Virginia granted to its veterans was located in the Virginia Military District of Ohio — not in Virginia itself. Post-war land claim records connect to Ohio and are held at the Virginia State Library.
2. **Kentucky:** Kentucky was still part of Virginia until 1792. If your ancestors moved westward during the war, their records for that period are **Virginia county records**, not Kentucky records.

---

**Recommended Next Step:** Identify the specific Virginia county where your ancestors lived, then focus searches on that county's court and deed records, church registers, and the 1782–1783 tax lists as the first population snapshot for that family.

NARA Record Group 15 pension application files for veterans' widows are among the richest genealogical sources for the period — a widow's application typically names the marriage date, witnesses, and children.

Anglican vestry records (poor-relief lists, vestry minutes) are held separately from baptism registers; vestry minutes name indigent parishioners not found in other church series and are a critical but underused source.

The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia-specific pages (Vital Records, Military Records, Land, Church, Probate, Census) all returned only generic content during this survey — consult them directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki before relying on their absence in this guide.

Volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779-1800, 341 images) is browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; it must be browsed image-by-image with no search shortcut.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies, admitted to the Union in 1788; during 1775-1783 it operated first as a colony and then, after July 1776, as an independent state
- **County seat / administrative center:** Williamsburg was the colonial capital; Richmond became the state capital in 1780
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colonial period), then independent Commonwealth of Virginia
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tool for this period
- **Economy:** Tobacco cultivation dominant in the Tidewater and Piedmont; mixed farming and trade in western counties
- **Ethnic composition:** English-descent settlers dominant in eastern counties; Scots-Irish, German, and Welsh immigrants concentrated in the Shenandoah Valley and western counties; large African enslaved population throughout
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (Episcopal after the Revolution — the established colonial church); Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian congregations active across the state; German Reformed and Lutheran congregations in the western/Valley counties
- **Key historical events:** Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War); Yorktown campaign concluded the war in 1781; the established Anglican church was disestablished after independence

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's county boundaries shifted frequently in this period as western settlement expanded — the specific county a family lived in must be established before searching court or deed records
- Kentucky was still part of Virginia (as Kentucky County, then three counties) until 1792 — records for families in Kentucky during 1775-1783 are Virginia county records
- The Virginia Military District of Ohio was set aside after the Revolution as bounty land for veterans — post-war land claim records connect to Ohio, not Virginia county deeds

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; the statewide registration start year cannot be confirmed from this tool result — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records directly
- **What exists:** No statewide civil registration existed during 1775-1783; church registers are the primary source for births, marriages, and deaths in this period
- **Where held:** Church registers at individual parishes and diocesan archives; copies microfilmed by FamilySearch (collection 1598230); county marriage bonds and licenses at county courthouses and Library of Virginia
- **Gaps:** Civil registration was absent statewide during the target period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers; county marriage bonds and licenses (collection 1734285); estate inventories naming heirs

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established colonial church), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian; German Reformed and Lutheran in Shenandoah Valley counties
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; Anglican vestry minutes (which also record poor-relief names and amounts)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598230 "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" contains approximately 1,234,567 records with associated images; original registers held at individual parishes, the Library of Virginia (Richmond), and diocesan archives
- **Gaps:** Anglican vestry records in some parishes were disrupted at the Revolution when the established church was disestablished; which specific parish served a particular locality in this period cannot be confirmed from tool results returned in this survey — say the affiliation is unconfirmed and direct to the Library of Virginia for parish boundary maps
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1790 federal census is the nearest federal enumeration; Virginia's portion was largely destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **State/provincial census:** No Virginia state census confirmed from tool results for this period
- **Other enumerations:** County personal property and land tax lists beginning 1782 are the primary substitute for the missing census
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (456,789 records) is name-indexed and searchable online; volume 005301449 (87 images, state enumerations/tax lists 1782-1799) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — keyword search only

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, inventories of personal property, guardianships, county court minute books
- **Testate or intestate:** Wills proved in county court (testate); administration bonds filed for intestate estates — both series name heirs and creditors
- **Date range:** Virginia county courts date from each county's formation; collection 2134567 covers 1650-1920
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2134567 "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (approximately 1,789,012 records); volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books 1775-1795, 158 images) is 61% name-indexed — indexed + images; original records at county courthouses and Library of Virginia

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land patents were granted by the Crown; after independence, the Commonwealth of Virginia issued state grants; bounty land for veterans was granted in the Virginia Military District of Ohio, with warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, bounty land warrants (post-1783), tax records
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1734285 "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" covers 2,567,890 records from 1600 onward
- **Where held:** County deed books at county courthouses; copies at Library of Virginia; collection 1734285 online; volume 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779-1800, 341 images) is browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783)
- **Record types:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls — NARA Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records — Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files — NARA Record Group 15

Researching Virginia families during the American Revolutionary War (1775-1783) puts you in one of the best-documented periods in American genealogy. Because no statewide civil registration existed yet, the most important records are the military files at the National Archives (service records, muster rolls, and pension applications for veterans and their widows), Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, and county personal property tax lists beginning in 1782, which are the standard substitute for the largely destroyed 1790 Virginia census. FamilySearch holds five indexed collections directly covering this period: military records, church records, land and will records, tax records, and county court records. One critical warning: the bounty land Virginia granted to its veterans was located in the Virginia Military District of Ohio, not in Virginia itself, so post-war land claim records connect to Ohio and are held at the Virginia State Library. A second warning: Kentucky was still part of Virginia until 1792, so if your ancestors moved westward during the war, their records for that period are Virginia county records.

The next step is to identify the specific Virginia county where your ancestors lived, then focus searches on that county's court and deed records, church registers, and the 1782-1783 tax lists as the first population snapshot for that family.

## Record Survival After Disasters — New Orleans, Early 1800s

### What Was Lost

New Orleans is an unusually disaster-prone archive. Two devastating fires — **1788** and **1794** — destroyed most of the colonial French Quarter and many early records. Repeated floods, hurricanes, and yellow fever epidemics caused further losses throughout the antebellum period.

### What Survived and Where to Find It

Despite the losses, a great deal survives because of Louisiana's **civil-law (notarial) system**, which produced a parallel record series that largely endured the fires:

1. **Catholic Sacramental Registers — St. Louis Cathedral**
   - Dating from **1731** (with gaps), covering baptisms, marriages, and burials
   - Preserved at the **Archdiocese of New Orleans** and microfilmed by FamilySearch
   - These are often the best substitute for lost civil records before state registration began

2. **Notarial Acts** (births, marriages, deaths, property transactions, manumissions, contracts)
   - Colonial French-era volumes (1718–1769) and Spanish-era volumes (1769–1803) are held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** at the Old U.S. Mint building in New Orleans
   - Post-1803 notarial acts are at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**
   - ⚠️ **Important:** These are organized by *notary name and date*, not by the subject's name — you need an approximate year and the notary's name to locate anything

### Key Caveats for Researchers

- Civil registration start dates for Louisiana could not be confirmed from specific FamilySearch Wiki pages during this session — verify those dates directly at [FamilySearch.org/wiki](https://FamilySearch.org/wiki)
- The archive is split between two custodians depending on the era (pre- vs. post-1803)

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Search the Archdiocese of New Orleans** for sacramental registers covering the specific years your ancestors lived in New Orleans
2. **Contact the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** with any approximate dates so they can direct you to the right notary's volume

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by France; passed to Spanish control 1763; returned briefly to France before the Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred the territory to the United States; Louisiana became a state in 1812, with New Orleans as the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of Orleans Parish; Louisiana uses "parishes," not "counties")
- **Parent jurisdiction:** State of Louisiana (1812–present); Orleans Territory (1804–1812); Louisiana Territory (1803–1804); Spanish colonial Louisiana (1769–1803)
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the population tool for this location.
- **Economy:** Major international port; cotton and sugar trade; enslaved labor was central to the antebellum economy.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, African (enslaved and free, including a large free-Black population), post-1803 American migrants, German and Irish immigrants growing through the period.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral, seat of the Diocese/Archdiocese of New Orleans); Protestant denominations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist) established congregations after 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Great fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial built environment and many records; Louisiana Purchase 1803; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods throughout the period.

## Boundary changes

- 1718–1769: French colonial Louisiana (Conseil Supérieur held governance and records)
- 1769–1803: Spanish colonial Louisiana (Cabildo governed; notarial and civil records maintained under the Spanish civil-law system)
- 1803–1804: Louisiana Territory (US), following the Louisiana Purchase
- 1804–1812: Orleans Territory (US)
- 1812–present: State of Louisiana, Orleans Parish
- Records created under each colonial regime are held by different custodians. A researcher working near 1803 must search both the Spanish colonial series (at the Louisiana Historical Center) and the early US-period series (at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center and Louisiana State Archives).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; no Louisiana-specific civil registration start date at any jurisdictional level was confirmed by tool results. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892) covers deaths from 1819, but whether this reflects a civil registration requirement or municipal recording was not confirmed. For 1800–1850, church sacramental registers are the documented primary vital source.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, 987,654 records with 493,827 images) covers the full research window. The "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892, 2,345,678 records, name index only, no images) supplements death searches from 1819 onward.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online collections cited above); Archdiocese of New Orleans (originals for St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers).
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires created gaps in the sacramental registers predating this research window; some early 1800s registers also have gaps from later flood and hurricane damage. Contact the Archdiocese directly to verify which specific registers survive for which years.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (see Church records); notarial acts for births/legitimations, marriage contracts, and succession (death) records; Cabildo records for the Spanish colonial period.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic — St. Louis Cathedral is the principal parish for colonial and antebellum New Orleans (baptisms, marriages, burials recorded from 1731, with gaps). Protestant denominations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist) arrived after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. The sacramental registers are the primary vital record series for this period.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans holds the original St. Louis Cathedral registers (1731–present, with gaps). Many registers have been microfilmed by FamilySearch and are accessible through collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925," 987,654 records, 493,827 images). (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic)
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed many early colonial sacramental records; surviving registers from 1731 contain gaps. The specific post-1800 years missing from the registers are not catalogued in this survey's tool results — contact the Archdiocese directly.
- **Language:** French (1718–1769), Spanish (1769–1803), English (after 1803). Working near 1803, researchers may encounter entries in any of the three languages. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic)

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** Federal censuses were enumerated for New Orleans in 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850. The 1810 and 1820 censuses are early nominal enumerations listing heads of household only; 1850 is the first to list all free household members by name.
- **State/provincial census:** This survey did not confirm a Louisiana territorial or state census supplement through tool results.
- **Other enumerations:** This survey did not confirm additional enumerations through tool results.
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and searchable at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and free on FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Louisiana uses "successions" (the civil-law equivalent of probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions, rather than standard common-law probate. Notarial acts also cover marriage contracts, estate inventories, emancipations, and slave transactions.
- **Testate or intestate:** For a testate decedent, look for succession records including the testament (will); for intestate, look for succession ab intestat filings in the notarial or district court records.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" covers the full research window (456,789 records, 228,394 images). The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (online, with images); Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for succession acts recorded notarially.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pre-US Louisiana lands used the French arpent system, not the rectangular survey; post-1803 federal grants used the rectangular system where applicable.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land grants were administered by the French and Spanish colonial governments. Post-1803 US land claims were adjudicated by the Board of Land Commissioners; the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office website holds some federal patents. The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Land and Property page returned only generic content during this survey.
- **Types:** Notarial acts cover all property transfers — they replace what deed books would contain in a common-law state. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds property transfer records from 1733 onward, organized by notary and date. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives)
- **Date range:** Notarial acts from 1733 to present; colonial-era acts (French 1718–1769, Spanish 1769–1803) at Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (1803–present, physical); Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building (French/Spanish colonial era, physical). One digitized browse-only volume covering 1803–1820 is on FamilySearch (image group 004990115, 167 images, 0% name-indexed, in French and English).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican-American War (1846–1848).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized military indexes and records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Louisiana State Archives may hold state militia records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (opened 1789), No. 2 (opened 1823), and No. 3 (opened 1854) are the principal Catholic cemeteries for this period; above-ground vaults were used because of the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed headstone records for many New Orleans cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers — contact the Archdiocese of New Orleans for the Catholic cemeteries.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** New Orleans had active French- and English-language newspapers from the early 1800s; this survey did not confirm specific titles and date ranges through tool results.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized historical newspapers; additional holdings at the Louisiana State Library and the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate sale notices, marriage announcements, and legal notices supplement gaps in formal vital records where registers were lost to fires or floods.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the busiest ports of entry in the United States during 1800–1850, receiving large numbers of Irish, German, and French immigrants.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); naturalization records (pre-1906 may appear in any court of record, including Orleans Parish courts).
- **Where held:** NARA; FamilySearch also holds some passenger and naturalization indexes.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property and poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** This survey did not confirm specific tax list date ranges through tool results.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can serve as a census substitute for years between federal enumerations and for enslaved persons not named in the census.

### Other record types — Notarial acts (unique to Louisiana)

- The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734, covering successions, marriage contracts, property transfers, tutorships, emancipations, and slave transactions. These are the single most important record class for 1800–1850 New Orleans research and serve as a substitute for missing vital, probate, and land records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives)
- Organized by notary name and date, not by party name — a researcher needs an approximate date and the notary's name to locate a specific act.
- FamilySearch holds one digitized browse-only volume covering 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, 0% name-indexed, in French and English); the bulk of the acts are physical-only at the Notarial Archives Research Center.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1612905) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (987,654 records, 493,827 images) | Primary vital records (baptism/marriage/burial) pre-civil registration | Free |
| FamilySearch (collection 1798054) | Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons, 283,945 images) | Marriage records from 1837 — does not cover marriages before 1837 | Free |
| FamilySearch (collection 2078341) | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (456,789 records, 228,394 images) | Successions and estate records | Free |
| FamilySearch (collection 1543892) | Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (2,345,678 records, name index only) | Death index from 1819 | Free |
| FamilySearch (image group 004990115) | Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies), Orleans, 1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only, French/English | Notarial acts 1803–1820 — browse image by image, no name index | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census records 1810–1850 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | War of 1812 and other service records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery transcriptions where no sexton record survives | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, estate/legal notices, marriage announcements | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, naturalization records, federal records | Free / In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans Parish covering 1803–1820 (notarial acts; image group 004990115); this appears to be the complete result set for the 1800–1850 window. The 4 named FamilySearch collections are the complete set returned by collections_search at Louisiana scope. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) was not available as a tool in this survey session and was not consulted; additional microfilm volumes may exist there.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts, 1734–present (successions, property, marriage contracts, emancipations, slave transactions) | In-person research; some finding aids online |
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building) | Colonial-era notarial records: French 1718–1769, Spanish 1769–1803 | In-person |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records, tax lists, court records | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans | St. Louis Cathedral original sacramental registers, 1731–present (with gaps from fires) | Contact archives for access |

## Records NOT online

- The vast majority of notarial acts are physical-only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (1803–present) and the Louisiana Historical Center (pre-1803); only one browse-only volume (1803–1820, image group 004990115) is on FamilySearch.
- Colonial-era records (French and Spanish) at the Louisiana Historical Center are physical.
- Tax lists and other territorial/early state records at the Louisiana State Archives are not confirmed as digitized by tool results in this survey.
- Original sacramental registers for St. Louis Cathedral (Archdiocese of New Orleans) are physical; the microfilmed copies are on FamilySearch (collection 1612905).
- Sexton records and burial registers for the St. Louis Cemeteries are physical at the Archdiocese of New Orleans.

## Known record losses

- **Fires of 1788 and 1794:** Both fires destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. (Sources: Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans; FamilySearch wiki search — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) These fires primarily affected colonial French records created before 1788. Spanish colonial notarial and Cabildo records (1769–1803) largely survived, as did St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers from 1731, with gaps introduced by the fires.
- **Ongoing flood, hurricane, and yellow fever damage:** Further archival losses occurred throughout the period from water damage; this survey did not confirm specific record series lost by name in tool results. (Source: Wikipedia)
- **What survives and where to look for copies or substitutes when a record is missing:**
  - *St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers* survive from 1731 with gaps. Originals: Archdiocese of New Orleans. Microfilmed copies: FamilySearch collection 1612905. These are the primary substitute for any missing civil vital record.
  - *Notarial acts* are exceptionally well-preserved from 1733 and cover births (legitimations), marriages (marriage contracts), deaths (succession acts), and property transactions. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the main corpus from 1803 onward; Louisiana Historical Center holds the colonial-era volumes. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives)
  - *Cabildo records* (the Spanish colonial governing body) survive and are relevant for the period before the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.
  - *Newspaper death notices, estate sale advertisements, and marriage announcements* fill gaps where no register survives; check Newspapers.com and inquire at the Historic New Orleans Collection.
  - *Tax lists* at the Louisiana State Archives serve as census and vital-record substitutes.
  - *FamilySearch death index* (collection 1543892, 1819–1964) can bridge the gap when no burial register is available from 1819 onward.

## Research tips

- Notarial records are the backbone of New Orleans research and replace what deed books, wills, and even some vital records would provide in a common-law state. They are organized by notary name and date, not by party name — you need an approximate date and the name of the acting notary. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives)
- Church records are in French (1718–1769), Spanish (1769–1803), or English (after 1803). Working near 1803, you may encounter entries in any of the three languages in the same register. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic)
- Louisiana uses successions (not probate), tutorships (not guardianship), and interdictions (not conservatorships) — search for these Louisiana-specific terms in finding aids and indexes.
- When a civil or church vital record is missing due to the 1788 or 1794 fires, turn first to the surviving sacramental registers (Archdiocese of New Orleans / FamilySearch collection 1612905), then to notarial acts (Notarial Archives Research Center for 1803 onward, Louisiana Historical Center for the colonial era).
- For families with records spanning the 1803 Louisiana Purchase boundary, search both the Spanish colonial notarial record series (Louisiana Historical Center, 1769–1803) and the early US-period notarial series (Notarial Archives Research Center, 1803 onward) — the same family's records may appear in both.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's specific topic pages for Louisiana returned only generic content during this survey — verify those pages directly at FamilySearch.org/wiki before relying on their absence from this guide.

The other major caution is that civil registration start dates for Louisiana could not be confirmed from the specific FamilySearch Wiki pages (they returned only generic content during this session) — re-check those pages directly at FamilySearch.org/wiki.

The next step is to search the Archdiocese of New Orleans for the specific sacramental register years your ancestors fall within, and to contact the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center with any approximate dates you have so they can direct you to the right notary's volume.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by France; passed to Spanish control 1763; returned briefly to France before the Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred the territory to the United States; Louisiana became a state in 1812, with New Orleans as the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of Orleans Parish; Louisiana uses "parishes," not "counties")
- **Parent jurisdiction:** State of Louisiana (1812–present); Orleans Territory (1804–1812); Louisiana Territory (1803–1804); Spanish colonial Louisiana (1769–1803)
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the population tool for this location.
- **Economy:** Major international port; cotton and sugar trade; enslaved labor was central to the antebellum economy.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, African (enslaved and free, including a large free-Black population), post-1803 American migrants, German and Irish immigrants growing through the period.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral, seat of the Diocese/Archdiocese of New Orleans); Protestant denominations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist) established congregations after 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Great fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial built environment and many records; Louisiana Purchase 1803; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods throughout the period.

## Boundary changes

- 1718–1769: French colonial Louisiana (Conseil Supérieur held governance and records)
- 1769–1803: Spanish colonial Louisiana (Cabildo governed; notarial and civil records maintained under the Spanish civil-law system)
- 1803–1804: Louisiana Territory (US), following the Louisiana Purchase
- 1804–1812: Orleans Territory (US)
- 1812–present: State of Louisiana, Orleans Parish
- Records created under each colonial regime are held by different custodians. A researcher working near 1803 must search both the Spanish colonial series (at the Louisiana Historical Center) and the early US-period series (at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center and Louisiana State Archives).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; no Louisiana-specific civil registration start date at any jurisdictional level was confirmed by tool results. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892) covers deaths from 1819, but whether this reflects a civil registration requirement or municipal recording was not confirmed. For 1800–1850, church sacramental registers are the documented primary vital source.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, 987,654 records with 493,827 images) covers the full research window. The "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection 1543892, 2,345,678 records, name index only, no images) supplements death searches from 1819 onward.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online collections cited above); Archdiocese of New Orleans (originals for St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers).
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires created gaps in the sacramental registers predating this research window; some early 1800s registers also have gaps from later flood and hurricane damage. Contact the Archdiocese directly to verify which specific registers survive for which years.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (see Church records); notarial acts for births/legitimations, marriage contracts, and succession (death) records; Cabildo records for the Spanish colonial period.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic — St. Louis Cathedral is the principal parish for colonial and antebellum New Orleans (baptisms, marriages, burials recorded from 1731, with gaps). Protestant denominations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist) arrived after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. The sacramental registers are the primary vital record series for this period.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans holds the original St. Louis Cathedral registers (1731–present, with gaps). Many registers have been microfilmed by FamilySearch and are accessible through collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925," 987,654 records, 493,827 images). (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic)
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed many early colonial sacramental records; surviving registers from 1731 contain gaps. The specific post-1800 years missing from the registers are not catalogued in this survey's tool results — contact the Archdiocese directly.
- **Language:** French (1718–1769), Spanish (1769–1803), English (after 1803). Working near 1803, researchers may encounter entries in any of the three languages. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic)

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** Federal censuses were enumerated for New Orleans in 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850. The 1810 and 1820 censuses are early nominal enumerations listing heads of household only; 1850 is the first to list all free household members by name.
- **State/provincial census:** This survey did not confirm a Louisiana territorial or state census supplement through tool results.
- **Other enumerations:** This survey did not confirm additional enumerations through tool results.
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and searchable at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and free on FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Louisiana uses "successions" (the civil-law equivalent of probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions, rather than standard common-law probate. Notarial acts also cover marriage contracts, estate inventories, emancipations, and slave transactions.
- **Testate or intestate:** For a testate decedent, look for succession records including the testament (will); for intestate, look for succession ab intestat filings in the notarial or district court records.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" covers the full research window (456,789 records, 228,394 images). The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (online, with images); Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for succession acts recorded notarially.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pre-US Louisiana lands used the French arpent system, not the rectangular survey; post-1803 federal grants used the rectangular system where applicable.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land grants were administered by the French and Spanish colonial governments. Post-1803 US land claims were adjudicated by the Board of Land Commissioners; the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office website holds some federal patents. The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Land and Property page returned only generic content during this survey.
- **Types:** Notarial acts cover all property transfers — they replace what deed books would contain in a common-law state. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds property transfer records from 1733 onward, organized by notary and date. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives)
- **Date range:** Notarial acts from 1733 to present; colonial-era acts (French 1718–1769, Spanish 1769–1803) at Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (1803–present, physical); Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building (French/Spanish colonial era, physical). One digitized browse-only volume covering 1803–1820 is on FamilySearch (image group 004990115, 167 images, 0% name-indexed, in French and English).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican-American War (1846–1848).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized military indexes and records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Louisiana State Archives may hold state militia records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (opened 1789), No. 2 (opened 1823), and No. 3 (opened 1854) are the principal Catholic cemeteries for this period; above-ground vaults were used because of the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed headstone records for many New Orleans cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers — contact the Archdiocese of New Orleans for the Catholic cemeteries.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** New Orleans had active French- and English-language newspapers from the early 1800s; this survey did not confirm specific titles and date ranges through tool results.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized historical newspapers; additional holdings at the Louisiana State Library and the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate sale notices, marriage announcements, and legal notices supplement gaps in formal vital records where registers were lost to fires or floods.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the busiest ports of entry in the United States during 1800–1850, receiving large numbers of Irish, German, and French immigrants.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); naturalization records (pre-1906 may appear in any court of record, including Orleans Parish courts).
- **Where held:** NARA; FamilySearch also holds some passenger and naturalization indexes.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property and poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** This survey did not confirm specific tax list date ranges through tool results.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can serve as a census substitute for years between federal enumerations and for enslaved persons not named in the census.

### Other record types — Notarial acts (unique to Louisiana)

- The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734, covering successions, marriage contracts, property transfers, tutorships, emancipations, and slave transactions. These are the single most important record class for 1800–1850 New Orleans research and serve as a substitute for missing vital, probate, and land records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives)
- Organized by notary name and date, not by party name — a researcher needs an approximate date and the notary's name to locate a specific act.
- FamilySearch holds one digitized browse-only volume covering 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, 0% name-indexed, in French and English); the bulk of the acts are physical-only at the Notarial Archives Research Center.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1612905) | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (987,654 records, 493,827 images) | Primary vital records (baptism/marriage/burial) pre-civil registration | Free |
| FamilySearch (collection 1798054) | Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons, 283,945 images) | Marriage records from 1837 — does not cover marriages before 1837 | Free |
| FamilySearch (collection 2078341) | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (456,789 records, 228,394 images) | Successions and estate records | Free |
| FamilySearch (collection 1543892) | Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (2,345,678 records, name index only) | Death index from 1819 | Free |
| FamilySearch (image group 004990115) | Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies), Orleans, 1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only, French/English | Notarial acts 1803–1820 — browse image by image, no name index | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census records 1810–1850 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | War of 1812 and other service records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery transcriptions where no sexton record survives | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, estate/legal notices, marriage announcements | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, naturalization records, federal records | Free / In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans Parish covering 1803–1820 (notarial acts; image group 004990115); this appears to be the complete result set for the 1800–1850 window. The 4 named FamilySearch collections are the complete set returned by collections_search at Louisiana scope. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) was not available as a tool in this survey session and was not consulted; additional microfilm volumes may exist there.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts, 1734–present (successions, property, marriage contracts, emancipations, slave transactions) | In-person research; some finding aids online |
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building) | Colonial-era notarial records: French 1718–1769, Spanish 1769–1803 | In-person |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records, tax lists, court records | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans | St. Louis Cathedral original sacramental registers, 1731–present (with gaps from fires) | Contact archives for access |

## Records NOT online

- The vast majority of notarial acts are physical-only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (1803–present) and the Louisiana Historical Center (pre-1803); only one browse-only volume (1803–1820, image group 004990115) is on FamilySearch.
- Colonial-era records (French and Spanish) at the Louisiana Historical Center are physical.
- Tax lists and other territorial/early state records at the Louisiana State Archives are not confirmed as digitized by tool results in this survey.
- Original sacramental registers for St. Louis Cathedral (Archdiocese of New Orleans) are physical; the microfilmed copies are on FamilySearch (collection 1612905).
- Sexton records and burial registers for the St. Louis Cemeteries are physical at the Archdiocese of New Orleans.

## Known record losses

- **Fires of 1788 and 1794:** Both fires destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. (Sources: Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans; FamilySearch wiki search — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) These fires primarily affected colonial French records created before 1788. Spanish colonial notarial and Cabildo records (1769–1803) largely survived, as did St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers from 1731, with gaps introduced by the fires.
- **Ongoing flood, hurricane, and yellow fever damage:** Further archival losses occurred throughout the period from water damage; this survey did not confirm specific record series lost by name in tool results. (Source: Wikipedia)
- **What survives and where to look for copies or substitutes when a record is missing:**
  - *St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers* survive from 1731 with gaps. Originals: Archdiocese of New Orleans. Microfilmed copies: FamilySearch collection 1612905. These are the primary substitute for any missing civil vital record.
  - *Notarial acts* are exceptionally well-preserved from 1733 and cover births (legitimations), marriages (marriage contracts), deaths (succession acts), and property transactions. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the main corpus from 1803 onward; Louisiana Historical Center holds the colonial-era volumes. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives)
  - *Cabildo records* (the Spanish colonial governing body) survive and are relevant for the period before the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.
  - *Newspaper death notices, estate sale advertisements, and marriage announcements* fill gaps where no register survives; check Newspapers.com and inquire at the Historic New Orleans Collection.
  - *Tax lists* at the Louisiana State Archives serve as census and vital-record substitutes.
  - *FamilySearch death index* (collection 1543892, 1819–1964) can bridge the gap when no burial register is available from 1819 onward.

## Research tips

- Notarial records are the backbone of New Orleans research and replace what deed books, wills, and even some vital records would provide in a common-law state. They are organized by notary name and date, not by party name — you need an approximate date and the name of the acting notary. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives)
- Church records are in French (1718–1769), Spanish (1769–1803), or English (after 1803). Working near 1803, you may encounter entries in any of the three languages in the same register. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic)
- Louisiana uses successions (not probate), tutorships (not guardianship), and interdictions (not conservatorships) — search for these Louisiana-specific terms in finding aids and indexes.
- When a civil or church vital record is missing due to the 1788 or 1794 fires, turn first to the surviving sacramental registers (Archdiocese of New Orleans / FamilySearch collection 1612905), then to notarial acts (Notarial Archives Research Center for 1803 onward, Louisiana Historical Center for the colonial era).
- For families with records spanning the 1803 Louisiana Purchase boundary, search both the Spanish colonial notarial record series (Louisiana Historical Center, 1769–1803) and the early US-period notarial series (Notarial Archives Research Center, 1803 onward) — the same family's records may appear in both.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's specific topic pages for Louisiana returned only generic content during this survey — verify those pages directly at FamilySearch.org/wiki before relying on their absence from this guide.

Here is the locality guide for tracing immigrants entering through Boston in the 1840s:

---

**Boston Port of Entry — 1840s Immigrant Records**

Boston was one of the five major US ports of entry in the 1840s, receiving tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants. The key records and repositories are:

---

### 1. Customs Passenger Lists (Most Direct Source)
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" on FamilySearch — over a million indexed entries
- **Originals held at:** National Archives, Waltham, Massachusetts
- **Limitation:** 1840s lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — no hometown, county, or townland — so they confirm arrival but rarely identify where someone came from within Ireland or Germany
- A digitized image volume covers 1840–1850 specifically, but only ~3% is name-indexed, so it largely requires page-by-page browsing

---

### 2. Naturalization Records (Push Past the Country of Origin Wall)
- **Collections:** FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (345,678 records); NARA federal court holdings at Waltham
- Declarations of intention and petitions for citizenship **often name a specific birthplace and arrival date**
- Before 1906, these could be filed in any court — federal, state, or local — so coverage is spread across repositories

---

### 3. Catholic Parish Registers (Essential for Irish Arrivals)
- **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** holds registers for parishes including the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's, documenting baptisms, marriages, and burials from the 1840s onward
- **FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (987,654 records) covers statewide denominations

---

### 4. 1850 Federal Census
- The first census to name every household member with age and birthplace — the single best tool for locating a family in the years immediately after arrival

---

### 5. Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" Notices (Unique Irish Resource)
- Relatives placed notices that **often named the immigrant's specific townland in Ireland** — invaluable for breaking through the country-of-origin barrier in passenger lists
- Boston newspapers are also available through Newspapers.com

---

### Key Warning
The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts returned only generic content during this survey. Check them directly at [familysearch.org/wiki](https://familysearch.org/wiki) before treating any absence of guidance as settled.

---

**Recommended next step:** Run a research plan targeting the Port of Boston passenger lists and Massachusetts naturalization records for the specific ancestor or family name you are tracing. If you share the name, I can help plan those searches.

# Locality Guide: Port of Boston, Massachusetts (1840s–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **City and county:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Port status:** One of five major US ports of entry in the 1840s, receiving tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Massachusetts Immigration, Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston))
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tools queried for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Major seaport and commercial hub; primary New England point of entry for trans-Atlantic European immigrants
- **Ethnic composition:** Large influx of Irish Famine immigrants during the 1840s; also German and other European arrivals
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant among Irish immigrants), Protestant (Congregationalist, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist), Jewish
- **Key historical events:** Irish Potato Famine (1845–1852) drove mass immigration; Boston was the nearest major US port for ships from the British Isles

## Boundary changes
- Boston has been in Suffolk County throughout the target period; no boundary changes affecting the 1840s–1870 record series were returned by the tools queried.

## Available record types

### Immigration and passenger records (primary source)
- **What exists:** Customs passenger lists for the Port of Boston, 1820–1891 (NARA Record Group 36). Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Massachusetts Immigration, Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)), 1840s lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not hometown or specific county of origin.
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume (DGS 003345210, 389 images) covering 1840–1850 for the Port of Boston. This volume is full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed — it must largely be browsed image by image. The indexed collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312, 1,234,567 records) covers the broader date range and is searchable by name.
- **Originals:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham, Massachusetts) holds the original records in NARA Record Group 36.
- **Gap:** 1840s lists do not give hometown or county of origin — they predate the detailed manifest format required after 1891.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children may appear only in a bundle with the parent's entry, not as separate lines.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts vital records returned only generic content during this survey; the specific year civil registration began at the state or town level cannot be confirmed from the tools queried.
- **What exists:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — 3,456,789 records. For immigrants who married or had children recorded in Boston after arrival, town-level vital records are a key source.
- **Holding level:** Town (Boston City Registrar) for local civil vital records during this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations documented:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Massachusetts Church Records, Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)), Catholic parish registers — especially the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's — document baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward.
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of Boston archives holds these records. FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) covers 987,654 records across denominations statewide.
- **Language:** Latin in Catholic sacramental registers; English in most Protestant registers.
- **Gaps:** Coverage for specific parishes and years varies. Contact the Archdiocese of Boston archives to determine which records survive for a specific parish. The parish that served a particular Boston neighborhood in the 1840s is not confirmed from this survey's tool results — establish that affiliation before requesting registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Boston appears in the 1840 and 1850 federal censuses. The 1850 census is the first to name every household member with age and birthplace — essential for locating newly arrived immigrants.
- **State census:** This survey did not confirm a Massachusetts state census for the 1840s–1870 period from the tools queried (the Massachusetts_Census wiki page returned only generic content).
- **Access:** The 1840 and 1850 censuses are name-indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Naturalization and court records
- **What exists:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection 1459213, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) — 345,678 records. A declaration of intention (first paper) or petition for naturalization often records country of origin, sometimes birthplace and date of arrival, and names witnesses who may be family members. These are especially valuable for the 1840s when passenger lists give minimal information.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has digitized a statewide collection. Originals are at NARA (federal courts) and the Massachusetts State Archives (state and local courts). Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record.

### Probate records
- **What exists:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — 567,890 records. For immigrants who acquired assets, probate files name heirs and sometimes next-of-kin in Ireland or Europe.
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Probate Court; also partially digitized on FamilySearch.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts land and property returned only generic content during this survey; which office holds grants or patents is not confirmed from tool results.
- **Types:** Deeds recorded at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds; city tax assessments.
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds. No specific digitized FamilySearch collection for Suffolk County deeds was confirmed from the tools queried.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865). Many 1840s immigrants enlisted.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (NARA); state adjutant general records (Massachusetts State Archives).
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/), Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers major Boston cemeteries including Catholic cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; may be held by the cemetery or the Archdiocese.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Boston had multiple active newspapers in the 1840s. The Boston Pilot published "Missing Persons" notices that named immigrants and often their townlands of origin in Ireland — a unique resource for Irish immigrant families.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized papers; the Boston Public Library holds microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, ship-arrival notices, and especially Missing Persons notices (Boston Pilot).

### Tax records
- **Types:** Boston city tax assessments naming property owners and residents.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists between census years can track an immigrant's residence.
- **Where held:** City of Boston Archives. No specific digitized collection was confirmed from the tools queried.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (1784312); Church Records, 1630–1920 (1921657); Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (1459213); Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (2061550); Probate Records, 1635–1991 (1678901) | Primary immigration, church, vital, and naturalization records | Free |
| Ancestry | Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (indexed) | Full name-indexed search of customs passenger lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Service records and pensions for immigrant veterans | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Death dates and burial locations | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Obituaries; Boston Pilot Missing Persons notices | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | NARA Record Group 36 originals | Original customs passenger lists at National Archives, Waltham | Free; in-person or mail request |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume (DGS 003345210, 389 images, 1840–1850) matched the Port of Boston passenger list series in the volume search; this is the complete result set for that query. Five indexed collections at the Massachusetts state level were also confirmed.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists, NARA RG 36 (1820–1891) | In-person or mail; archives.gov |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (Cathedral of Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, others) for 1840s immigrant baptisms, marriages, burials | Contact archives directly |
| Massachusetts State Archives | State court naturalization records; alien passenger reports | In-person or online request |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds | Deed books, land records | In-person |
| Suffolk County Probate Court | Probate files | In-person |
| City of Boston Archives | City tax records, municipal records | In-person |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm, local history collections | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Complete access to all years of Port of Boston passenger lists requires searching the indexed collection (1784312) or visiting NARA at Waltham; the 1 digitized volume (DGS 003345210) covers only 1840–1850 and is only 3% name-indexed.
- Boston city tax assessments: not confirmed as digitized from the tools queried.
- Suffolk County deed books: not confirmed as comprehensively digitized from the tools queried.
- Many individual Catholic parish registers: may be held only at the Archdiocese of Boston archives or individual parishes.

## Known record losses
The tools queried did not identify specific record losses for 1840s Boston. Contact the repositories named above to verify what survives for a particular record series.

## Research tips
- The 1840s Boston customs passenger lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — to identify the specific origin in Ireland or Europe, cross-reference the 1850 census birthplace field, naturalization declarations, and Catholic church records. ([Massachusetts Immigration, Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston))
- The Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" database is a unique resource for Irish immigrant families: notices named immigrants and often their specific townlands in Ireland, submitted by relatives searching for lost family members.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — not just federal courts. Search FamilySearch collection 1459213 and also check Suffolk County Superior Court records and U.S. Circuit/District Court records at NARA Waltham.
- Catholic parish registers named by the wiki search (Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's) document Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward and are held at the Archdiocese of Boston archives ([Massachusetts Church Records, Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)). Confirm which parish served your ancestor's neighborhood before requesting registers.
- The 1850 federal census is the first to name every household member with age and birthplace — it is the most powerful first step for locating a 1840s immigrant family in Massachusetts; the 1840 census names only the head of household.
- FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts (Massachusetts_Vital_Records, Massachusetts_Immigration, etc.) returned only generic content during this survey — re-verify those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki before relying on their absence.

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists, NARA RG 36 (1820–1891) | In-person or mail; archives.gov |

Here is the locality guide the research agent compiled for tracing Native American families in Oklahoma (Indian Territory) during the mid-1800s:

---

**Locality Guide — Indian Territory / Oklahoma, mid-1800s**
*(Saved as loc_001 in your project)*

**Jurisdictional Context**

The region of present-day Oklahoma was organized as Indian Territory — set aside for Native American tribes from 1830 through Oklahoma statehood in 1907. It was governed by the **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole) under their own tribal governments and courts, with federal oversight through the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Because no county-level civil government existed in the tribal portion until 1907, **there are no civil birth, marriage, or death records** for the mid-1800s.

---

**Key Record Series**

| Record Type | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Dawes Rolls** (enrollment cards) | 1898–1914 | Most important tribal enrollment; digitized and name-indexed |
| **Old Settler Cherokee Roll** | 1851 | For Cherokees who emigrated before the main Removal |
| **Earlier tribal census rolls** | 1840–1870 | FamilySearch collection 1987432 |
| **Annuity payment rolls** | Various | BIA records; list family members receiving treaty payments |
| **Removal-era emigration lists** | 1830s–1840s | Covers families during forced removal from southeastern states |
| **Federal Indian census schedules** | 1860+ | Separate from regular federal census; covers tribal nations |
| **Mission church registers** | Mid-1800s | Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions |
| **BIA agency correspondence** | Ongoing | Original files at National Archives Southwest Region, Fort Worth |
| **Tribal court files** | Various | Fort Worth NARA; not fully digitized |

---

**Important Caveats**
- The **1890 federal census was destroyed nationwide** — that gap affects all researchers.
- **Freedmen rolls** (for freedpeople of the tribes) are **separate** from blood-quantum rolls and require a distinct search.
- For ancestors present before Removal, extend your search into the **southeastern states of origin** (Georgia, Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee, North Carolina, etc.).

---

**Repositories**
- **FamilySearch** — tribal censuses, rolls, early land records, mission church records, county marriages from 1890
- **National Archives Southwest Region, Fort Worth, TX** — original Dawes Commission records, BIA agency files, tribal court records not yet digitized

---

**Recommended Next Step**

Identify which specific tribe or tribal nation the ancestor was affiliated with, then search the relevant tribal census series in **FamilySearch collection 1987432**, working backward through sequential rolls toward the mid-1800s. If the family was present before Removal, extend the search into their southeastern state of origin.
