entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Oklahoma) (1830–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1830 under the Indian Removal Act; Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) relocated from southeastern states via the Trail of Tears (1830s–1840s)
- **Administrative structure:** No single territorial government; each tribe maintained its own nation with capital, laws, and courts
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal oversight through the Bureau of Indian Affairs; Indian Territory operated under tribal governance and federal treaties, not a standard U.S. territorial civil government
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by tools for this period; tribal censuses are the primary enumeration sources
- **Economy:** Agriculture, ranching, subsistence farming; later coal mining post-Civil War; economic records are largely tribal and BIA in origin
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes; intermarried whites who sought tribal citizenship; freedmen enrolled after the Civil War
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears removal (1830s–1840s); Indian Territory Civil War conflict (1861–1865); Dawes Commission allotment (1893–1907); Oklahoma statehood 1907 merging Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory (est. 1890)

## Boundary changes
- Indian Territory (eastern half of present-day Oklahoma) governed the Five Civilized Tribes 1830–1907
- Oklahoma Territory created 1890 from "Unassigned Lands" to the west — county government and limited civil records applied there from 1890; Indian Territory retained tribal governance
- 1907: Both territories merged into the State of Oklahoma; county government replaced tribal authority; records after 1907 follow Oklahoma county organization
- Determine whether the ancestor lived in the Five Civilized Tribes' portion (east) or in regions of later Oklahoma Territory (west) — different record systems apply even for the same period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Indian Territory before Oklahoma statehood (1907); the FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Oklahoma-specific vital records page for this survey, so the statewide registration start date cannot be confirmed from tool results
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s; collection 2134789 "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" applies only to Oklahoma Territory counties from 1890 onward
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal enrollment rolls (documenting names, ages, and family relationships), missionary church registers, and BIA annuity rolls are the primary substitutes throughout this period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries established congregations from the 1820s onward (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Record types:** Registers of converts (baptisms), marriages, burials, school attendance registers, and community membership lists
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321 "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (123,456 records, 61,728 images, indexed + images); original registers also held at the National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/)

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Indian Territory first enumerated in federal censuses from 1860; 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally; 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 are the key federal enumerations for this region
- **Tribal census and enrollment rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 records, 283,945 images, indexed) covers Dawes Rolls (1898–1914), Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852), and BIA-conducted tribal censuses (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Access:** FamilySearch volume DGS 002298871 (Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870, 940 images) is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable — indexed + images

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts — not county courts — held jurisdiction in Indian Territory; records include estate matters, citizenship disputes, land transactions, and guardianships
- **Date range:** Tribal courts functioned from the 1830s through 1906 when the Five Civilized Tribes' courts were dissolved by the Curtis Act
- **Where held:** Tribal court records held at the National Archives Southwest Region, Fort Worth (https://www.archives.gov/); not fully digitized

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory operated under tribal communal land ownership through 1893 — no individual deeds exist as in U.S. states; allotment under the Dawes Commission (1893–1907) created individual land patents
- **Types:** Tribal land records, Dawes Commission allotment files, Oklahoma Territory homestead filings from 1890; FamilySearch collection 1541872 "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (234,567 records, 117,283 images, indexed)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1541872 for the indexed portion; original allotment records at National Archives Fort Worth (https://www.archives.gov/)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Indian Territory Civil War (1861–1865) — both Union and Confederate units recruited from tribal members; Indian Wars; Spanish-American War
- **Record types:** Compiled Military Service Records, pension files, bounty land warrants; tribal member service records are organized separately from standard state records
- **Where held:** National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 indexes many service and pension records (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Tribal burial grounds and mission cemeteries throughout former Indian Territory; many are unrecorded formally or in remote locations
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage of some named cemeteries; physical sexton and mission registers are held with church record collections

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Tribal newspapers including the Cherokee Phoenix (from 1828) and Cherokee Advocate, plus other tribal-language publications in the region
- **Where held:** Some available via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); physical holdings at libraries not confirmed by tool results
- **Content value:** Obituaries, tribal council notices, land sale announcements, legal notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** The Five Civilized Tribes were forcibly removed from southeastern states; removal-era emigration rolls document families at the time of removal and are primary genealogical sources; for pre-removal history, extend research into Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, and North Carolina
- **Record types:** Removal rolls, emigration lists, annuity rolls; naturalization records for intermarried whites who sought tribal citizenship
- **Content note:** Examine removal rolls for the full family party — children including infants appear on emigration rolls alongside parents and household members; FamilySearch collection 1987432 covers some of these records

### Tax records
- **Types:** No county property tax existed in Indian Territory before 1907; BIA annuity payment rolls functioned as the equivalent, listing enrolled tribal members receiving federal treaty payments
- **Date range:** Annuity rolls date from various treaty periods, 1830s onward; held at National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/), not fully digitized
- **Substitute value:** Annuity rolls are a critical substitute for census records and document family composition across the period

### Other record types
- **BIA agency records:** Bureau of Indian Affairs maintained agency correspondence, school records, medical records, and Indian census schedules for each tribal agency; held at National Archives Fort Worth — source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records
- **Freedmen records:** After the Civil War, tribal freedmen were enrolled as citizens; the Dawes Rolls include a separate Freedmen schedule that must be searched independently from the blood-quantum rolls
- **School records:** BIA-operated and mission school registers are held at denominational archives and the National Archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (1987432); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (1541872); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (1654321); Tribal Enrollment Cards DGS 002298871 | Tribal rolls, land, church records — the gap left by no civil vital registration | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Federal censuses covering Indian Territory from 1860, including 1860–1900 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Civil War service and pension records for tribal members | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Named cemeteries lacking formal sexton registers | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Tribal newspapers and territorial papers | Subscription |
| National Archives | NARA online catalog and digital records (https://www.archives.gov/) | Dawes Commission records, BIA agency records, tribal court records not digitized on FamilySearch | Free (in-person) / some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 1 digitized volume for Indian Territory (DGS 002298871, Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870, 940 images) — this is the complete result set for that query. Collections search returned 4 indexed FamilySearch collections. Additional undigitized volumes and collections may exist beyond what FamilySearch has indexed for this place and period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives — Southwest Region, Fort Worth, TX | Dawes Commission records, BIA agency records, tribal court records, Freedmen records, annuity rolls | In-person; many items microfilmed at FamilySearch |

## Records NOT online
- BIA annuity payment rolls (many pre-1860)
- Tribal court records (most held at NARA Fort Worth, not fully digitized)
- Removal-era emigration lists (partially at NARA, not fully digitized)
- Many pre-1850 missionary church registers

## Known record losses
- The 1890 U.S. federal census was largely destroyed nationally — this affects Indian Territory coverage for that census year. No tool result identified specific record losses unique to Indian Territory itself.

## Research tips
- Start with the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) even for mid-1800s research — they document living and recently deceased members with stated ages, enabling birth-year calculation back to the 1830s–1850s; indexed at FamilySearch collection 1987432 and Ancestry (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Oklahoma) (1830–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1830 under the Indian Removal Act; Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) relocated from southeastern states via the Trail of Tears (1830s–1840s)
- **Administrative structure:** No single territorial government; each tribe maintained its own nation with capital, laws, and courts
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal oversight through the Bureau of Indian Affairs; Indian Territory operated under tribal governance and federal treaties, not a standard U.S. territorial civil government
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by tools for this period; tribal censuses are the primary enumeration sources
- **Economy:** Agriculture, ranching, subsistence farming; later coal mining post-Civil War; economic records are largely tribal and BIA in origin
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes; intermarried whites who sought tribal citizenship; freedmen enrolled after the Civil War
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears removal (1830s–1840s); Indian Territory Civil War conflict (1861–1865); Dawes Commission allotment (1893–1907); Oklahoma statehood 1907 merging Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory (est. 1890)

## Boundary changes
- Indian Territory (eastern half of present-day Oklahoma) governed the Five Civilized Tribes 1830–1907
- Oklahoma Territory created 1890 from "Unassigned Lands" to the west — county government and limited civil records applied there from 1890; Indian Territory retained tribal governance
- 1907: Both territories merged into the State of Oklahoma; county government replaced tribal authority; records after 1907 follow Oklahoma county organization
- Determine whether the ancestor lived in the Five Civilized Tribes' portion (east) or in regions of later Oklahoma Territory (west) — different record systems apply even for the same period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Indian Territory before Oklahoma statehood (1907); the FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Oklahoma-specific vital records page for this survey, so the statewide registration start date cannot be confirmed from tool results
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s; collection 2134789 "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" applies only to Oklahoma Territory counties from 1890 onward
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal enrollment rolls (documenting names, ages, and family relationships), missionary church registers, and BIA annuity rolls are the primary substitutes throughout this period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries established congregations from the 1820s onward (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Record types:** Registers of converts (baptisms), marriages, burials, school attendance registers, and community membership lists
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321 "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (123,456 records, 61,728 images, indexed + images); original registers also held at the National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/)

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Indian Territory first enumerated in federal censuses from 1860; 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally; 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 are the key federal enumerations for this region
- **Tribal census and enrollment rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 records, 283,945 images, indexed) covers Dawes Rolls (1898–1914), Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852), and BIA-conducted tribal censuses (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Access:** FamilySearch volume DGS 002298871 (Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870, 940 images) is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable — indexed + images

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts — not county courts — held jurisdiction in Indian Territory; records include estate matters, citizenship disputes, land transactions, and guardianships
- **Date range:** Tribal courts functioned from the 1830s through 1906 when the Five Civilized Tribes' courts were dissolved by the Curtis Act
- **Where held:** Tribal court records held at the National Archives Southwest Region, Fort Worth (https://www.archives.gov/); not fully digitized

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory operated under tribal communal land ownership through 1893 — no individual deeds exist as in U.S. states; allotment under the Dawes Commission (1893–1907) created individual land patents
- **Types:** Tribal land records, Dawes Commission allotment files, Oklahoma Territory homestead filings from 1890; FamilySearch collection 1541872 "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (234,567 records, 117,283 images, indexed)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1541872 for the indexed portion; original allotment records at National Archives Fort Worth (https://www.archives.gov/)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Indian Territory Civil War (1861–1865) — both Union and Confederate units recruited from tribal members; Indian Wars; Spanish-American War
- **Record types:** Compiled Military Service Records, pension files, bounty land warrants; tribal member service records are organized separately from standard state records
- **Where held:** National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 indexes many service and pension records (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Tribal burial grounds and mission cemeteries throughout former Indian Territory; many are unrecorded formally or in remote locations
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage of some named cemeteries; physical sexton and mission registers are held with church record collections

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Tribal newspapers including the Cherokee Phoenix (from 1828) and Cherokee Advocate, plus other tribal-language publications
- **Where held:** Some available via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); physical holdings at libraries not confirmed by tool results for this survey
- **Content value:** Obituaries, tribal council notices, land sale announcements, legal notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** The Five Civilized Tribes were forcibly removed from southeastern states; removal-era emigration rolls document families at the time of removal and are primary genealogical sources
- **Record types:** Removal rolls, emigration lists, annuity rolls; naturalization records for intermarried whites who sought tribal citizenship; FamilySearch collection 1987432 covers some of these records

- **Date range:** Annuity rolls date from various treaty periods, 1830s onward; held at National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/), not fully digitized
- **Substitute value:** Annuity rolls are a critical substitute for census records and document family composition across the period

### Other record types
- **BIA agency records:** Bureau of Indian Affairs maintained agency correspondence, school records, medical records, and Indian census schedules for each tribal agency; held at National Archives Fort Worth (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Freedmen records:** After the Civil War, tribal freedmen were enrolled as citizens; the Dawes Rolls include a separate Freedmen schedule that must be searched independently from the blood-quantum rolls
- **School records:** BIA-operated and mission school registers are held at denominational archives and the National Archives

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, Quaker Community Records (ca. 1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Proprietary colony established 1681 by William Penn; became a U.S. state 1787.
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial capital)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colonial period); United States from 1776
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by survey tools for this period.
- **Economy:** Agricultural, mercantile trade, iron manufacture
- **Ethnic composition:** English and Welsh Quakers (founding population concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties); German pietist groups (Mennonite, Moravian, Lutheran, Reformed); Scots-Irish. Quakers constituted a significant share of the colonial population in the southeastern counties per Wikipedia.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Moravian, Catholic
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) — both directly affected Quaker communities through disownment proceedings for members who took up arms.

## Boundary changes
Pennsylvania's outer borders were largely established at founding and remained stable through the late 1700s. County-level creation was ongoing: Philadelphia, Chester, and Bucks were the original three counties (1682); Lancaster (1729), York (1749), Cumberland (1750), and others were carved from them across the period. Records from a newly formed county before its formation date are held by the parent county. Always identify the parent county for records predating any target county's formation.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births or deaths until 1906 (state level). Philadelphia County began county-level vital registration in 1860; Allegheny County in 1870. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records), there was no statewide requirement during the late 1700s.
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** Marriage records were kept at the county level from the colonial period — marriage licenses and bonds at the county courthouse. No civil birth or death registration existed.
- **Where held:** County courthouse. FamilySearch collection 1571957, "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (312,045 records with images), and collection 1502909, "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (198,765 records, index only, no images), both cover the period.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death records exist for this period. The civil marriage record series is the only civil vital source for 1750–1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting records are the essential substitute — they recorded births, marriages, and deaths comprehensively before any civil requirement existed.

### Church records — Quaker meeting records (primary focus)
- **Denominations present:** Society of Friends (Quakers) — dominant in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties through the late 1700s per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania). Other denominations (Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Presbyterian) also maintained registers but are not the focus of this guide.
- **Record types:** Monthly meeting minutes, registers of births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfer between meetings), and disownment proceedings. Marriage certificates were signed by all attendees — an extraordinary witness list. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records), these records directly substitute for civil registration.
- **Where held:**
  - **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, PA:** The largest collection of American Quaker records per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) and Wikipedia. Original custodian of most Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers.
  - **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, Haverford, PA:** Also a primary original repository per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania).
  - **FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 001188322):** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, 145 images. Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image. Access at FamilySearch.org by imageGroupNumber.
  - FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states and is a major finding aid per the FamilySearch Wiki. This is a derivative source; originals are at Swarthmore and Haverford.
- **Gaps:** The specific collection lists at Swarthmore and Haverford were not confirmed by the survey tools; contact those repositories directly to identify available minute books for a specific monthly meeting.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790. For 1750–1789, no federal census existed.
- **Tax records as substitutes:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records), county tax assessment lists and tax duplicates survive from the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties and serve as census substitutes before 1790. The 1693 Chester County tax list is cited as one of the earliest surviving examples.
- **Other enumerations:** This survey did not confirm any state or territorial census for the late 1700s period.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and widely available online. County tax lists vary by county and survival; held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives, with some on FamilySearch microfilm.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships — at the county Register of Wills from the colonial period per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records).
- **Date range:** Colonial period onward.
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills; also at the Pennsylvania State Archives. FamilySearch collection 1999196, "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (3,200,560 images, no name index) covers this period — browse-only, no search capability.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records), land records begin with William Penn's original grants (1681). The Pennsylvania Land Office in Harrisburg holds warrant, survey, and patent records. County deed books begin at the date of each county's formation.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds, mortgages, tax duplicates.
- **Date range:** 1681 onward.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Land Office records, Harrisburg); county courthouse Recorder of Deeds for deed books. Many Quaker families were landowners — land records cross-reference meeting membership and can confirm residence.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Quaker note:** Quakers were largely pacifist and many refused military service; some were disowned by their meetings for taking up arms or for other war-related activities. Disownment records in the monthly meeting minutes document these individuals by name and date — a unique finding tool for identifying Quakers who were active in the conflicts.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov); Pennsylvania state militia records at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov); Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Most monthly meetings maintained their own burying grounds, often adjacent to the meetinghouse. Deaths and burials were recorded in meeting registers — not in separate sexton books as in many other denominations.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) indexes many Pennsylvania Quaker cemeteries, though coverage varies by county and meetinghouse.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are part of the monthly meeting records held at Swarthmore and Haverford.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, founded 1728) and other Philadelphia-area papers published marriage and death notices in the late 1700s.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription) for digital access. The Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold paper and microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, and legal/estate notices may supplement meeting records.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary colonial port of entry.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA for maritime immigration; Quaker certificates of removal for internal and transatlantic migration between meetings. Naturalization records (pre-1906) are scattered across any court of record.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov) for passenger lists; certificates of removal are within the meeting records at Swarthmore and Haverford.
- **Content note:** Certificates of removal are unique to Quaker practice — they certify good standing, name both origin and destination meeting, and give the date of transfer. They function as the Quaker equivalent of a migration record and can precisely document family moves between Pennsylvania meetings or across the Atlantic.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Assessment lists, tax duplicates (personal property and real estate).
- **Date range:** Surviving from the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records).
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Essential census substitute before the 1790 federal enumeration. Tax lists can track household heads through the 1750–1789 gap.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1999196: Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (3,200,560 images, browse-only); Collection 1571957: Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (312,045 records with images); Collection 1502909: Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (198,765 records, index only); Digitized volume 001188322: Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Probate before 1906; county marriages; Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790 federal census (first enumeration) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com) | Quaker burying grounds not covered elsewhere online | Free |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov) | Revolutionary War service/pension records; passenger arrivals at Philadelphia | Free/In-person |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com) | Marriage and death notices in Pennsylvania Gazette and other late-1700s papers | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Pennsylvania, 1750–1800 across all record types (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images). No summary counts were returned by the tool. Additional volumes may exist under county-level place names rather than the state-level search used here — a county-by-county volume search would provide fuller coverage.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest collection of American Quaker monthly meeting records, registers, certificates of removal, disownment files | In-person; contact Swarthmore College library |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Primary repository for Quaker records including Pennsylvania meetings | In-person; contact Haverford College library |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records, militia records, colonial-era county records | In-person / online request |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware, Lancaster and other counties) | Deed books, Register of Wills, marriage licenses | In-person / mail request |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Published abstracts, manuscript collections, newspapers | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Manuscript monthly meeting minutes and registers at Swarthmore and Haverford (beyond the single 145-image Philadelphia Yearly Meeting volume found by this survey)
- Certificates of removal between meetings
- Disownment records in monthly meeting minutes
- County tax assessment lists (most pre-1790)
- Pennsylvania Land Office warrant and survey files at Harrisburg
- County deed books (the browse-only FamilySearch probate collection does not include deeds; deed books require county courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives access)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey reported specific losses of Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore and the Quaker and Special Collections at Haverford College are the authoritative custodians. Contact them directly to confirm survival and availability for a specific monthly meeting.

## Research tips
- Quaker meeting records directly substitute for civil vital registration in the late 1700s — Pennsylvania had no statewide requirement until 1906 (per the FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records). Start with the meeting records before looking for civil records.
- Identify which monthly meeting the family belonged to before searching — that is the record-keeping unit. Chester County, Bucks County, Philadelphia County, and Delaware County had the densest Quaker populations in this period (per the FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- Use William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) as a finding aid and index to meeting records. It is a published abstraction — verify any finding against the original registers at Swarthmore or Haverford.
- The one digitized FamilySearch volume covering this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, imageGroupNumber 001188322) must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
- Tax assessment lists from the 1690s onward are the main census substitute for 1750–1789, before the 1790 federal census. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records), the 1693 Chester County tax list is among the earliest surviving examples; other counties have comparable series.
- Certificates of removal in the meeting records track family moves between meetings — a family that disappears from one monthly meeting likely transferred to another, and the certificate names both origin and destination meetings with the date of transfer.

- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial capital)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colonial period); United States from 1776
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by survey tools for this period.
- **Economy:** Agricultural, mercantile trade, iron manufacture
- **Ethnic composition:** English and Welsh Quakers (founding population concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties); German pietist groups (Mennonite, Moravian, Lutheran, Reformed); Scots-Irish. Quakers constituted a significant share of the colonial population in the southeastern counties per Wikipedia.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Moravian, Catholic
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) — both directly affected Quaker communities through disownment proceedings for members who took up arms.

## Boundary changes
Pennsylvania's outer borders were largely established at founding and remained stable through the late 1700s. County-level creation was ongoing: Philadelphia, Chester, and Bucks were the original three counties (1682); Lancaster (1729), York (1749), Cumberland (1750), and others were carved from them across the period. Records from a newly formed county before its formation date are held by the parent county. Always identify the parent county for records predating any target county's formation.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births or deaths until 1906 (state level). Philadelphia County began county-level vital registration in 1860; Allegheny County in 1870. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records), there was no statewide requirement during the late 1700s.
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** Marriage records were kept at the county level from the colonial period — marriage licenses and bonds at the county courthouse. No civil birth or death registration existed.
- **Where held:** County courthouse. FamilySearch collection 1571957, "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (312,045 records with images), and collection 1502909, "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (198,765 records, index only, no images), both cover the period.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death records exist for this period. The civil marriage record series is the only civil vital source for 1750–1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting records are the essential substitute — they recorded births, marriages, and deaths comprehensively before any civil requirement existed.

### Church records — Quaker meeting records (primary focus)
- **Denominations present:** Society of Friends (Quakers) — dominant in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties through the late 1700s per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania). Other denominations (Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Presbyterian) also maintained registers but are not the focus of this guide.
- **Record types:** Monthly meeting minutes, registers of births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfer between meetings), and disownment proceedings. Marriage certificates were signed by all attendees — an extraordinary witness list. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records), these records directly substitute for civil registration.
- **Where held:**
  - **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, PA:** The largest collection of American Quaker records per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) and Wikipedia. Original custodian of most Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers.
  - **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, Haverford, PA:** Also a primary original repository per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania).
  - **FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 001188322):** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, 145 images. Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image. Access at FamilySearch.org by imageGroupNumber.
  - FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states and is a major finding aid per the FamilySearch Wiki. This is a derivative source; originals are at Swarthmore and Haverford.
- **Gaps:** The specific collection lists at Swarthmore and Haverford were not confirmed by the survey tools; contact those repositories directly to identify available minute books for a specific monthly meeting.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790. For 1750–1789, no federal census existed.
- **Tax records as substitutes:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records), county tax assessment lists and tax duplicates survive from the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties and serve as census substitutes before 1790. The 1693 Chester County tax list is cited as one of the earliest surviving examples.
- **Other enumerations:** This survey did not confirm any state or territorial census for the late 1700s period.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and widely available online. County tax lists vary by county and survival; held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives, with some on FamilySearch microfilm.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships — at the county Register of Wills from the colonial period per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records).
- **Date range:** Colonial period onward.
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills; also at the Pennsylvania State Archives. FamilySearch collection 1999196, "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (3,200,560 images, no name index) covers this period — browse-only, no search capability.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records), land records begin with William Penn's original grants (1681). The Pennsylvania Land Office in Harrisburg holds warrant, survey, and patent records. County deed books begin at the date of each county's formation.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds, mortgages, tax duplicates.
- **Date range:** 1681 onward.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Land Office records, Harrisburg); county courthouse Recorder of Deeds for deed books. Many Quaker families were landowners — land records cross-reference meeting membership and can confirm residence.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Quaker note:** Quakers were largely pacifist and many refused military service; some were disowned by their meetings for taking up arms or for other war-related activities. Disownment records in the monthly meeting minutes document these individuals by name and date — a unique finding tool for identifying Quakers who were active in the conflicts.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov); Pennsylvania state militia records at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov); Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Most monthly meetings maintained their own burying grounds, often adjacent to the meetinghouse. Deaths and burials were recorded in meeting registers — not in separate sexton books as in many other denominations.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) indexes many Pennsylvania Quaker cemeteries, though coverage varies by county and meetinghouse.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are part of the monthly meeting records held at Swarthmore and Haverford.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, founded 1728) and other Philadelphia-area papers published marriage and death notices in the late 1700s.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription) for digital access. The Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold paper and microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, and legal/estate notices may supplement meeting records.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary colonial port of entry.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA for maritime immigration; Quaker certificates of removal for internal and transatlantic migration between meetings. Naturalization records (pre-1906) are scattered across any court of record.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov) for passenger lists; certificates of removal are within the meeting records at Swarthmore and Haverford.
- **Content note:** Certificates of removal are unique to Quaker practice — they certify good standing, name both origin and destination meeting, and give the date of transfer. They function as the Quaker equivalent of a migration record and can precisely document family moves between Pennsylvania meetings or across the Atlantic.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Assessment lists, tax duplicates (personal property and real estate).
- **Date range:** Surviving from the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records).
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Essential census substitute before the 1790 federal enumeration. Tax lists can track household heads through the 1750–1789 gap.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1999196: Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (3,200,560 images, browse-only); Collection 1571957: Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (312,045 records with images); Collection 1502909: Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (198,765 records, index only); Digitized volume 001188322: Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Probate before 1906; county marriages; Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790 federal census (first enumeration) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com) | Quaker burying grounds not covered elsewhere online | Free |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov) | Revolutionary War service/pension records; passenger arrivals at Philadelphia | Free/In-person |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com) | Marriage and death notices in Pennsylvania Gazette and other late-1700s papers | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Pennsylvania, 1750–1800 across all record types (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images). No summary counts were returned by the tool. Additional volumes may exist under county-level place names rather than the state-level search used here — a county-by-county volume search would provide fuller coverage.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest collection of American Quaker monthly meeting records, registers, certificates of removal, disownment files | In-person; contact Swarthmore College library |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Primary repository for Quaker records including Pennsylvania meetings | In-person; contact Haverford College library |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records, militia records, colonial-era county records | In-person / online request |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware, Lancaster and other counties) | Deed books, Register of Wills, marriage licenses | In-person / mail request |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Published abstracts, manuscript collections, newspapers | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Manuscript monthly meeting minutes and registers at Swarthmore and Haverford (beyond the single 145-image Philadelphia Yearly Meeting volume found by this survey)
- Certificates of removal between meetings
- Disownment records in monthly meeting minutes
- County tax assessment lists (most pre-1790)
- Pennsylvania Land Office warrant and survey files at Harrisburg
- County deed books (the browse-only FamilySearch probate collection does not include deeds; deed books require county courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives access)

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey reported specific losses of Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore and the Quaker and Special Collections at Haverford College are the authoritative custodians. Contact them directly to confirm survival and availability for a specific monthly meeting.

## Research tips
- Quaker meeting records directly substitute for civil vital registration in the late 1700s — Pennsylvania had no statewide requirement until 1906 (per the FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records). Start with the meeting records before looking for civil records.
- Identify which monthly meeting the family belonged to before searching — that is the record-keeping unit. Chester County, Bucks County, Philadelphia County, and Delaware County had the densest Quaker populations in this period (per the FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- Use William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) as a finding aid and index to meeting records. It is a published abstraction — verify any finding against the original registers at Swarthmore or Haverford.
- The one digitized FamilySearch volume covering this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, imageGroupNumber 001188322) must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
- Tax assessment lists from the 1690s onward are the main census substitute for 1750–1789, before the 1790 federal census. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records), the 1693 Chester County tax list is among the earliest surviving examples; other counties have comparable series.
- Certificates of removal in the meeting records track family moves between meetings — a family that disappears from one monthly meeting likely transferred to another, and the certificate names both origin and destination meetings with the date of transfer.

Here is the locality guide produced for Pittsburgh in the late 1800s steel era:

---

**Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (c. 1870–1900) — Occupational & Industrial Research Guide**

Pittsburgh during the steel boom was a magnet for Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrant workers. Because **Pennsylvania had no statewide vital registration during this period**, the most effective strategy combines occupational records with ethnic parish registers. Key points:

### Vital Records — Church Registers First
- Pennsylvania did not require statewide birth/death registration in the late 1800s, so **ethnic Catholic parish registers** are the primary substitute.
- Each Pittsburgh parish typically served one national community and kept its own baptism, marriage, and burial books. **Knowing your ancestor's ethnic/national background first** is essential before searching church records.

### Occupational & Industrial Sources
- **Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh)** — holds fragmentary company employment records and steel-industry materials.
- **Rivers of Steel Archives** — additional industrial employer records.
- **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** — state factory inspector reports that can name individual workers.
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh — City Directory Collection** — directories run from the 1810s onward; following a worker year-by-year between census enumerations is a powerful technique during the gap created by the destruction of the 1890 federal census.

### Census Records
- **1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses** are fully indexed on both Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- The **1890 census was largely destroyed** nationally — city directories, tax lists, and church records fill that gap for Pittsburgh families.

### FamilySearch Collections (Confirmed Available)
- **Pennsylvania marriages, 1677–1950** — indexed.
- **Pennsylvania probate records, 1683–1994** — browse-only images.
- **Pennsylvania naturalizations, 1790–1915** — approximately 15% indexed; important for immigrant steel workers.

### Key Repository to Consult
The FamilySearch Wiki's Allegheny County page is the recommended starting point for a full county research guide:
👉 [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy)

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County established 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland Counties; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population figures for this place and period were not returned by tools in this survey.
- **Economy:** Center of the American steel industry; Carnegie's steel empire and numerous other iron and steel firms dominated; glassmaking and coal extraction also major.
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive in-migration of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers throughout the period (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the dominant denomination for immigrant groups), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Presbyterian, and various ethnic-national parishes.
- **Key historical events:** Steel boom 1870s–1900; Homestead Strike 1892; wave immigration from Central and Eastern Europe from the 1880s onward.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County has been stable since 1788; no internal boundary changes affect the 1870–1900 period as returned by tools.
- Pittsburgh annexed surrounding boroughs through this period — records for residents of those boroughs before annexation may be filed under the borough's own name, not Pittsburgh.
- place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions for this place and period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The specific Pennsylvania Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content and no level-specific registration dates could be confirmed. The death certificates collection (1921317) dates from 1906, indicating statewide death registration began after the 1870–1900 target period. County-level marriage registration appears from at least 1885 per collections_search. Birth registration dates by level were not confirmed by any accessible tool result.
- **What exists (online):** Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317): 524,189 records, 1,048,378 persons, 312,045 images — indexed + images. Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957): 312,045 records — indexed + images. Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909): 198,765 records — index only (0 images). Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196): 3,200,560 images — browse-only, not name-indexed. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317) starts after the target period but covers deaths of people who were active workers in the 1870–1900 period.
- **Where held:** Online at FamilySearch; original civil records at the Allegheny County courthouse.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration existed for 1870–1900; church records are the essential substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; city directory entries; probate records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with distinct ethnic parishes for Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian communities), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Presbyterian, Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic ethnic parish registers are often the only documentary source for immigrant vital events in 1870–1900.
- **Where held:** Individual parish archives and diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh); FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church records. The FamilySearch Wiki specifically notes that Catholic parish registers for immigrant communities are often the best source for family data for this period (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- **Gaps:** Coverage varies by parish; not all parishes are online or microfilmed. The specific parish that served a family depends on their ethnicity and neighborhood — the parish affiliation is not confirmed by any tool result in this survey; consult the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives for a complete parish list.
- **Language:** Registers for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian parishes may be in those languages or in Latin.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, 1900 all cover Pittsburgh and Allegheny County; the 1870–1900 censuses list each person's occupation — an especially valuable column for identifying steel workers. Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding the census per the FamilySearch Wiki generic content.
- **State/provincial census:** The FamilySearch Wiki census page returned only generic content; Pennsylvania state census availability was not confirmed by tools in this survey.
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and available online at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, guardianships, inventories — filed at the county level.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1788).
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) on FamilySearch: 3,200,560 images, browse-only (must be browsed image-by-image; not name-indexed). Volume 008120441 covers Probate Records 1683–1994 (1,180 images, browse-only). Originals held at the Allegheny County courthouse.
- **Note on naturalization:** Court records also contain naturalizations. Naturalization volume 008120443 covers 1790–1915 (351 images, 15% name-indexed, English and German); originals are at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was a proprietary/warrant-and-survey state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The specific Pennsylvania Land and Property FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content; the tool confirmed that county courthouses hold deed books.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (Recorder of Deeds); originals not confirmed online by any tool result.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many Pittsburgh-area men served; Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, draft registrations — available at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration; state adjutant general records may be at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny County had numerous denominational and municipal cemeteries serving the steel-era workforce.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online index.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries or their successor organizations.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had multiple daily papers throughout this period.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, which holds an extensive local history collection.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, industrial accident reports, labor dispute coverage — all especially valuable for steel-era families.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Pittsburgh is inland; immigrants arrived principally through the port of New York (Ellis Island opened 1892 for this period) or Baltimore, then traveled inland.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); naturalization petitions at the Allegheny County courthouse and National Archives at Philadelphia.
- **Where held:** Naturalization records before 1906 could be filed in any court of record; Allegheny County courthouse and National Archives at Philadelphia are the primary custodians.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax records.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives; online availability not confirmed by tools in this survey.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can serve as annual census substitutes, especially for years between federal enumerations.

### Other record types — Industrial and occupational sources (specialized for this research context)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary survival; some held at the Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records). Not all companies or time periods are covered.
- **Union membership lists:** Available through surviving labor union archives; query the AFL-CIO archives and Rivers of Steel.
- **City directories:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from the 1810s — these list occupation and address annually and are the most consistent occupational source available between censuses.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Published reports can name workers involved in accidents or labor conditions; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Federal census occupation column:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal census schedules all record each person's occupation — a direct route to identifying steel workers and their mill.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, browse-only); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (15% indexed); County Marriages 1885–1950; Civil Marriages 1677–1950; Death Certificates 1906–1968 | Marriage records; probate; naturalization; post-period deaths | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1870, 1880, 1900 census; occupation column | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Cemetery inscriptions and burial data | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, labor news | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Civil War service, pension files | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Naturalization; passenger lists | Pre-1906 naturalizations; immigration manifests | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a complete set of 3 digitized volumes matching Pennsylvania in this period. FamilySearch collections_search returned 5 substantive Pennsylvania-level collections (a sixth marked as a synthetic test fixture was excluded). These may not represent the full extent of Allegheny County-specific digitized holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse (Pittsburgh) | Deed books, marriage licenses, naturalization records, probate files | In-person / mail |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | Local history collection; city directories from the 1810s; local newspaper archives | In-person |
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Industrial and immigration records; company employment records (fragmentary) | In-person |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area Archives | Company employment records; union records (fragmentary) | Contact institution |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State factory inspector reports; adjutant general military records | In-person / online request |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Pre-1906 naturalization records; federal court records | In-person / NARA request |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers by ethnic community | Contact institution |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1906 birth records (no statewide registration existed; most are in church registers)
- Pre-1906 death records for Allegheny County (church burial registers are the primary source)
- City directories (physical at Carnegie Library; some may be on Ancestry)
- State factory inspector reports
- Company employment records at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel
- Union membership lists
- County property and personal property tax records
- Probate Records collection (1999196) is images-only and must be browsed without a name index

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified the destruction of a specific Allegheny County record set for the 1870–1900 period. The generic FamilySearch Wiki content noted that federal census records are available "with gaps" but did not name a specific loss for this county. Researchers should contact the Allegheny County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives to confirm the survival status of any specific series before concluding a record does not exist.

## Research tips
- **Start with the occupation column in census records.** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal census schedules all record each person's occupation — a direct filter for steel mill workers, puddlers, rollers, and furnace tenders; use that column to identify the mill, then work backward to find the company name.
- **City directories are an annual census substitute.** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds directories from the 1810s — check every year of the 1870–1900 period for a subject to track addresses, employers, and occupational titles between federal enumerations.
- **Identify the ethnic parish before searching church records.** Catholic parishes of this era served specific nationalities; a Slovak family belonged to a Slovak parish, not necessarily the geographically nearest one. Query the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives for a list of ethnic parishes and their founding dates (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- **For immigrant workers, naturalization records are essential biographical sources.** Declarations of intention (first papers) name the country and sometimes the specific town of birth; these were filed in any court of record before 1906 — check Allegheny County courthouse, Common Pleas Court, and the National Archives at Philadelphia.
- **Company records are fragmentary but high-value when they survive.** Contact the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel before concluding a company left no employment records — some payroll ledgers and personnel files do survive in private archive deposits.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, and Pennsylvania returned only generic content during this survey** — the specific guidance pages (Allegheny County Genealogy, Pennsylvania Vital Records, Pennsylvania Church Records) may exist and contain additional searcher advice; visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly to check.
