# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County established 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties; Pittsburgh is the county seat
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by survey tools; Pittsburgh was one of the fastest-growing industrial cities in the United States during this period
- **Economy:** Steel production dominated; Carnegie Steel and other large firms made the Pittsburgh region the center of American iron and steel manufacture; associated industries included coal mining, coke production, glass manufacturing, and railroad operations
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive immigrant labor force — Irish and German populations from earlier decades joined by large Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian communities in the 1880s and 1890s (Wikipedia search result)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal
- **Key historical events:** Industrial expansion after the Civil War drove rapid urbanization across the county; the Homestead Strike of 1892 at Carnegie Steel's Homestead plant is the dominant labor event of the period

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries were stable throughout the 1870–1900 period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Allegheny County maintained county-level birth and death records from 1870, earlier than Pennsylvania's statewide mandate of 1906 (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** County-level births and deaths 1870–1905; statewide death certificates beginning 1906 (FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records, indexed + images, 1906–1968); marriage licenses at the county level from 1885 (FamilySearch collections 1921317, 1571957, 1502909)
- **Where held:** Allegheny County for pre-1906 county records; FamilySearch for digitized marriage records; Pennsylvania State Archives for statewide records from 1906
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth registration before 1906; county-level birth records for 1870–1905 are not confirmed as fully digitized; the death certificate collection (2255317) begins after the 1870–1900 research window
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; city directories; census mortality schedules (1870, 1880); newspaper death and marriage notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (ethnically organized parishes — Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish parishes from the 1840s onward), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Methodist (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Original registers at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives and individual parishes; FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church registers; the Heinz History Center holds some local church materials
- **Gaps:** Not all ethnic Catholic parishes have digitized records for this period; coverage should be confirmed directly at the Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives
- **Language:** German-language registers for German Lutheran and German Reformed congregations; Polish, Slovak, and other Slavic languages for ethnic Catholic parishes

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 all survive and list each resident's occupation; the 1900 census also records each immigrant's year of arrival in the United States (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census); the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed and is not available for Allegheny County
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules accompany the 1870 and 1880 censuses and record deaths in the preceding twelve months
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses are fully indexed and available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships, petitions
- **Date range:** Allegheny County records from 1788 onward
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (physical); FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) has 3,200,560 browse-only images — must be browsed image by image with no name index; digitized volume 008120441 (1,180 images, 1683–1994) is likewise browse-only

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania Land Office in Harrisburg holds warrant, survey, and patent records from 1681; county deed books at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds hold transfers from 1788 (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, warrants, surveys, patents; tax assessment lists
- **Date range:** Allegheny County deed books from 1788; tax lists from the late 18th century
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for Land Office records

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the dominant event of the preceding generation; veterans' pension files are a major genealogical resource for men living in Pittsburgh 1870–1900; Spanish-American War (1898) falls at the end of the target period
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files; draft registrations; state adjutant general records for Pennsylvania volunteers
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal service and pension records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records including Civil War pension files; Pennsylvania State Archives for state-level military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, est. 1844), Homewood Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic cemeteries associated with specific parishes
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers major Allegheny County cemeteries; coverage of smaller ethnic parish cemeteries varies
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for major cemeteries; burial registers in ethnic parish archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (1786–present) and Pittsburgh Dispatch were the leading papers; foreign-language papers (Polish, Slovak, German) served immigrant communities
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized Pittsburgh newspapers; Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds microfilm of local papers; ethnic-press papers may be held at the Heinz History Center
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices, labor news; union meeting notices sometimes named officers and members

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Castle Garden through 1892, Ellis Island from 1892) was the primary arrival point for Eastern European immigrants; Baltimore was secondary
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests; declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization (Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records 1798–1930 are at the National Archives at Philadelphia — source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) and Ancestry for passenger manifests; National Archives at Philadelphia for Allegheny County pre-1906 naturalizations; FamilySearch digitized volume 008120443 (Naturalization Records, 1790–1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed)
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests list every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents; examine the full manifest for all family members when researching an immigrant family

### Tax records
- **Types:** Annual county tax assessment lists (personal property and real estate)
- **Date range:** Assessment lists from Allegheny County formation (1788) onward
- **Where held:** Allegheny County archives and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax lists fill the gap left by the destruction of the 1890 federal census and can establish residence and property holdings year by year

### Occupational and industrial records
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary — some Carnegie Steel and associated company records survive at the Senator John Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives; these are not online and require an in-person visit or inquiry (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Union membership lists:** Some survive at the Heinz History Center and in union archives; the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers had local lodges throughout Allegheny County
- **City directories:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from 1813 onward; every annual directory lists head-of-household names, addresses, and occupations — invaluable for locating workers between censuses (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual reports from 1872; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives; they document workplace conditions but do not list individual workers by name
- **Federal census occupation data:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 schedules list each resident's occupation; for steel workers, entries such as "iron worker," "puddler," "roller," "heater," and "laborer in iron mill" appear

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885–1950 (coll. 1921317, 524,189 records); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (coll. 1571957, 312,045 records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (coll. 1502909, index only); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (coll. 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906–1968 (coll. 2255317, 4.2M indexed records); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (vol. 008120443, 15% indexed) | Marriage records across the period; probate; post-1906 deaths; some naturalizations | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1870, 1880, 1900 censuses fully indexed; mortality schedules | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Major cemetery coverage; fills gap where no death cert exists before 1906 | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, marriage notices, labor news 1870–1900 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Civil War pension files for veterans in Pittsburgh 1870–1900 | Subscription |
| NARA | Federal Records (https://www.archives.gov/) | Immigration manifests; Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalizations 1798–1930 | Free (some digitized) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania state level (the full result set, complete: true). These are broad statewide series; Allegheny County-specific volumes may exist in the FamilySearch Catalog and were not surfaced by this survey — the catalog search was not run.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh | Company employment records; industrial archives; local history; immigration materials | In-person; contact history center |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives | Steel industry company records; mill photographs; labor history | In-person; contact archive for appointment |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania Room | City directories from 1813; local history; newspapers | In-person; some items digitized |
| Allegheny County Register of Wills | Probate records from 1788 | In-person or mail request |
| Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds | Deed books from 1788 | In-person |
| Allegheny County Courthouse (Prothonotary / Common Pleas) | Naturalizations 1798–1930 (originals at NARA Philadelphia), civil court records | In-person |
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Original Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | In-person; contact archives |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records; tax assessments; factory inspector reports; state vital records post-1906 | In-person or online request |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region) | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records 1798–1930; federal records | In-person or online request |

## Records NOT online
- Allegheny County birth and death records 1870–1905 (county-level, pre-statewide registration) — not confirmed as digitized; contact Allegheny County Department of Health and Pennsylvania State Archives
- Company employment records at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel — physical access only; not comprehensively indexed
- Union membership lists — physical archives; access varies
- Pennsylvania factory inspector annual reports — largely physical or microfilm at Pennsylvania State Archives
- Allegheny County tax assessment lists (annual) — physical at county archives and Pennsylvania State Archives
- Original Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh parish registers — in-person at the Diocesan Archives

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed; no tool result identified any Pittsburgh-specific census substitute from that year, but annual city directories and tax lists serve as functional substitutes for the 1880s and 1890s

## Research tips
- For immigrant steel workers, start with the church register of the ethnic parish that served their community — Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized by nationality, so a Slovak family would have been registered at a Slovak parish; original registers are at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records)
- City directories from the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (from 1813) are an overlooked but powerful tool: they appear annually and list occupation and address, letting you track a worker through the 1890 census gap year by year (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)
- The 1880 and 1900 federal census schedules record each person's occupation and birthplace of parents; the 1900 schedule also records the year of immigration, making it particularly valuable for narrowing European origin before searching passenger manifests
- Naturalization records are rich for this period: the declaration of intention and final petition both name birthplace and sometimes the town of origin in Europe; Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records 1798–1930 are now at the National Archives at Philadelphia (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)
- The Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives hold company and labor records for the steel industry that exist nowhere else; plan a visit or inquiry early, as these collections are not uniformly catalogued (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- Because the 1890 census was destroyed, use the 1880 and 1900 censuses to bracket that decade, supplemented by annual city directories and county tax assessment lists to establish residence and occupation in the intervening years

- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by survey tools; Pittsburgh was one of the fastest-growing industrial cities in the United States during this period
- **Economy:** Steel production dominated; Carnegie Steel and other large firms made the Pittsburgh region the center of American iron and steel manufacture; associated industries included coal mining, coke production, glass manufacturing, and railroad operations
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive immigrant labor force — Irish and German populations from earlier decades joined by large Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian communities in the 1880s and 1890s (Wikipedia search result)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal
- **Key historical events:** Industrial expansion after the Civil War drove rapid urbanization across the county; the Homestead Strike of 1892 at Carnegie Steel's Homestead plant is the dominant labor event of the period

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries were stable throughout the 1870–1900 period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Allegheny County maintained county-level birth and death records from 1870, earlier than Pennsylvania's statewide mandate of 1906 (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** County-level births and deaths 1870–1905; statewide death certificates beginning 1906 (FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records, indexed + images, 1906–1968); marriage licenses at the county level from 1885 (FamilySearch collections 1921317, 1571957, 1502909)
- **Where held:** Allegheny County for pre-1906 county records; FamilySearch for digitized marriage records; Pennsylvania State Archives for statewide records from 1906
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth registration before 1906; county-level birth records for 1870–1905 are not confirmed as fully digitized; the death certificate collection (2255317) begins after the 1870–1900 research window
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; city directories; census mortality schedules (1870, 1880); newspaper death and marriage notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (ethnically organized parishes — Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish parishes from the 1840s onward), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Methodist (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Original registers at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives and individual parishes; FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church registers; the Heinz History Center holds some local church materials
- **Gaps:** Not all ethnic Catholic parishes have digitized records for this period; coverage should be confirmed directly at the Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives
- **Language:** German-language registers for German Lutheran and German Reformed congregations; Polish, Slovak, and other Slavic languages for ethnic Catholic parishes

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 all survive and list each resident's occupation; the 1900 census also records each immigrant's year of arrival in the United States (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census); the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed and is not available for Allegheny County
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules accompany the 1870 and 1880 censuses and record deaths in the preceding twelve months
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses are fully indexed and available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships, petitions
- **Date range:** Allegheny County records from 1788 onward
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (physical); FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) has 3,200,560 browse-only images — must be browsed image by image with no name index; digitized volume 008120441 (1,180 images, 1683–1994) is likewise browse-only

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania Land Office in Harrisburg holds warrant, survey, and patent records from 1681; county deed books at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds hold transfers from 1788 (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, warrants, surveys, patents; tax assessment lists
- **Date range:** Allegheny County deed books from 1788; tax lists from the late 18th century
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for Land Office records

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the dominant event of the preceding generation; veterans' pension files are a major genealogical resource for men living in Pittsburgh 1870–1900; Spanish-American War (1898) falls at the end of the target period
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files; draft registrations; state adjutant general records for Pennsylvania volunteers
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal service and pension records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records including Civil War pension files; Pennsylvania State Archives for state-level military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, est. 1844), Homewood Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic cemeteries associated with specific parishes
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers major Allegheny County cemeteries; coverage of smaller ethnic parish cemeteries varies
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for major cemeteries; burial registers in ethnic parish archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (1786–present) and Pittsburgh Dispatch were the leading papers; foreign-language papers (Polish, Slovak, German) served immigrant communities
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized Pittsburgh newspapers; Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds microfilm of local papers; ethnic-press papers may be held at the Heinz History Center
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices, labor news; union meeting notices sometimes named officers and members

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Castle Garden through 1892, Ellis Island from 1892) was the primary arrival point for Eastern European immigrants; Baltimore was secondary
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests; declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization (Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records 1798–1930 are at the National Archives at Philadelphia — source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) and Ancestry for passenger manifests; National Archives at Philadelphia for Allegheny County pre-1906 naturalizations; FamilySearch digitized volume 008120443 (Naturalization Records, 1790–1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed)
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests list every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents; examine the full manifest for all family members when researching an immigrant family

### Tax records
- **Types:** Annual county tax assessment lists (personal property and real estate)
- **Date range:** Assessment lists from Allegheny County formation (1788) onward
- **Where held:** Allegheny County archives and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax lists fill the gap left by the destruction of the 1890 federal census and can establish residence and property holdings year by year

### Occupational and industrial records
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary — some Carnegie Steel and associated company records survive at the Senator John Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives; these are not online and require an in-person visit or inquiry (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Union membership lists:** Some survive at the Heinz History Center and in union archives; the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers had local lodges throughout Allegheny County
- **City directories:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from 1813 onward; every annual directory lists head-of-household names, addresses, and occupations — invaluable for locating workers between censuses (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual reports from 1872; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives; they document workplace conditions but do not list individual workers by name
- **Federal census occupation data:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 schedules list each resident's occupation; for steel workers, entries such as "iron worker," "puddler," "roller," "heater," and "laborer in iron mill" appear

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885–1950 (coll. 1921317, 524,189 records); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (coll. 1571957, 312,045 records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (coll. 1502909, index only); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (coll. 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906–1968 (coll. 2255317, 4.2M indexed records); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (vol. 008120443, 15% indexed) | Marriage records across the period; probate; post-1906 deaths; some naturalizations | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1870, 1880, 1900 censuses fully indexed; mortality schedules | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Major cemetery coverage; fills gap where no death cert exists before 1906 | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, marriage notices, labor news 1870–1900 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Civil War pension files for veterans in Pittsburgh 1870–1900 | Subscription |
| NARA | Federal Records (https://www.archives.gov/) | Immigration manifests; Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalizations 1798–1930 | Free (some digitized) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania state level (the full result set, complete: true). These are broad statewide series; Allegheny County-specific volumes may exist in the FamilySearch Catalog and were not surfaced by this survey — the catalog search was not run.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh | Company employment records; industrial archives; local history; immigration materials | In-person; contact history center |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives | Steel industry company records; mill photographs; labor history | In-person; contact archive for appointment |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania Room | City directories from 1813; local history; newspapers | In-person; some items digitized |
| Allegheny County Register of Wills | Probate records from 1788 | In-person or mail request |
| Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds | Deed books from 1788 | In-person |
| Allegheny County Courthouse (Prothonotary / Common Pleas) | Naturalizations 1798–1930 (originals at NARA Philadelphia), civil court records | In-person |
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Original Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | In-person; contact archives |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records; tax assessments; factory inspector reports; state vital records post-1906 | In-person or online request |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region) | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records 1798–1930; federal records | In-person or online request |

## Records NOT online
- Allegheny County birth and death records 1870–1905 (county-level, pre-statewide registration) — not confirmed as digitized; contact Allegheny County Department of Health and Pennsylvania State Archives
- Company employment records at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel — physical access only; not comprehensively indexed
- Union membership lists — physical archives; access varies
- Pennsylvania factory inspector annual reports — largely physical or microfilm at Pennsylvania State Archives
- Allegheny County tax assessment lists (annual) — physical at county archives and Pennsylvania State Archives
- Original Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh parish registers — in-person at the Diocesan Archives

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed; no tool result identified any Pittsburgh-specific census substitute from that year, but annual city directories and tax lists serve as functional substitutes for the 1880s and 1890s

## Research tips
- For immigrant steel workers, start with the church register of the ethnic parish that served their community — Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized by nationality, so a Slovak family would have been registered at a Slovak parish; original registers are at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records)
- City directories from the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (from 1813) are an overlooked but powerful tool: they appear annually and list occupation and address, letting you track a worker through the 1890 census gap year by year (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)
- The 1880 and 1900 federal census schedules record each person's occupation and birthplace of parents; the 1900 schedule also records the year of immigration, making it particularly valuable for narrowing European origin before searching passenger manifests
- Naturalization records are rich for this period: the declaration of intention and final petition both name birthplace and sometimes the town of origin in Europe; Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records 1798–1930 are now at the National Archives at Philadelphia (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)
- The Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives hold company and labor records for the steel industry that exist nowhere else; plan a visit or inquiry early, as these collections are not uniformly catalogued (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- Because the 1890 census was destroyed, use the 1880 and 1900 censuses to bracket that decade, supplemented by annual city directories and county tax assessment lists to establish residence and occupation in the intervening years

# Pittsburgh, Allegheny County — Late 1800s Steel Boom Locality Guide

*(Guide saved as **loc_001** in your project.)*

---

## Overview

Pittsburgh and Allegheny County were the epicenter of American steel production from roughly 1870–1900. Carnegie and other firms drew massive waves of Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, and German immigrants into the mills, making ethnic community records as important as civil ones.

---

## Critical Limitations to Know Up Front

| Issue | Impact |
|---|---|
| **No Pennsylvania statewide birth/death registration until 1906** | Church registers, newspaper accounts, and city directories substitute for vital records |
| **1890 federal census largely destroyed** | Leaves a gap in the most crowded decade of the boom; 1880 and 1900 are the bookends |
| **Company employment records fragmentary and not digitized** | Coverage varies drastically by employer; much of what survives is unindexed |

---

## Key Repositories

### 1. Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh)
The primary repository for Pittsburgh regional history. Holds surviving company employment records and community collections. Much of this material must be searched on-site — it is not digitized.

### 2. Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area (Homestead)
Focuses specifically on the steel industry and the communities that grew around the mills. Relevant for Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, and surrounding mill towns.

### 3. FamilySearch (Free Online)
- **Pennsylvania probate records** — browse-only or partially indexed volumes
- **Naturalization records** — partial coverage; immigrants in the mills naturalized frequently to qualify for certain jobs
- **Death records** — county and later state-level coverage
- **Marriage records** — county courthouse filings
- Searching most Pennsylvania volumes for this period requires **page-by-page browsing** (not name-indexed)

### 4. Ancestry (Subscription)
- **Federal census 1880 and 1900** — occupation columns are your first industrial source; look for entries like "Puddler," "Roller," "Heater," "Laborer Carnegie," etc.
- Includes some Pittsburgh city directories

### 5. Newspapers.com / Chronicling America
- **Mill accident reports** — injuries and deaths in the mills were heavily reported; a fatality often gives age, nationality, neighborhood, and survivors
- Obituaries in ethnic-language papers (Polish, Slovak, Croatian press in Pittsburgh)

### 6. Find A Grave / BillionGraves
- Burial records fill in death dates absent from vital records before 1906
- Mill-town cemeteries are well represented

---

## Record Types by Priority

### Tier 1 — Start Here
1. **Federal census (1880, 1900)** — occupation column, street address, neighbors (often co-workers or relatives), birthplace and parents' birthplace
2. **City directories** (Pittsburgh, Allegheny City) — annual; show employer and address year by year
3. **Ethnic parish registers** — baptism, marriage, burial; Poles went to St. Stanislaus, Slovaks to St. Gabriel, Croatians to St. Nicholas, Irish to various Catholic parishes

### Tier 2 — Fill Gaps
4. **Naturalization records** — Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas; declarations and petitions name birthplace and sometimes employer
5. **Newspaper mill-accident and strike reports** — Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, Pittsburgh Press, ethnic papers
6. **Probate records** — wills and administration files at Allegheny County Courthouse; list real property, next of kin

### Tier 3 — Specialized / On-Site
7. **Company employment records** at Heinz History Center or Rivers of Steel — when they survive, they give hire date, department, wage, and sometimes address
8. **Union records** — Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers had locals in Pittsburgh; surviving lodge records occasionally name members

---

## Ethnic Community Strategy

Because Pennsylvania vital registration was absent, **the ethnic parish is the de facto civil registry** for immigrant steel workers:

- **Polish** → St. Stanislaus Kostka (Strip District); also St. Adalbert
- **Slovak** → St. Gabriel, St. Joachim, St. Matthew
- **Croatian** → St. Nicholas Croatian Catholic
- **Italian** → St. Peter, Immaculate Heart of Mary
- **Irish/German** → long-established Catholic and Protestant parishes throughout Allegheny County

Many of these registers have been partially microfilmed by FamilySearch and are available to browse; others remain in the parish archives.

---

## Recommended First Steps

1. **Search the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses** for your ancestor by name — note the ward/street, occupation, and neighbors
2. **Check Pittsburgh city directories** for the intervening years to track address and employer changes
3. **Identify the ethnic parish** from the neighborhood and national origin, then browse its baptism/marriage registers
4. If your ancestor was injured or died at work, **search Pittsburgh newspapers** for mill accident reports
5. Contact the **Heinz History Center** directly for any surviving employment records tied to a specific company

---

The natural next step is a research plan for a specific ancestor, starting with the census occupation columns (1880, 1900), then ethnic parish registers, then city directories and the Heinz History Center for employment documentation.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland counties; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city 1816
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Allegheny County, Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by this survey's tools; Pittsburgh grew rapidly as the center of American steel production — Wikipedia identifies it as the leading steel city of the era
- **Economy:** Steel and iron manufacturing dominated; Andrew Carnegie's empire and related firms attracted massive industrial labor; glass and coke also significant
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrants poured into the city and mill towns (Wikipedia)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal
- **Key historical events:** Steel industry boom under Carnegie; Homestead Strike (1892); rapid population growth through immigration

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries were stable throughout 1870–1900
- The city of Allegheny (now Pittsburgh's North Side) was a separate municipality; it was not annexed by Pittsburgh until 1907 — events before 1907 for residents of that city may be recorded under "City of Allegheny," not Pittsburgh

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey and did not state specific start dates. The earliest FamilySearch collection for Pennsylvania death certificates (collection 2255317) begins in 1906, indicating statewide death registration was not in place before that year. County marriage records are available from 1885 (collection 1921317). No statewide birth or death registration exists for 1870–1900.
- **What exists for 1870–1900:** County marriage records indexed in collections 1921317 ("Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950") and 1571957 ("Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950"); compiled marriages 1700–1900 indexed in collection 1502909. No searchable statewide birth or death records for this period.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse for original marriage licenses; FamilySearch at https://www.familysearch.org for the above collections
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth registration and no statewide death registration for 1870–1900
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers are the primary source for births and deaths in this period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with distinct ethnic parishes for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers), German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal — per FamilySearch Wiki search results from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Parish and diocesan archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed Pennsylvania church records generally, but this survey found no confirmed digitized collection specifically for Allegheny County churches beyond the statewide collections listed above
- **Gaps:** Coverage varies by parish; not all ethnic parishes have been microfilmed or indexed
- **Language:** Registers for ethnic parishes (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) may be in those languages or in Latin

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, 1900 are indexed and searchable; the occupation column in all three is a primary tool for identifying steel workers and their trade designations — per FamilySearch Wiki search results from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records
- **1890 census:** Largely destroyed; this is the most significant gap for the steel boom period
- **State census:** This survey did not confirm any Pennsylvania state census series for the late 1800s
- **Mortality schedules:** Generic wiki content returned in this survey noted that mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding the census — these may partially compensate for the absence of death registration
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses are indexed and available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch; 1890 is largely absent

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 ("Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994") covers the full period — 3.2 million images available but 0 records are name-indexed (browse-only)
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 008120441, 1,180 images, covering 1683–1994, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (originals); FamilySearch collection 1999196 for digitized browse images

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is not a rectangular survey state)

This survey covered Pittsburgh and Allegheny County, Pennsylvania during the late 1800s steel boom (1870-1900), when Carnegie and other firms drew enormous waves of Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, and German immigrants into the mills. Here is what the locality-guide found for you:

---

## Tracing Philadelphia Families Affected by the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic

**The core challenge:** Philadelphia had no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793 — that system didn't exist in Pennsylvania until 1906. Research depends on church registers, epidemic-specific sources, and surrounding paper trails.

---

### Most Direct Sources for the Epidemic

**Mathew Carey's Published Account**
The single most useful starting point: Carey's published narrative lists the dead by street. It is available digitized online. Search it first for your specific surnames.

**Citizen Relief Committee Records (Bush Hill Hospital)**
The manuscript minutes of the committee chaired by Mayor Clarkson and Bush Hill hospital patient records are held at:
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**
- **Philadelphia City Archives**

These are physical collections — plan to write or visit.

---

### Church Burial Registers

Church registers are the primary vital records. Key congregations include:
- **Christ Church**
- **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes')**
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (Quaker)**

Most are not name-indexed online. FamilySearch holds one browse-only Quaker meeting volume for 1750–1800 (145 images, no index). The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** has compiled printed indexes to many Philadelphia church registers that can direct you to the right archive.

---

### Census Records as a Before-and-After Check

- **1790 federal census** (three years before the epidemic) and the **1800 census** together serve as a household survival check — look for households that disappear or shrink dramatically between the two.

---

### Probate Records

**Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994** on FamilySearch (3.2 million browse-only images) are likely to show a spike in estate filings in late 1793 and early 1794 as victims' estates were settled. Probate is a productive fallback for families with no other surviving 1793 record.

---

### Critical Geographic Note

In 1793, the *city* of Philadelphia was much smaller than *Philadelphia County*. Residents of **Northern Liberties, Southwark**, and other adjacent townships had records filed under those township names — **always search the full county, not just the city proper.**

---

### Recommended Research Sequence

1. Search Mathew Carey's list of the dead for your surnames.
2. Cross-reference any matches against the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses.
3. Search the **Pennsylvania Probate Records** browse collection on FamilySearch.
4. Write to the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** for Committee minutes and church register microfilm.

For place-specific FamilySearch Wiki guidance: [Philadelphia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy)

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, with focus on the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; City of Philadelphia incorporated 1701
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, the largest city and national capital at the time; the yellow fever epidemic killed approximately 5,000 — roughly one-tenth of the population (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). The place population tool returned no figures for this period.
- **Economy:** Shipping, Atlantic trade, finance, printing, and skilled crafts; the waterfront districts were the epicenter of the 1793 epidemic
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers, German Lutherans and Reformed, Scots-Irish Presbyterians, Swedish Lutherans, Irish Catholics, African Americans (a significant free Black community that organized much of the epidemic's emergency burial and nursing work), and recent European immigrants
- **Religious denominations:** Episcopal/Anglican (Christ Church, St. Peter's, St. Paul's), Quaker (Friends Meeting), Lutheran (Zion and St. Michael's), German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, St. Joseph's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), and the Free African Society (predecessor to Bethel AME)
- **Key historical events:** Yellow fever epidemic August–November 1793, killing ~5,000; thousands fled the city; Philadelphia was then the U.S. capital under the new Constitution

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was established 1682 and was stable throughout 1780–1810
- In 1793 the City of Philadelphia occupied only a portion of the county; Northern Liberties, Southwark, Kensington, and other townships were separate jurisdictions within the county — records for their residents were created under those township names, not the city
- The 1854 Act of Consolidation merged city and townships into one city-county unit; this postdates the target period and does not affect where 1793 records were filed

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed for births, marriages, or deaths in Pennsylvania in 1793. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317) confirms statewide death registration began in 1906. No earlier civil vital registration is confirmed by the sources consulted in this survey.
- **What exists for 1793:** No birth, marriage, or death certificates. Church registers and epidemic-specific published sources (see below) are the only vital sources for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; Mathew Carey's list of the yellow fever dead; Committee of the Citizens minutes; city directories; probate estate files

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's, St. Paul's), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Lutheran (Zion, St. Michael's), German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, St. Joseph's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei), African Methodist Episcopal (Free African Society/Bethel)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and (for some denominations) confirmations and communicant lists
- **Where held:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records); the Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds manuscript registers; FamilySearch has one digitized browse-only volume, Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed page by page)
- **Gaps:** No denomination's burial registers for the epidemic year of 1793 were confirmed as fully name-indexed online in this survey. The epidemic's burial pace (peak deaths exceeding 100 per day in October 1793) may have disrupted normal record-keeping; some burials may be unrecorded.
- **Language:** English for most denominations; German for Lutheran and German Reformed records; Swedish for Gloria Dei

### Epidemic-specific records (1793)
These record types are unique to the yellow fever crisis and have no equivalent in routine years:
- **Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793):** Lists names of the dead by street; widely reprinted; accessible in digitized form at HathiTrust and other online libraries. The single most useful named-dead source for the epidemic. (Cited at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Committee of the Citizens of Philadelphia minutes and reports:** The emergency relief committee chaired by Mayor Matthew Clarkson compiled lists of the sick, dead, and assisted. Manuscript records at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Bush Hill was converted into a fever hospital; patient records document those treated there. Some records at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Free African Society records:** The Free African Society organized much of the emergency burial labor; their records document African American involvement and may name persons who died or were buried.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (pre-epidemic snapshot), 1800, and 1810 censuses cover Philadelphia. A household present in 1790 and absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic losses or flight. No state census for Pennsylvania in this period was confirmed by the tools surveyed.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia city directories from 1785 onward list residents by name and address between census years.
- **Access:** 1790, 1800, and 1810 federal censuses are name-indexed and searchable on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships, petitions — filed with the Philadelphia County Register of Wills
- **Date range:** From Philadelphia County's formation in 1683
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196), 3,200,560 images — browse-only (0 name-indexed records); physical originals at the Philadelphia Register of Wills / Philadelphia City Archives
- **Note:** Probate filings spiked in late 1793 and early 1794 as epidemic victims' estates were administered. A person with no other 1793 record may appear in an estate file from that year.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Proprietary grants under the Penn family; subsequent deeds at the county level. The Pennsylvania Land and Property wiki page was not available during this survey; the specific holding office for 1793 patents was not confirmed.
- **Types:** Deed books (grantee/grantor indexes), mortgages, ground rents (common in Philadelphia), city lot records
- **Date range:** Deed records from the 1680s
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Recorder of Deeds (City Hall). Physical records; extent of online access was not confirmed in this survey.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (ended 1783, pre-period); Quasi-War with France (1798–1800); War of 1812 (post-period)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/). Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military records including pension files.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground (Episcopal), Gloria Dei Churchyard (Swedish Lutheran), St. Peter's Churchyard, Friends (Quaker) burial grounds. During the 1793 epidemic, emergency burial grounds were pressed into service.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcriptions for many Philadelphia cemeteries, including epidemic-related burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at the respective church or cemetery archives; some have been published or microfilmed.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia Gazette, Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser (daily from 1784), Federal Gazette, and others published throughout this period. Papers carried death notices, estate notices, quarantine orders, and the official daily death toll during the epidemic.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project; the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Free Library of Philadelphia hold original runs on microfilm.
- **Content value:** Death notices, estate notices and probate calls, marriage announcements, legal notices, and epidemic reporting

### Immigration and naturalization records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major Atlantic port of entry throughout the 18th century.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; naturalization petitions (filed in any court of record before 1906); declarations of intent
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry holds indexed Philadelphia passenger lists. Philadelphia naturalization records are scattered across the courts of common pleas, district court, and state Supreme Court.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard; check the full manifest for all family members, including infants.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County annual tax assessments; city ward assessments list residents by name and property
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the colonial period
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold assessment ledgers; some are on microfilm at FamilySearch.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists confirm a family's continued presence in a specific ward after the epidemic and fill gaps between census years.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198K records, no images); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Probate; marriage; Quaker minutes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790, 1800, 1810); Philadelphia passenger lists | Census; immigration | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia | Burial records not fully indexed elsewhere | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Philadelphia titles | Death notices; epidemic reporting | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military records including pensions and service files | Revolutionary War pensions for epidemic-era veterans | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including naturalization and passenger lists | Immigration; federal court records | Free catalog — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matched the volume search for Philadelphia 1750–1800 (complete result set, totalResults: 1). Collections search returned 6 statewide Pennsylvania collections; 3 overlap the 1780–1810 target period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Committee of the Citizens minutes; Bush Hill hospital records; church registers; manuscript collections; newspapers on microfilm; city directories | In-person; some digitized via HSP Digital Library |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Municipal records; Register of Wills probate files; deed records; ward tax assessments | In-person; online finding aids |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State-level records for the period | In-person; online finding aids |
| Free Library of Philadelphia | Newspaper runs on microfilm; city directories | In-person; some digitized |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Published indexes to church records; compiled genealogies | In-person; some published volumes in libraries |
| National Archives (Mid-Atlantic region) | Federal court records including naturalizations; passenger lists; military pensions | In-person; request via archives.gov |

## Records NOT online
- Philadelphia church burial registers for most denominations in the 1793 period are not confirmed as name-indexed online in this survey — many are in manuscript at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania or at the churches themselves
- Committee of the Citizens of Philadelphia manuscript minutes — physical at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives
- Bush Hill hospital patient records — physical at HSP
- Philadelphia County deed and mortgage records for 1780–1810 — primarily physical at Philadelphia City Archives
- Annual ward tax assessment lists — primarily physical at Philadelphia City Archives and HSP
- Free African Society records — physical at Bethel AME Church archives and HSP

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey specified the confirmed destruction of a particular Philadelphia record set for 1780–1810. The pace of deaths during the epidemic (up to 100+ per day at the October 1793 peak) may have disrupted normal church record-keeping for some congregations, but no tool result confirms specific register losses. For any surname with no church record in the epidemic year, Mathew Carey's list and the Committee minutes are the recommended substitutes.

## Research tips
- **Start with the epidemic death list.** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) lists names of the dead by street; it is the quickest confirmation that a family member died in the outbreak. Cited in the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793
- **Check probate records within 6–12 months of August 1793.** Epidemic victims' estates were administered in late 1793 and early 1794. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994) holds 3.2M browse-only images; use the county-level index at the Philadelphia City Archives to identify the correct file before browsing images.
- **Search the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses together.** A household present in 1790 and absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic losses or flight. Both are name-indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Identify the family's denomination before searching church records.** Philadelphia had over a dozen active denominations in 1793 with separate registers. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's compiled indexes (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) can direct you to the right register before an archive visit.
- **Consider that many families evacuated.** Those who left during August–November 1793 may appear in Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, or Bucks County records for that period rather than Philadelphia records. Check neighboring county church registers and tax lists for the same window.
- **Use city directories to track movement.** Philadelphia city directories from 1785 onward list residents by name and address in years between census enumerations; a person who disappears from the directory after 1793 may be a victim, an evacuee, or a death not otherwise recorded.

- **Religious denominations:** Episcopal/Anglican (Christ Church, St. Peter's, St. Paul's), Quaker (Friends Meeting), Lutheran (Zion and St. Michael's), German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, St. Joseph's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), and the Free African Society (predecessor to Bethel AME)
- **Key historical events:** Yellow fever epidemic August–November 1793, killing ~5,000; thousands fled the city; Philadelphia was then the U.S. capital under the new Constitution

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was established 1682 and was stable throughout 1780–1810
- In 1793 the City of Philadelphia occupied only a portion of the county; Northern Liberties, Southwark, Kensington, and other townships were separate jurisdictions within the county — records for their residents were created under those township names, not the city
- The 1854 Act of Consolidation merged city and townships into one city-county unit; this postdates the target period and does not affect where 1793 records were filed

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed for births, marriages, or deaths in Pennsylvania in 1793. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317) confirms statewide death registration began in 1906. No earlier civil vital registration is confirmed by the sources consulted in this survey.
- **What exists for 1793:** No birth, marriage, or death certificates. Church registers and epidemic-specific published sources (see below) are the only vital sources for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; Mathew Carey's list of the yellow fever dead; Committee of the Citizens minutes; city directories; probate estate files

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's, St. Paul's), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Lutheran (Zion, St. Michael's), German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, St. Joseph's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei), African Methodist Episcopal (Free African Society/Bethel)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and (for some denominations) confirmations and communicant lists
- **Where held:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records); the Historical Society of Pennsylvania holds manuscript registers; FamilySearch has one digitized browse-only volume, Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed page by page)
- **Gaps:** No denomination's burial registers for the epidemic year of 1793 were confirmed as fully name-indexed online in this survey. The epidemic's burial pace (peak deaths exceeding 100 per day in October 1793) may have disrupted normal record-keeping; some burials may be unrecorded.
- **Language:** English for most denominations; German for Lutheran and German Reformed records; Swedish for Gloria Dei

### Epidemic-specific records (1793)
These record types are unique to the yellow fever crisis and have no equivalent in routine years:
- **Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793):** Lists names of the dead by street; widely reprinted; accessible in digitized form at HathiTrust and other online libraries. The single most useful named-dead source for the epidemic. (Cited at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Committee of the Citizens of Philadelphia minutes and reports:** The emergency relief committee chaired by Mayor Matthew Clarkson compiled lists of the sick, dead, and assisted. Manuscript records at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Bush Hill was converted into a fever hospital; patient records document those treated there. Some records at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Free African Society records:** The Free African Society organized much of the emergency burial labor; their records document African American involvement and may name persons who died or were buried.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (pre-epidemic snapshot), 1800, and 1810 censuses cover Philadelphia. A household present in 1790 and absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic losses or flight. No state census for Pennsylvania in this period was confirmed by the tools surveyed.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia city directories from 1785 onward list residents by name and address between census years.
- **Access:** 1790, 1800, and 1810 federal censuses are name-indexed and searchable on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships, petitions — filed with the Philadelphia County Register of Wills
- **Date range:** From Philadelphia County's formation in 1683
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196), 3,200,560 images — browse-only (0 name-indexed records); physical originals at the Philadelphia Register of Wills / Philadelphia City Archives
- **Note:** Probate filings spiked in late 1793 and early 1794 as epidemic victims' estates were administered. A person with no other 1793 record may appear in an estate file from that year.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Proprietary grants under the Penn family; subsequent deeds at the county level. The Pennsylvania Land and Property wiki page was not available during this survey; the specific holding office for 1793 patents was not confirmed.
- **Types:** Deed books (grantee/grantor indexes), mortgages, ground rents (common in Philadelphia), city lot records
- **Date range:** Deed records from the 1680s
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Recorder of Deeds (City Hall). Physical records; extent of online access was not confirmed in this survey.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (ended 1783, pre-period); Quasi-War with France (1798–1800); War of 1812 (post-period)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/). Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military records including pension files.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground (Episcopal), Gloria Dei Churchyard (Swedish Lutheran), St. Peter's Churchyard, Friends (Quaker) burial grounds. During the 1793 epidemic, emergency burial grounds were pressed into service.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcriptions for many Philadelphia cemeteries, including epidemic-related burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at the respective church or cemetery archives; some have been published or microfilmed.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia Gazette, Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser (daily from 1784), Federal Gazette, and others published throughout this period. Papers carried death notices, estate notices, quarantine orders, and the official daily death toll during the epidemic.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project; the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Free Library of Philadelphia hold original runs on microfilm.
- **Content value:** Death notices, estate notices and probate calls, marriage announcements, legal notices, and epidemic reporting

### Immigration and naturalization records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major Atlantic port of entry throughout the 18th century.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; naturalization petitions (filed in any court of record before 1906); declarations of intent
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry holds indexed Philadelphia passenger lists. Philadelphia naturalization records are scattered across the courts of common pleas, district court, and state Supreme Court.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard; check the full manifest for all family members, including infants.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County annual tax assessments; city ward assessments list residents by name and property
- **Date range:** Tax records survive from the colonial period
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold assessment ledgers; some are on microfilm at FamilySearch.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists confirm a family's continued presence in a specific ward after the epidemic and fill gaps between census years.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K indexed records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198K records, no images); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Probate; marriage; Quaker minutes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790, 1800, 1810); Philadelphia passenger lists | Census; immigration | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia | Burial records not fully indexed elsewhere | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Philadelphia titles | Death notices; epidemic reporting | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military records including pensions and service files | Revolutionary War pensions for epidemic-era veterans | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including naturalization and passenger lists | Immigration; federal court records | Free catalog — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matched the volume search for Philadelphia 1750–1800 (complete result set, totalResults: 1). Collections search returned 6 statewide Pennsylvania collections; 3 overlap the 1780–1810 target period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Committee of the Citizens minutes; Bush Hill hospital records; church registers; manuscript collections; newspapers on microfilm; city directories | In-person; some digitized via HSP Digital Library |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Municipal records; Register of Wills probate files; deed records; ward tax assessments | In-person; online finding aids |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State-level records for the period | In-person; online finding aids |
| Free Library of Philadelphia | Newspaper runs on microfilm; city directories | In-person; some digitized |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Published indexes to church records; compiled genealogies | In-person; some published volumes in libraries |
| National Archives (Mid-Atlantic region) | Federal court records including naturalizations; passenger lists; military pensions | In-person; request via archives.gov |

## Records NOT online
- Philadelphia church burial registers for most denominations in the 1793 period are not confirmed as name-indexed online in this survey — many are in manuscript at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania or at the churches themselves
- Committee of the Citizens of Philadelphia manuscript minutes — physical at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives
- Bush Hill hospital patient records — physical at HSP
- Philadelphia County deed and mortgage records for 1780–1810 — primarily physical at Philadelphia City Archives
- Annual ward tax assessment lists — primarily physical at Philadelphia City Archives and HSP
- Free African Society records — physical at Bethel AME Church archives and HSP

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey specified the confirmed destruction of a particular Philadelphia record set for 1780–1810. The pace of deaths during the epidemic (up to 100+ per day at the October 1793 peak) may have disrupted normal church record-keeping for some congregations, but no tool result confirms specific register losses. For any surname with no church record in the epidemic year, Mathew Carey's list and the Committee minutes are the recommended substitutes.

## Research tips
- **Start with the epidemic death list.** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) lists names of the dead by street; it is the quickest confirmation that a family member died in the outbreak. Cited in the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793
- **Check probate records within 6–12 months of August 1793.** Epidemic victims' estates were administered in late 1793 and early 1794. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994) holds 3.2M browse-only images; use the county-level index at the Philadelphia City Archives to identify the correct file before browsing images.
- **Search the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses together.** A household present in 1790 and absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic losses or flight. Both are name-indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Identify the family's denomination before searching church records.** Philadelphia had over a dozen active denominations in 1793 with separate registers. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's compiled indexes (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) can direct you to the right register before an archive visit.
- **Consider that many families evacuated.** Those who left during August–November 1793 may appear in Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, or Bucks County records for that period rather than Philadelphia records. Check neighboring county church registers and tax lists for the same window.
- **Use city directories to track movement.** Philadelphia city directories from 1785 onward list residents by name and address in years between census enumerations; a person who disappears from the directory after 1793 may be a victim, an evacuee, or a death not otherwise recorded.

Here is the locality guide for Chicago around the 1871 Great Fire:

---

## Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Records for the 1871 Great Fire Era

**The Core Problem: The Courthouse Fire**
The Great Chicago Fire (October 8, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and with it virtually all pre-fire civil records: deeds, probate files, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers. Research strategy for affected families must pivot almost entirely to substitutes.

---

### Pre-Fire Records That Survived

| Record | Why It Survived | Where Found |
|---|---|---|
| **1870 Federal Census** | Originals held in Washington, D.C. | FamilySearch, Ancestry (fully indexed) |
| **City Directories (1840s onward)** | Held off-site | Newberry Library |
| **Insurance Records** | Chicago Title and Trust Company holdings | Chicago History Museum |
| **Newspaper Archives (1871)** | Fire victim lists, missing persons notices | Newberry Library; Newspapers.com; Chronicling America |
| **Surviving Church Registers** | Stored outside the courthouse | FamilySearch (collection 1803978 — ~285,000 church records, 1833–1925) |

---

### Post-Fire Records Built from Scratch

Cook County rebuilt its civil registration after the fire:

- **Birth certificates** from 1871 — ~1.45 million records (FamilySearch, free)
- **Death records** from 1871 — ~980,000 records (FamilySearch, free)
- **Marriage records**, 1871–1920 — ~620,000 records (FamilySearch, free)
- **Reconstructed property records** under the **Burnt Record Act of 1872** — digitized FamilySearch volume covering 1871–1880

---

### Key Repositories

1. **Newberry Library** (Chicago) — city directories, pre-fire newspapers, some church records
2. **Chicago History Museum** — Chicago Title and Trust insurance records; fire-era materials
3. **Archdiocese of Chicago / Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** — Catholic parish records predating the fire
4. **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University** — Cook County records not held elsewhere
5. **FamilySearch.org** — post-fire Cook County vitals and surviving church registers (free)

---

### Research Strategy

> **Important warning:** A negative result in an online database does not mean the record is gone. Many pre-fire records were physically reconstructed but have never been digitized. Always check the Newberry Library, Chicago History Museum, and IRAD before concluding a record does not exist.

**Recommended sequence:**
1. Start with the **1870 federal census** as your pre-fire anchor for the family
2. Search **newspaper archives from 1871** for fire victim lists and missing persons notices
3. Check **post-fire Cook County vital records** (birth, death, marriage) on FamilySearch
4. Consult **city directories** at the Newberry Library for residence and occupation evidence
5. Search **surviving church registers** (FamilySearch collection 1803978)
6. For property ownership, check the **Burnt Record Act reconstructions** (1871–1880 digitized volume)

For the most current guidance, consult the [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy page on the FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy).
